10008.name: Loop/iteration variable declarations: the variable name (and preceding "for", "(int", commas between tuple variables) introduced in for/foreach loops and lambda parameters (e.g. "for i in", "for k, v in", "(x =>", "|n|"). Weak echoes appear on prose phrases like "for each X".

10025.name: Diffuse, weak activation on words that start or carry a contrasting, concessive, or qualifying clause, i.e. a caveat or limitation on what came before. Typical carriers are "but", "even though", "although", "however" and "while". Hedges and negations also fire, such as "can be a challenge", "not going to", "possibly", "mainly" and "I would never say that". Peaks fall on the connective and the following few words, as in "but will not be", "but please keep in mind that" and "even though we remain".

10067.name: Tokens in the middle of multi-token proper names or fixed compound terms, such as institution, organization and person names, chemical or technical terms. The feature fires on interior pieces like connectors (of, on, de, &, -, the), name-continuation subword fragments and middle words, where the earlier tokens predict how the name continues.

10069.name: Delimiter and boundary tokens that close one item or row and begin the next in a structured, repeating sequence: line breaks after affiliation addresses, table/list row separators ("|⏎|", " \\⏎", "), ("), code line endings and indentation, and sentence- or stanza-ending punctuation. Activation is strongest on the row breaks of tables and aligned numeric columns.

10132.name: Expository, formal prose, firing most strongly on the opening sentences that follow a section heading such as "Introduction" or "Abstract" in scientific papers, where the background topic is first being set up. Weaker, scattered activation appears on content words and punctuation throughout other informative or encyclopedic text.

10144.name: Tokens inside bibliographic citations and references, such as years, page numbers, volume numbers, DOI segments, journal names with their punctuation, dates, and legal case names (e.g. 'v.'). Activation is weak and spread across these elements, peaking on page ranges and DOI or date parts.

1015.name: A broad, low-specificity feature that fires on content words in noun phrases, such as proper names, organizations, product and technical terms, and title-like phrases. It is strongest in formulaic or boilerplate text: website menus and buttons, affiliate disclaimers, attributions and bylines, license notes, regulatory listings and technical specs. Function words and running prose are largely ignored.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on short content words, mostly nouns and name or term fragments. It is strongest on formulaic boilerplate, especially website UI and navigation text such as 'Post Your Answer', privacy/cookie policy, 'Press J to jump to the feed', keyboard shortcuts, 'Create Account', 'Popular' and 'user group'. Lower-level hits occur on code identifiers, headings and other key terms.

10284.name: Whitespace and line-break tokens, chiefly newlines that come after spaces or tabs (blank or trailing-whitespace lines). It is strongest on indented empty lines inside code and LaTeX blocks, and weaker on ordinary paragraph breaks after punctuation. Scattered word-fragment tokens get only faint activation.

1032.name: Words or word-pieces starting with the letter "A" (either case), including names, acronyms, and ordinary words. Capitalized onsets and acronyms such as AME, AMZN and A. tend to be strongest, and continuation pieces are weaker.

Words or tokens beginning with the letter "A" (either case), such as names, nouns, code identifiers and fragments like "Am", "Ak", "Agency", "Action". Activation is strongest on the first, A-initial token, with weaker activation on the following subword pieces.

10376.name: The predicate right after a subject or relative pronoun (that/which/who/could/to) that describes how something behaves, performs or functions, e.g. 'scales up well', 'pays out large', 'tend to cook', 'utilize less power', 'deliver'. It is mostly verbs and their short complements expressing a characteristic capability or quality of the subject.

A weak, diffuse feature on predicate words right after a subject, mostly verbs and verb phrases (sometimes adjectives or adverbs) that describe how something functions, performs or behaves. Typical cases are "runs on", "handles", "measures", "outputs", "won't close right", "seem to work properly", "respond to" and "sold for". Activation is strongest on descriptions of a product's or entity's capabilities and performance.

10378.name: A weak, diffuse feature on the head nouns or final subword pieces of noun phrases. These are mostly concrete or technical nouns naming the substance, tool, carrier, medium or location involved in a described action or process. Examples include solvents, water, sand, mosquito, UAVs, vectors, instruments and arms. They often follow prepositions or verbs of means and location such as by, using, through, in, on and with.

Nouns (and occasionally phrases) denoting a carrier, holder, or medium through which something is held, conveyed, or delivered (carrier oil, envelope, backpack, vehicle, funnel, string for beads, setting, lap, rod, tick-borne, delivering a missile). Activations are weak and diffuse, peaking on 'carrier oil'.

10383.name: Fires mainly on numbers, digits and variables inside math, code or numeric contexts (fraction denominators, exponents, decimal digits, LaTeX symbols and closing delimiters). It is strongest on the final token of a numeric or mathematical expression, just before a closing bracket, '$' or punctuation. Weaker, scattered hits land on ordinary words, commas and newlines in prose.

10398.name: Words in the body of a result or conclusion statement, mostly in scientific or technical abstracts. It fires on the claim itself rather than its subject, e.g. "is significantly reduced", "is strongly influenced by", "has better performance", "was achieved in", "outperforms". It is strongest right after reporting verbs such as "show/conclude/suggest that" and on evaluative words like significantly, better, best, consistent with, and achieved.

10446.name: Fires most strongly on "HTML"/"html" and the ".html"/".htm" file extension, plus related markup or format terms like "Markup", ".xml" and "SQL". It fires weakly on other document and text-format words such as "prose", "Contents", "abstract", "summary", "APA" and "paperback".

10480.name: The opening argument or parameter token right after a function or operator name, typically a merged token like "(x", "(n", or "<T" that starts the argument list in math notation (f(x), a(n), P(S)) or code (function parameters, generic type parameters). Subscripts and indices right after a symbol also fire, more weakly.

10495.name: Weak, diffuse activation that is strongest on technical/scientific text, especially methods and results passages of papers. It fires on nouns naming the measured quantity, method or subject (volume, imaging, data, parameters, size), on passive reporting verbs (was measured, were analysed, assessed), and on sentence boundaries that introduce them ('. The', '. Inf').

10521.name: Head nouns (occasionally pronouns or word fragments) that end a noun phrase, typically preceded by a determiner or possessive (the, that, my, his, her) and referring back to an entity already established in context, e.g. "the casino", "the drug", "the former", "my advisor", "his organization". Activations are generally weak and fire on the head word that completes the phrase.

10602.name: A weak, diffuse feature found mostly in health, medical and scientific prose. It peaks in passages about obesity, chronic disease and risk, especially causal or prevalence phrasing such as 'can contribute to', 'reduced risk of chronic diseases', 'puts you at the same significant risk' and 'has increased substantially'. Elsewhere in academic or abstract-like text it fires weakly on function words, punctuation and DOI/citation markers.

10622.name: Structural formatting tokens that open or separate items in a structured list or block: indentation whitespace after opening braces and newlines in code/JSON/struct/dict literals (strongest), commas between fields, leading spaces before bullet/numbered list items, and markup like <thead>, \item, or header labels. Weak scattered activations on filler words in prose.

10628.name: Terms from developmental biology and embryology, especially organismal growth, embryos and tissue or limb or wing patterning, with the strongest response to phrases like 'limb buds', 'patterning' and 'skeletal development'. Weak, scattered activations also appear on other biomedical terms and on unrelated text.

10651.name: Phrases describing how a product or thing is built, composed, tested or certified: technical specs, materials and ingredients ("made from", "composed of", "free from"), technologies used, and quality claims ("upgraded hardware", "undergone thorough testing", "Premium Selected certificate", "scientifically proven"). Activation is strongest in promotional or technical product descriptions.

10671.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on junction tokens between two phrases or list items, especially coordinating conjunctions ('and', 'or', 'but') right after a noun. It also fires faintly on sentence-ending periods, list markers and code statement separators, i.e., points where a new coordinated element or clause is about to begin.

10822.name: A diffuse feature that fires on tokens inside structured, repetitive, non-prose text such as code, HTML/XML tables and tags, LaTeX math, file paths, and spec lists. It is strongest on HTML table markup (td/tr tags, closing brackets and newlines between cells) and on parts of identifiers in code. It seems to respond to tokens whose form is predictable from a repeating template or syntax pattern.

10828.name: Noun-phrase objects of prepositions or verbs, typically an indefinite article plus noun (a team, a solution, a woman, a market), peaking on relative pronouns (that/who/is) that start a clause modifying the noun. Activation builds across the phrase and is strongest on the 'that' or 'who' introducing the modifier.

1087.name: Language about purpose, goals and future benefit: phrases expressing aims, importance, or enabling outcomes ("important to understand", "to improve the", "mission to develop", "paves the way to", "opens up new possibilities for", "can help", "critical to advancing"). Activation is strongest on the purpose 'to' and the following verb in promotional, scientific or mission-statement prose.

10896.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on terms naming measurement or assessment methods, indices, scales and evaluation tools (e.g., drought severity index, assessment tool, numeric scale, quantify, Delphi method, JC-10 assay, OEE) in scientific and technical text. Activation is strongest inside the names of these methods, with only scattered weak hits elsewhere.

1093.name: Diffuse, low-level activation over text with an Indian or South Asian flavor: Indian names and places (Patel, Sundaram, Sankaranarayanan, Satish, Hyderabad, Kautilya, Bhatt, Bollywood films). It fires most strongly on wordy, formal or non-native English phrasing typical of Indian English, such as "are of much significance", "I shall go on with", "paves a way to encourage", "give a lot of information on" and "As of now, the answer is No".

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on ordinary words and phrases in the middle of running clauses, mostly descriptive or instructional prose. It is strongest where natural-language explanation or instructions sit inside noisy, garbled, code-like or machine-generated text (e.g. "is displayed as per the value of", "Following are the sectors where we can add"). Activation is spread over spans of function and content words rather than tied to any specific token.

10933.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires at discourse transition points in expository text. It is strongest at sentence and paragraph boundaries, such as periods, '.\n\n', commas and closing parentheses, and on the words that open the next clause ('The', 'In', 'We also', 'What'). It is especially active in scientific or technical passages that report methods and findings ('characterization of', 'showed', 'we observed', 'measurements reveals', 'tests', 'investigated').

11014.name: Line breaks and other separator punctuation (newlines, periods, pipes, dashes, closing brackets) that end a short metadata field, most often right after a date or number in a header, byline or catalog listing, just before the next field or the main text begins.

Separator tokens (newlines, pipes, slashes, parentheses, periods) that immediately follow a date, year, timestamp or price in document headers and metadata, marking the shift from that metadata to the next field or the main text.

11039.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on words about political power and governance, such as parties, majorities, regimes, administrations, elections, parliaments and rising to or achieving power. The strongest activations are on "majority," "Party" and "elected," with "elected" appearing inside an election passage. Weaker activations land on related notions of control or influence (gaining access, ground or pressure) and occasionally on unrelated tokens.

1106.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires weakly across many tokens in varied contexts (prose, code, citations, headings). It is somewhat denser at the start of documents or sections, such as titles, bylines, headers, SQL/C++ code and citation lists, and on content nouns, proper-name fragments, and year/date pieces (e.g. '201', date commas). It has no clear single semantic meaning.

A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires broadly on unnatural, noisy, or machine-like text rather than on any one concept. Typical contexts are code snippets and markdown fences, numbered or enumerated lists, repetitive or degenerate sequences, garbled token salad, and fragments in non-Latin scripts. Activation is spread across many tokens in these contexts. It peaks on stray tokens, especially the bare space before a digit (e.g., '= 0', 'in 1'), plus odd items like 'python', 'order' in 'in order to', and oddly split words such as 'capt' or 'mitig'.

1111.name: Words about safety, security, protection and risk: secure, safe, security, protect/protective, ensure/sure, threat, danger, risk, insecure, stability, integrity. The strongest activations are on "security", "secure" and "safe".

11110.name: Mostly the equals sign (and sometimes other relational symbols like <) between the two sides of a math equation or assignment. It fires most strongly when an algebraic expression comes before it and a value or expression follows. Weak activations also land on separators or transition points just before an answer or value, such as score hyphens, periods ending a numeric statement, and colons.

1120.name: Tokens at the very start of a document, the first few words of a title, header, or opening line (often split from the first token), plus lead-in material such as dates, versions, and section starts right after a title. Activation is highest on the first tokens and fades over the next few words.

Position-driven feature that fires on the first few tokens of a document or passage, regardless of content: titles, headings, code-block openers (```python, import, \documentclass), opening phrases of a sentence or question. Activation peaks on the first content token or two and fades over the following tokens, with weaker blips at nearby line breaks or punctuation.

11242.name: Mainly the word "south" in its forms (South, southern, southwest, Chinese 南), especially naming regions, often right after "the". Weaker activation on other directional or positional words (lower, bottom, northern) and on "King/Queens/Kings", plus scattered weak, noisy tokens.

11254.name: Short numeric constants, especially small integers, that serve as operands, mostly divisors and moduli (e.g. after %, mod, "divided by", "multiple of", /=, *) in code and math. Weaker activations land on list items or values that complete an expression.

11276.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature on structural boundary tokens in formatted or scraped text: paragraph breaks (often right after a sentence-final period), list and enumeration spacing, separators such as hyphens and slashes, LaTeX \begin, and HTML tag ends. It fires most where the content shifts abruptly to a new, often unrelated segment, such as spliced spam sentences or a change of section.

11314.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on nouns and phrases denoting the outcome, product, or new or modified version of a process, such as "new act", "revised decision", "resulting signal", "obtained products", "generated systems", "proposed deals", "oxide product" and "simulated pressure", and on output variables like "out =". It is often triggered by a preceding modifier like new, resulting, generated, proposed, revised or obtained. Scattered low activations also appear on punctuation and code tokens.

11324.name: Weak, diffuse feature centered on words about naming, expressing, and representing things: language, terms, names, notation, word, syntax, metaphor, verse, symbolism, labeling, citing, "name for", "referred to", "state that in a creative way". It responds mainly to nouns and verbs about the way something is called, phrased, or symbolically conveyed, often in meta-linguistic or definitional contexts.

11402.name: Fires where a just-mentioned term or entity is about to be defined, explained, or glossed: copulas and appositive starters like "is a", ", which is", ", or", ", a", "commonly known as", open parentheses before abbreviations or formulas, and dashes or quotes introducing a definition.

Tokens that start a definition or description of a just-named term, strongest on the copula ('is', 'which is', 'is a', 'an escape in') and on definition openers after a colon or parenthetical (e.g. 'Beech (Fagus) is', 'Threat: A simulated', 'Boolean is a value type'). Weak, scattered activation also appears on delimiters (parentheses, '=', colons, newlines) in code, lists and noisy synthetic text.

11417.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single clear trigger. It mostly fires on tokens that complete a phrase, especially the head noun at the end of a noun phrase or prepositional object, such as "database", "fractures", "goods", "parking lot", "customer base" and "Higher Education". It also fires on the closing parts of set multi-word expressions or names and on some punctuation ending a clause. These tokens tend to be fairly predictable continuations given the preceding context.

11422.name: The head noun or noun phrase that completes a prepositional phrase of setting or scope, most often after "in" (also "at", "of", "for", "from"). It names where, when or in what domain something holds: places (Bermuda, Uganda, your yard, the Pacific), contexts or sections (this section, the field, the modern world), times (that day, Saturday morning) and levels or uses (atomic levels, industrial use).

The final word (usually a noun) completing an adverbial phrase that sets the scope or context of a clause: a place (in the world, on campus, in the village, in Iraq), a time (on Monday, this month, so far, in the past), or a domain/group (academia and industry, her generation). These typically come at the end of a clause, right before punctuation or a continuation.

11487.name: Nouns for professional roles, especially legal representatives who act on someone's behalf. "Lawyer", "lawyers", "counsel", "attorney", "Defense" and "counsellor" activate most strongly. Weaker hits include other advisors and agents (broker, aide, ambassador, coach, doctor, advocate) and related words like "representing" and "advice".

Nouns for professionals who act on behalf of or advise a client, especially lawyers, attorneys and counsel, and also coaches, doctors, agents and providers. Activation is strongest for legal representatives tied to a specific party ("his lawyer", "plaintiff's counsel").

115.name: Author bylines and affiliation blocks, especially at the start of academic papers. It fires on author names, the commas and 'and' between them, superscript affiliation numbers/markers (strongest), institution/department names, and nearby emails, dates and headers. It fires weakly on similar credit or attribution text elsewhere (bylines, 'Author', contact info).

11514.name: Abstract or general head nouns (sometimes verbs) that complete a noun phrase or clause, typically right after a modifier, determiner or preposition. Examples include objectives, solutions, information, trust, forces and community. It fires most strongly on conceptual nouns that finish an idea, often in business, analytical or reflective prose.

11566.name: Induction/copying: fires on a word or subword that repeats one appearing earlier in the same text (names, acronyms, terms, numbers, code strings), usually at the start of the repeated phrase, where it can be predicted by copying the earlier occurrence.

11619.name: References to lists, arrays, sequences and other collections, firing most strongly in code on list-holding variables and operations on them (.split(), list(...), len(x), x[0], sys.argv[1], shape[i], .ToList()). It fires weakly on prose and math words for sequences, series and sets.

11646.name: Names of actors and performers, especially the final token of a surname, in casting or role contexts (e.g., "played by X", "starring", cast lists, "X would be playing"). Other personal names and name fragments activate weakly.

11696.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature in expository technical/academic prose that triggers on ordinary function words, nouns and sentence punctuation rather than any specific token. It is strongest in mathematical or research-abstract language describing proofs, conjectures, relations and validation, e.g. 'conjectured', 'related by', 'empirical validation'.

A diffuse feature of expository, mostly academic or technical prose. It fires weakly on scattered content words, verbs and punctuation at clause boundaries. It peaks on predicate phrases that state a relationship between concepts, such as "are shown to be equivalent", "provides the connecting link", "belongs to" and "Now the" after a math expression. It responds most to the main verb or connective that carries an argument forward.

11733.name: Tokens naming one side of a binary contrast or choice between alternatives, such as male/female, true/false, 1/0, North/South, object/background, heat instead of ice, or one species dominating another. Activation is strongest on the chosen or winning option, e.g. “adopts $1$” and “dominance of M. domesticus”.

11797.name: Newline tokens (single or double) ending a line that has no closing punctuation, such as after list items, headings, titles, code statements, or lines broken mid-sentence, marking a structural line break rather than a sentence end.

1181.name: Tokens inside descriptive or defining phrases that explain what a subject is, usually right after the subject, as in appositives (", a global leader in…"), "X is a…" definitions, parenthetical glosses and "such as" lists. Activation is highest on the article and the connecting prepositions (a, in, of, by, to) of encyclopedic, explanatory text.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires on the content of expository or explanatory clauses: the predicate that defines or describes a term, concept or entity. Typical spans are "X refers to a shared, virtual space", "also known as web harvesting… is the process of", "a trust allows a grantor to transfer" and "which are common in traffic signs". The strongest activations fall in the middle of these definitional or descriptive phrases. Scattered function words in factual prose get only low activation.

11858.name: Words that open a hypothesis or setup in mathematical/technical writing, chiefly "Let" (as in "Let X be…"), plus "Suppose", "Assume", "Consider", "If". They typically come at the start of a sentence or clause and introduce variables or premises. Activation is strongest for "let/suppose" right before a definition.

11879.name: The word "void" in all its senses: emptiness or a gap left by absence ("left a void"), outer space or the abyss, invalidating something ("void the warranty"), and the C/C++/C# return type keyword, which activates most strongly. It also fires on "devoid". Rare weak activations on unrelated tokens are noise.

The word "void" (and "devoid") in every sense: the programming return/parameter type (strongest, especially "(void" and void in parameter lists), legal invalidity ("null and void"), emptiness or gaps ("fill the void"), and "devoid of" meaning lacking.

11938.name: Items inside sequences or lists of repeated or patterned elements, mostly numbers (e.g., comma- or space-separated values, grids, repeated digits, doubling series). It fires on later entries once a pattern is established and grows stronger as the sequence continues and becomes predictable.

Items within a repetitive list or sequence, mostly numbers or short codes (chords, letters, scores, citation numbers, lottery numbers, data values) separated by commas, dashes, slashes or newlines. It fires on elements in the middle or later part of the series, once the repeating pattern is established.

12022.name: Values assigned to layout, spacing, and dimension settings, especially the separator and number in key-value pairs such as CSS 'margin: 0; padding: 0', Tkinter 'padx=1, pady=1', 'labelsize=20' and 'width="100%"'. These fire most strongly. Weak, diffuse activations also appear on measurements and units (mm, ms, dimensions) and on scattered tokens in code, markup and technical text.

1204.name: Fires broadly on nearly every token at the very start of a document: titles, headlines, paper titles and author lines, headers, and the first sentences or code lines that follow. Activation is strongest on the title or headline and fades as the text continues. Very common words like "the" are often skipped.

A dense feature that fires on nearly every token near the start of a document. It appears across many kinds of content: code, headings, lists, math word problems and multilingual snippets. Activation is strongest in short, low-coherence or synthetic-looking text that repeats itself or echoes a title. It seems to track generic 'early, low-context document' text rather than any specific word or meaning.

1222.name: Negation words and constructions (not, n't, no, never, cannot, nobody, neither, without) and the words right after them that complete the negated predicate (e.g. "not necessary to", "never be a", "no reason to see"). Weaker activation on implicitly negative or limiting words such as few, low, avoid, restrictions and without.

Negation: words like "not", "never", "no", "nothing", "without", contractions such as "n't", and the words that follow inside the negated phrase (e.g. "not sure", "never made sense to"). Activation is highest on the negator and weaker on the rest of the phrase.

12244.name: A weak, diffuse feature on technical or procedural prose that explains how a tool, function or method works. It peaks on phrases about mechanism and inputs, such as "uses", "combines information from", "references", "based on", "to specify", "by using placeholders", "constraints" and "criteria". It also fires faintly on scattered tokens in code, config and math snippets.

12255.name: Operators and operands inside mathematical equations, formulas and code expressions: mainly '=', '+', '-', '–' signs, plus nearby numbers, terms and separators (commas, brackets) in equations, matrices and function arguments. Activation is weak and diffuse, peaking on equals signs and arithmetic operators in linear or algebraic equations.

12313.name: Reports of casualties, damage, or other tallied outcomes: counts and quantities (numbers, "000", "dozens", "many, many") of people or things affected, along with death, injury, destruction, and loss words (died, killed, destroyed, injured). Activation is strongest in clauses like "387 people were...", "24 have sadly died", "teen killed". It is weaker for neutral number tallies and occasional stray tokens.

Counts and quantities of people or things affected by events, especially in news reporting: numbers and quantifiers (more than 50, dozens, thousands of, millions, many, some) and the nouns and verbs that go with them. It fires most strongly on casualty statements, e.g. 'six people were killed' or 'killed three people and injured hundreds'.

12335.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on the last token of a phrase, clause or sentence: the final word right before a period, comma, question mark, bracket or line break, or on that closing punctuation or newline token itself. It is strongest on sentence-final nouns (e.g. "temperatures.", "mode.") and on date separators.

12364.name: Text describing negative consequences, harms, or drawbacks, especially causal language linking a cause to a bad outcome (e.g. 'leads to', 'can all cause', 'results in', 'is a barrier to', 'wreaking havoc', 'harmful to', 'difficult to') in critical or cautionary statements.

12384.name: Punctuation or markup that comes right after a heading, title, name, or section label (e.g., "Introduction", a username, a headword) and opens the metadata, label, or content that follows. Typical forms are opening brackets/parentheses, pipes, colons, LaTeX \label, HTML <td> tags, table-of-contents dot leaders with page numbers, and spacing before timestamps.

12415.name: Separator tokens (equals signs, arrows, colons, question marks followed by newlines, line breaks, spaces) that sit right before an answer, result or value is given, e.g. a calculation result, conversion value, the answer after a question, or the next field in a list or table. They mark the point where the following content is expected to be predicted.

12419.name: Weak, diffuse activation on words in clauses that deliver a turn or payoff after an earlier setup. These are typically contrastive or resolving phrases following a premise, such as "but it didn't help much", "but at long last… confirmed", "Well, we can!", "Now… raises another cause for concern", "the result is" and "be in vain". Activation is strongest on "but", "now", hedges like "may" and "might have been", and the key outcome nouns and verbs.

12426.name: Answer selections and option labels, i.e. letters, Roman numerals, numbers or Yes/No given as the chosen answer, especially in answer keys ("1.D 2.C", "Answer: B.", "I, III and V"). It is strongest on letter choices that follow a question number or an "Answer:" label. Weaker activation appears on other enumerated list items and indexed values.

12433.name: Tokens containing the letter sequence "cal"/"kal"/"alc" (or close variants such as "Call", "Kal", "alo", "alm"). The strongest hits are word-initial fragments like "cal" in caliber/calibre, calculus and calibration. Weaker hits include California, calendar, calculation/calculating and name fragments (Kalak, Kalousi, Falciani, chalcogenides).

12570.name: Words that open a hypothesis or setup statement, chiefly mathematical problem/proof language like "Suppose", "Let", "Consider", "Assume", usually at the start of a sentence before variable definitions (strongest for "Suppose"). Weak activations also appear on similar statement- or block-opening tokens such as code declarations (var, auto, public) and HTML <thead>.

12578.name: A diffuse, low-strength feature that mostly fires on highly predictable tokens which complete a fixed phrase, collocation, compound term or split word, such as "top of page", "lingua franca", "state of the art", "par-agon" and "penetration depth". Its strongest activation is on an opening brace in code syntax.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words inside an introductory or conditional clause that sets up the main statement. Typical frames are "If…", "For every…", "so for/from…" and "the higher the…, the more…". The activating word is usually the head noun or key word of that setup phrase, just before the clause resolves, as in "if it were O(n) then…" or "If a player draws any numbered card…".

12585.name: Tokens that open a structured element: field or label names in key–value or spec-sheet layouts (e.g., 'Last Update', 'General details', 'Longitude', 'director'), section headings, and the tag, element, or identifier name right after a delimiter such as '<', '@', '[', or '.' in markup and code (e.g., <item>, <map>, <input>, @NotNull). Activation is strongest on HTML/XML tag names.

12646.name: The definite article "the"/"The", mostly right after a verb or preposition (e.g. "of the", "in the", "request the") and often in formal, legal, academic or instructional prose. It also fires on sentence-initial "The" starting a new paragraph, such as "The following...". There are rare weak hits on non-article tokens.

12671.name: Sentence- and clause-ending punctuation, mostly periods (often with following newlines), placed right after a long descriptive clause or noun phrase finishes a statement. Similar boundary tokens such as commas, closing parentheses, list bullets, and line breaks also fire.

1268.name: Diffuse, low-intensity activation on technical and procedural text that describes how something is done, such as the method, tool, or means used for a task. It is strongest in code comments (e.g. "//Use D3 to retrieve data", "De-allocate any memory here") and in instructional phrases like "how would we write this as", "have to use the HTTP Request node to interact with", "accessed in the same way" and "controlled through a".

Explanatory or instructional prose in technical/coding contexts, especially in assistant-style answers, code comments, and walkthroughs. It fires on phrases that describe how to implement, structure, or fix something ("you might add a call to", "use cmd instead", "here's how you could"), along with nearby section headers and transitions into code blocks.

12824.name: Mainly the subword fragment "oph" inside longer words (biopharmaceutical, nanophotonics, homophonic, fluorophore, Drosophila, cacophony). It also fires weakly on stray spaces and odd whitespace or encoding characters (non-breaking or zero-width spaces, mojibake like "Â", HTML entities, unusual quote marks) and on other mid-word fragments.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens that are fragments of a longer unit whose continuation is unusual or split. It is strongest on a plain space just before a rare Unicode symbol (‡, non-breaking hyphen). It is moderate on mojibake bytes like "â" (from a garbled ’ or ™) and on daggers. It is weak on word-piece prefixes that start a multi-token word (oph, gly, hyper, aster), on zero-width spaces, and on URL or markup fragments.

12855.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single topic. It fires on a token that completes a highly predictable fixed phrase, collocation or word, given the immediately preceding context. Examples include 'Public Domain', 'in press', 'laid off', 'free shipping', 'promoted to partner', 'No. 1', 'IP67', 'arrow-up', 'click OK', 'Rated 6/10' and \in'fty'. Subword pieces finishing a word, such as 'bacteric-idal', 'Havild-ar' and 'mon-oph-yly', also count.

12983.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on incomplete subword fragments, where a word, name, LaTeX command or number is split across tokens and the next piece is highly predictable. Examples include ' Commod'-ities, ' Lau'-ndering, ' Zh'-uge, '\r'-ho, 'til'-de, the middle of katakana or Cyrillic words, and DOI or phone-number chunks. It also fires weakly on whitespace and indentation inside code.

13058.name: A weak, diffuse feature on document-opening boilerplate and metadata, such as titles, headers, datelines, timestamps, page and part numbers, citation and bibliographic fields, and the line breaks separating these header elements from body text.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on formal, official or bureaucratic document language, especially headers and metadata near the start of a text: press or news release labels, legislative titles ("AN ACT TO AMEND TITLE"), booking or arrest records, requests for proposals, filings, bug and issue numbers, datelines and timestamp separators. It also fires weakly on nouns in formal, report-like prose (record, request, submission, document).

13059.name: Tokens that introduce the divisor in a division or modulo operation. Most often this is "by" after divide/divided/divisible, but it also covers equivalents such as "with", "por", "of" (in "multiple of"), and "_by". Symbolic forms fire too: ÷, /, /=, %, mod, the }{ between numerator and denominator in \frac, and the comma before the divisor argument in function calls. Weaker activations appear on other arithmetic operators like "multiply by", minus and "equal to".

13106.name: Document header and metadata text, chiefly bibliographic and publication details at the start of a page: journal volume, issue and number labels, dates, page counts and boilerplate such as 'Skip to content'. Activation is strongest on issue numbers, like the digit after 'No.' or 'Issue number' in a citation.

Bibliographic and publication-metadata tokens, mainly the month, day, year digits and issue numbers in citations of periodicals (e.g., "the Feb. 12, 2018 issue of", "(Nov-Dec 1985)"), plus words like "issue", "edition" and "magazine". Weaker activations land on other header or locator elements such as page and chapter numbers, breadcrumb "Home", and dateline punctuation.

13138.name: Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repeated or templated text. It fires where a phrase, list pattern or format seen earlier in the context recurs, so the next token can be copied from before. Examples include a duplicated headline, "Image Credit: …", "Belgrade … ME - 4918", "Examples of … include" and "end their career". Most hits are punctuation, separators, newlines, spaces or digits within these repeating structures.

13169.name: Fires broadly on formulaic, highly predictable tokens in technical or structured text, mostly code syntax (assignments, brackets, colons, indentation, method calls, loop headers, template tags), plus math notation, URLs, file paths and emails. It also catches the predictable final word of proper names (Institute, Association, City). Activation is strongest inside dense code blocks such as Python loops, class definitions and template conditionals.

13184.name: Tokens tied to time, duration and waiting, such as timers, timeouts, delays, sleep calls, refresh/retry intervals, freezes and pauses, patience, "long enough", and units like minutes or seconds. Activation is strongest for technical timing parameters like timeouts, timers, thread sleep and TTL values.

13203.name: Function words directly after a word that sets up a question, task, or quantity, most strongly "of" following "probability/probabilities" (and similar heads like "possibility", "complexity", "number", "example"). Weaker hits fall on the next word after imperative or question openers in exam and problem text ("Find the", "Calculate", "What is", "determine whether"), where the token anticipates the object being asked about.

1321.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on the substantive, topic-carrying content of a passage: domain-specific nouns, noun phrases and their predicates (e.g., technical, medical, scientific, product or subject-matter terms such as 'deployment', 'vessel structures', 'psychosis', 'coursework', 'corrosive chemicals'). It spans whole clauses describing what is being done or discussed, peaking on key subject nouns and staying weak on generic framing words.

A broad, low-specificity feature that fires across spans of substantive content rather than on any particular word. It covers noun phrases and clauses that follow a verb or preposition, code statements and identifiers, and math expressions. Activation is strongest on the key content nouns of descriptive or definitional phrases (e.g. 'movie tickets', 'business partner's failure', 'education system's financial practices'). Connecting function words and boilerplate are mostly skipped.

1323.name: Sentence and clause boundaries: mostly the period that ends a sentence (plus closing parens, line breaks), and sometimes the conjunction or first word that opens the next clause ("But", "In", "and", "So"). Activation is strongest on the period right after a complete statement, just before a new sentence starts.

Clause and sentence boundaries. It fires mostly on the period (or comma, dash, or newline) that ends a full clause, especially a general statement, and sometimes on the first words of the next sentence ("We", "But", "It", "In").

13278.name: Structural markers in log or machine-generated text, strongest on log-level prefixes and their delimiters (e.g. "DEBUG (MainThread) [", "INFO|", "[INFO]") right after timestamps. Weak activations land on formatting and separator tokens in code, markup, lists and metadata, such as pipes, brackets, @, list bullets, chat-nick prefixes and newlines before headers.

13388.name: Language about hitting, shooting, or scoring against a target, plus related success measures. The strongest cases are sports performance and stats, such as batting averages, home runs, balls faced, boundaries, shot charts, landed punch combinations and scoring goals. Weaker cases cover accuracy, hitting a jackpot, missing, success rates and percentages.

Words about attempts, shooting, hitting and scoring accuracy, mostly in sports: shots, field goals, free throws, swings, hits, doubles, shooting percentages (FG%/FT%), and related success-rate stats. Weaker activations occur on general words about aiming, attempts, effectiveness or hitting a target.

13421.name: Words for streets and other named places, strongest on "street/Street/streets" and on the type word that ends a street name in an address (Avenue, Road, Close, strasse, Plaza). Weaker on other location words such as Hill, River, village, neighborhood and intersection.

13427.name: The word "method(s)"/"methodology" and other research-paper section headings (Materials and Methods, Experimental Procedures, Introduction, Results, Related Work, References), strongest on "Methods" headers in scientific abstracts and papers.

13431.name: Fires most strongly on color specifications, especially RGBA tuples like (0,0,0,1), alpha channel/alpha value mentions, ARGB/RGB formats, and Color3f. Weaker, diffuse activation appears on delimiters and parameter tokens in technical, code and scientific notation, such as commas in argument lists, separators and units.

13451.name: Opening or separator tokens that come just before a value. Most often this is a space, '(', '=', ',' or '_{' placed directly before a number or function argument in math, code or word problems, as in 'after 5 years', 'f(1)' or 'x_0 = 0.2'. It also fires on the '<tr' that opens the first header row after '<table><thead>' in HTML tables.

13483.name: Words naming or describing statistical and empirical findings in scientific or analytical writing, such as reports of significance, effects, changes, trends, evidence and test results. It peaks on "significant"/"significantly" and p‑values after phrases like "showed", "were" or "found".

Words that express measured or evaluated magnitude, comparison, or outcome, especially statistical or quantitative judgments ("significant", "significantly", "statistically", "evidence of", "expectations", "exceeds", "over budget", "double-digit", "greater than", "disparity"). Activation is strongest for "significant" in a statistical sense.

13598.name: Fires on the modifier or first part of a multi-word compound term or technical noun phrase (e.g., 'chemical' warfare, 'surgical' intervention, 'student' housing, 'volumetric' efficiency, 'image' search), i.e., the adjective, noun, or word-piece that anticipates a specific head noun to follow, mostly in technical or expository text.

1362.name: Tokens inside conventional, formulaic multi-word phrases and collocations (e.g. “have to do with”, “a long way to go”, “shadow of its former glory”, “years of experience”, “rather than”, “means that”, “contrary to what one might expect”). Activation is strongest on the predictable continuation words that complete a stock expression. Many of the marked tokens are the function words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries) that glue these phrases together, rather than any particular content word.

Diffuse, low-intensity activations on common function words and generic connective phrases in fluent prose, such as prepositions, auxiliaries, determiners, and discourse markers like "also", "for example", "that suits", "not necessarily", "ensure", and "the ability to". The strongest hits are mid-sentence phrase heads that predict a common continuation; there is no clear topical content.

13632.name: Words referring to family and domestic life, mainly offspring and dependents (children, kids, sons, daughters, baby boy, family, offspring), often after possessives like "my" or "their". It also fires more weakly on related ideas such as home, marriage, loved ones, relationships and upbringing.

1364.name: Fires most strongly on non-English and non-Latin-script text split into subword pieces (Chinese, Arabic, Persian, Cyrillic, Vietnamese), and weakly on accented letters in European languages. It also responds faintly to unusual or rare tokens such as emoji, mojibake, long runs of table-of-contents dots, HTML table tags, LaTeX fragments and odd word fragments.

Non-English and non-Latin script tokens (especially Chinese characters, also Cyrillic, Japanese, Arabic, Amharic, odd Unicode) that show up in mostly English or code text, frequently as garbled or code-switched fragments. Activation peaks on the first character of a Chinese word. Weak firing also occurs on stray symbols, emoji and markdown separators.

1365.name: Forms of the copula "to be" (is, are, was, be, Chinese 是) right after the subject noun phrase, introducing the predicate or a definition. Adverbs directly following the verb (not, only, generally, just) are weakly included.

1380.name: Short single-letter (or very short) symbols used as variable, function, or label names, especially math variables (f, g, b, t, D, rho, Delta), loop indices (i, j), type parameters, and list/section labels (D), IV, (e)). Strongest when a new variable or function is being introduced or defined.

13809.name: A weak, diffuse feature on low-content connective tokens inside running phrases, such as commas, “and/or”, “of/the/a/in”, hyphens, slashes, spaces before numbers, and mid-word subword fragments of rare names. It is strongest within lists, addresses, place names, citations and numeric specifications, at points where the next token continues an ongoing list item or multi-token entity.

13835.name: The token right after the opening word of a line, tag or label. It fires most strongly on HTML/shortcode attribute names that follow a tag name, such as type, id, src and http in <input type=, <button id=, <iframe src=, <meta http- and [slideshow_deploy id=. It fires weakly on the word after a leading header or label word, as in Posted March, Study Section and Import P, or after a command name, as in dig + and serverless logs.

Mostly weak, diffuse activations on the token right after a tag, label or heading word. The strongest cases are attribute names that directly follow a markup or shortcode tag name, such as id, url, name, alt and href in [caption id=,

13842.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on words in phrases about deliberate intervention, meaning an agent actively manipulating, controlling or acting on something. The strongest cases are "manually control … position" and "medical intervention allows women to". Similar phrases include "cut the cord", "addition of", "overexpression of", "directly admonish", "take charge" and "government policies … supporting". Most other activations are low and scattered across unrelated technical or descriptive words.

13848.name: Weak, diffuse activations, mostly on subword pieces inside multi-token proper names, acronyms or technical terms. These are usually the first or middle fragment, as in "Gro|ys|man", "Craw|ley", "Cad|ie" and "T|GB". It tends to fire when the name or term was already seen earlier in the context, so the rest of the word can be predicted by copying. It also fires occasionally on ordinary nouns that refer back to an entity already mentioned.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on the head or first subword token of a specific referent. These are usually proper names of people, products, places or organizations (e.g., the first piece of a multi-token surname or brand), often an entity already mentioned or being referred back to. It also fires on a few ordinary nouns naming a specific object or entity.

1385.name: A diffuse, weakly activating pattern centered on the final content token of a short phrase, title, question, or argument, typically just before a boundary such as a question mark, closing quote or parenthesis, comma, or line break. It is strongest in templated, SEO-style query headings, for example "Convert Decimal 0.01 to Percent", "rooms in the Bellagio?" and "on a computer?". Weaker activations land on phrase-ending nouns, date and number fields, and function-call arguments.

1387.name: Words and name fragments beginning with the letter "h" (e.g. hence, health, hard, hydro, Hong, Hart, hospital). Activation lands on the h-initial token, usually at the start of a word, and sometimes continues weakly onto the following subword pieces.

Fires on tokens that begin with the letter "h"/"H" (e.g. hex, hooves, hours, high, headers, heights, Hidden, HMM, Here, His, Hyper-, .h), strongest on bare or capitalized H and short h-initial fragments, often in noisy code or garbled text.

13899.name: A diffuse, weak feature that peaks in historical or war-time narratives about people fleeing, being evacuated, hiding or being mobilized. Examples include escaping Hungary as tanks rolled in, the Soviet government leaving Moscow, raising a regiment in WWI, and children hidden in a safe room. It fires across the clause describing the people and their movement or refuge, such as subject pronouns, verbs like escaped, evacuated, fleeing and tasked, and destinations. Elsewhere it shows only sparse low activation on ordinary function words.

1399.name: Pieces of identifiers and names, strongest in code. It fires on the later sub-tokens of compound identifiers (CamelCase or snake_case function, class and method names), especially names about to be called or defined, i.e. just before an opening parenthesis or argument list. Weaker activations land on word fragments inside URLs, email addresses, domain names and technical terms.

14030.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single clear concept. It fires on content tokens that complete a predictable phrase or parallel structure, such as "rural compared with urban", "lost or stolen", "warm or cool" and "25 years in about 25 weeks". It also fires on the first piece of a proper noun or multi-token word (Kenyan, Makati, Bland-Altman, unbeatable). The strongest activation is on Wikipedia-style citation brackets such as "[4]".

A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single topic. It fires on a word or subword inside a familiar multi-token unit, usually a noun or the start of a name, at a point where the continuation is highly predictable. Examples include fixed names and collocations ("US Food [and Drug]", "Edgar Allan [Poe]", "bed [and breakfast]", "Gust[avo]"), set phrases ("For example", "future generations", "warm and friendly", "Located in", "Dear"), and structured strings ("java[.lang]", "Twitter @", "GIVEAW[AY]").

14039.name: Operators and connective symbols inside mathematical formulas, LaTeX, or code expressions, especially binary operators such as +, -, * and >= (strongest when they join operands inside parentheses), along with LaTeX commands, subscripts and method-chain tokens. Weaker activations appear on similar joining tokens in plain text, such as spaces, hyphens and 'to'/'No' between numbers or names.

14061.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens that begin or continue a proper name, identifier, title or technical term, often one that repeats or is predictable from earlier context. Typical cases are code identifiers (Game, Forum, _remove), product or event names, math variables and subscripts, and numbered references (Part, page, 205). It fires mostly right after a preposition, article or assignment that introduces the name.

14080.name: Names and nouns for political or geopolitical entities, such as empires, dynasties, republics, territories, provinces, colonies, regions and countries. These are often adjectives like "Imperial" or "colonial" or nouns like "territory", "province" or "republic" in historical or governmental contexts. The strongest activation is on colonial/territorial concepts. Activation is weak and noisy on other proper-noun fragments.

14095.name: Completion tokens of multi-token names and specialized terms: the later subword or second word of proper nouns, acronyms and compound phrases (e.g. Go-Da|igo, Pal|ma, El Ni|ño, deep vein throm|bus, CGI|AR). Activation is strongest when the term is predictable, often because it already appeared earlier in the context.

Tokens that complete a named entity or a multi-token term, typically the final subword of a proper noun (person, place, brand, organization, or acronym), e.g. the end of a surname, place name, or company name that was split into pieces. These tokens are largely predictable from the preceding fragment. Activation is strongest on rare foreign or political names.

14184.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature that fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens in factual, expository or narrative prose, mainly function words, verbs and nouns that carry a statement forward. It is strongest on reporting and predicate phrases that relay facts or claims, such as "says that", "claims that", "was included in", "has risen to" and "until". It is not tied to any specific word or topic.

14211.name: A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires in technical, scientific or technology writing, especially about engineered materials, devices and methods such as nanostructures, polymers, porous carriers, sensors, assays and therapies. It lands on the content nouns of these passages (materials, devices, approaches) and on the connective words that follow them when describing function or purpose ("that", "to overcome", "to reduce", "and", "itself").

14263.name: A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on connectors and separators inside lists, series, or parallel structures, where the next item continues a predictable pattern. Typical tokens are commas, "and", "or even", "to", and "|" between items. It also fires on the repeated elements of enumerations, such as fourth/fifth/sixth, Office 2003/2007, stage 7/8, Oa/Ob/Oc, and indexed math terms like i_1, i_2 or \mathbf i, j, k.

1432.name: A broad, low-intensity feature in informational, press-release-style prose about named organizations, companies, institutions and products. It fires on the words immediately following such names, especially the remainder of a multi-token name ("-Benz E-Class", "Labs, China"). It also fires on the descriptive clauses that state what the entity is, does or offers ("is responsible for the administration of", "have successfully developed and deployed", "is gathering the best"). Peaks fall on sentence boundaries and transitions (periods, line breaks, commas) within these entity-centered descriptions.

A diffuse, weak feature of formal expository or promotional prose, typical of AI-assistant or marketing writing. It fires on function words and structural tokens in definitional or descriptive passages ("X is a … that …", "Here's how…", "We design our services…"). It also fires on transitions such as line breaks, bullets, list numbers and header endings that introduce an explanation or definition. It is strongest at the start of a new descriptive sentence after a list or heading.

14348.name: Tokens at points of textual discontinuity or formatting artifacts: line breaks that separate unrelated segments of scraped web text (titles, navigation, headers giving way to new content) and words split mid-word by hyphenation, line wrapping, or bad tokenization (e.g. 'profes-⏎sional', 'commentar y', 'Intermedi ate'). Mid-word breaks activate most strongly.

14433.name: Comparative and superlative constructions: comparative adjectives/adverbs ("-er" forms, "more", "less", "better", "larger", "easier") and intensifiers like "much" or "even" preceding them, plus words expressing a degree of change or improvement (e.g., "improve", "enough", "as ... as"). Activation peaks on the comparative word itself and sometimes spreads to the word it modifies.

14453.name: Weak, diffuse activation on nouns and names (people, companies, organizations, groups, countries) that serve as the agent, subject or referent of a clause, typically an entity performing or receiving an action, often appearing just before a verb or a possessive 's. The strongest cases are named people and movements (e.g. a surname followed by 'claimed', 'Black Lives Matter').

14462.name: Tokens tied to TV shows, films and other screen entertainment, peaking on words like series/show/TV shows, show titles (Downton Abbey, Profiler, Maid In India, Homecoming, telenovela) and the descriptive phrases that introduce them ("is a comedy web series where", "is a 1988 film that"). Weak, scattered activations occur elsewhere.

14483.name: Primarily fires on code expressions that reference variables and data structures, especially array/dictionary indexing and subscripts (e.g. data['key'][, chart[me][, cout << array, (input), plus assignment and return statements. Weaker analogous activation appears on symbolic variables and subscripts in math. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are faint and scattered.

14488.name: Mostly physics, chemistry and other technical terms, with "electron" firing most strongly (also electron density, spin, photon, quarks, charge, bonding, DFT). Weak activations land on word-piece fragments in scientific or technical contexts, such as the inner parts of words, acronyms and names.

14511.name: Relative pronouns (mostly "that", also "which", "what", French "qui") that start a relative clause right after the noun they modify.

14516.name: Phrases in news-style sports recaps describing athletes’ or teams’ performance and results. The strongest cases are box-score statistics and outcomes such as “led a balanced attack with a game-high 14 points,” “scored nine runs in the fifth inning” and “winless in two matches.” Much weaker activation appears on similar report-style quantity or condition words in weather and nutrition text, such as clouds, rains and carbs.

1453.name: Mostly word-internal subword fragments containing the short vowel 'i' (ib, imb, idip, ilit, isc, ique, ik, iox, ig, piez, mish, ric, sic, Vir/ilio), typically inside rare names, foreign words and technical terms that get split into several tokens. The fragment is usually the first or a middle piece of an unfamiliar word. Weaker hits fall on ordinary words and code identifiers with an 'i' (Pick, bit, PID, ZIP, kill, dip).

Tokens containing the vowel 'i' (or its equivalent in other scripts, e.g. Cyrillic 'и' or Persian 'ی'), most often short subword fragments in the middle of rare words, names, code identifiers or foreign text (e.g. 'ich', 'iss', 'ir', 'id', 'ik', 'is'). Activation is strongest on fragmentary i-syllables and weaker on whole common words that merely contain an 'i'.

14559.name: Fires most strongly on the Dutch surname particle "van"/"Van" (as in Van Halen, van de Flierdt). Weaker activations appear on look-alike name or subword fragments that contain "v" or "an"/"am" sounds, such as ivan, Evan, anders, Camp, wander, Vill, VW, visc and vagr. These are often parts of proper names.

1457.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires on salient content noun phrases and named entities (people, places, companies, products, technical terms) in running prose. Proper names that act as a clause subject activate most strongly (Cicero, Ghent, Ukrainian, Apple, President). Activation sometimes spills onto the following verb phrase, relative clause ("who", "which") or trailing punctuation and newlines.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on content tokens such as nouns, noun phrases, numbers and code identifiers, especially items in lists or repeated structured patterns (number sequences, typedefs, key/value lines, 'coffee, tea, soft…'). It often appears in rambling, garbled or low-coherence text rather than marking any specific meaning.

14580.name: Runs of whitespace (spaces, tabs, blank lines) and filler characters such as dot leaders or dashed lines used for indentation, alignment, or layout, mostly in code, ASCII diagrams, tables, and tables of contents. The strongest activations are on spacing that aligns columns or tree diagrams. Weak, scattered activations also appear on stray separators and symbols.

14584.name: Weak activations on structural boundary tokens, mostly newlines (often fused with a preceding period, question mark or tag close) that end a sentence, heading or list item just before a new segment starts. It also fires on related layout markers such as bullets, list numbers, indentation spaces, and HTML table tags. A few stray hits fall on garbled or ungrammatical text.

14603.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural and boilerplate tokens in scraped web text, such as metadata separators (|, :, —, •), URL and domain fragments, page labels (Posts, Info, Results, "Failed" to load), and query-string parameters. It is strongest on attribute syntax inside HTML tags and shortcodes, like class="prettyprint lang" and id=. Occasional activations on ordinary prose words are low and uninformative.

A weak, diffuse feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on tokens in formulaic, boilerplate or structured text (feed and page metadata, field labels and colons, recipe and manual phrasing) where the next token is highly predictable. Examples include word fragments mid-completion ("Sh"→ourly, "vac"→uums, "traff"→icked) and labels or colons just before a value.

14636.name: Comment-start markers in source code (//, #, ///, ##), particularly inline or line-leading comments that introduce a natural-language explanation of the following code. There is weaker activation on similar transitions from code or formatting into explanatory prose (e.g., "Now", "We" after headings).

14638.name: Words about crowds and mass public gatherings, especially protests and demonstrations: rallies, protesters gathering, petitions, protest votes, days of action, parades, celebrations, applause and cheering crowds, plus collective nouns such as multitude, groups and armada. The strongest responses are on explicit protest or demonstration terms, with weak scattered firing on surrounding context words.

14698.name: Binary operator tokens in math and code, mainly exponent operators (^, **, )^, ^{, ).^) placed just before a power such as 2. Weaker hits on other operators and casts (as, >=, -, /, <<) and on a few stray punctuation and whitespace tokens.

Exponentiation operators ("^", "^{", "**", ")^", Math.pow's comma) placed between a base and its exponent in math/code, especially polynomial terms like x^3. Weaker hits land on other binary operators (%, >=, >>) and on list-separating commas.

Exponentiation operators: the caret (^, ^{, ^\) or ** that raises a base to a power, especially right before an exponent like 2 or 3 in math, LaTeX or code. It also fires weakly on other operators and separators (/, ::, -, commas, periods, spaces).

14708.name: The second item in a paired or binary construction, usually the token right after "and"/"or" in phrases like "between X and Y" or "both X and Y" (e.g., young and old, transmitting and reflecting, crop and animal). Activation is strongest on the final word of that second conjunct, especially when it completes a contrast or relationship between two entities.

14724.name: The first piece of a compound noun or multi-token word, i.e. a modifier or word fragment whose meaning depends on what follows (scale→ups, rain→forests, coast→ers, transcription→factors, wind→farms, best→practices). It is often a noun used attributively in technical or domain-specific terms. Activation is generally weak.

1483.name: Fires on the final subword pieces that complete a word split across several tokens (e.g. bellig-erents, Repet-ition, non-perturb-ative, Crockp-ots), often spilling onto the next one or two tokens of the same noun phrase or name. It shows up mostly in technical terms, proper names, acronyms and version or code strings, and peaks on the token where the multi-token word is resolved.

A diffuse, weak feature. It fires most strongly on subword pieces that finish a word split across several tokens, such as "ude" in Jean-Claude, "ers" in man-agers, "ship", "eness", "ical" and the Cyrillic and Korean endings. It also often fires on the next one or two tokens that continue the phrase. This is common in noisy, garbled, code, multilingual or repetitive text, and it is not tied to any clear meaning.

14858.name: Titles, offices and role nouns for people (President, Minister, Prime Minister, CEO, director, chief, Gov., Queen, coach), typically right before a person's name. Activation is strongest for political leadership titles such as President, Prime Minister and Gov.

Titles of positions, offices and ranks (President, Prime Minister, Pope, Chancellor, Sheriff, Queen, director, mayor), firing most strongly on high-ranking political, religious or royal titles placed just before a person's name.

1487.name: City and town names (and other place names), with activation strongest on the final token completing the name (e.g. 'sburgh', 'sha', 'Angeles') and sometimes the comma after it in datelines or addresses. Weak firing on other proper nouns or generic place words like 'city'.

14893.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires weakly on function words and punctuation at phrase or clause junctions, such as prepositions, conjunctions, articles, auxiliaries, commas and sentence or paragraph breaks. These are positions where the sentence is about to continue into a new constituent (e.g. 'is the ability to', ', which we have', 'and has').

A diffuse, weakly selective pattern with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words and clause connectors such as "to", "of", "that", "the", "was a", "yet you have a" and "with the". It also fires on sentence boundaries and paragraph breaks. These tokens tend to sit at points where a new clause or the main content of a phrase is about to begin.

14954.name: Final token of a proper name (usually a person's surname or last subword piece of a name, also ships, Pokémon, products), marking completion of a multi-token named entity.

14964.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires across scientific and technical expository prose, especially biology/biomedical research writing such as abstracts and papers. It activates on scattered content words, word-piece fragments and function words, peaking on explanatory claims about mechanisms or capabilities (e.g. "can", "can be", "resulted in", "which eventually").

15095.name: Tokens at boundaries within web-page boilerplate and metadata, such as the newline ending a field value (IDs, ISBNs, DOIs, dates, namespaces, "pages on⏎this wiki") just before the next label, and the word "navigation" in wiki "Jump to: navigation, search" headers. Generally marks where one structured, templated element ends and the next begins.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on boundary tokens ending a segment in structured or boilerplate text, just before a new field or line begins. Typical spots are line breaks between header or diff lines (strongest after an #ifndef include-guard line), the final digit of an ISBN, URL fragment words like 'comments' or 'respond' that precede a timestamp, and punctuation or delimiters in code, URLs and metadata. It fires only rarely on ordinary prose.

15108.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no single dominant token. It fires mostly at structural boundaries in text, such as sentence-ending periods, commas separating clauses or list items, paragraph breaks and closing tags like "</". It also fires on the words immediately after these boundaries, typically sentence or clause openers like "In addition,", "Coming up," and "However,". Within running prose it picks up scattered content words, often nouns and verbs describing events or outcomes such as "losses", "progress" and "lost a bunch of".

15113.name: Descriptions of research study design and data sources in scientific or academic writing, especially methods-section details about who or what was studied, where, when and how. Typical phrases cover participants and cohorts, sites, protocols, surveys, screening, monitoring, measurements, models and date ranges. The strongest activations fall on participant and sample descriptions such as 'children were screened', 'participants', 'protocols' and 'sites in'.

15273.name: Definite article "The"/"the" (occasionally other determiners like "These"/"A") at the start of a new sentence, paragraph, or clause, opening a fresh noun phrase that introduces the next topic. Activation is strongest right after a period or paragraph break.

Sentence-initial definite determiners (mostly "The", sometimes "the"/"This") that open a new sentence or clause and begin a noun phrase referring back to something already introduced. Activation is strongest right after a sentence break or paragraph break in news-style prose.

15355.name: Opening punctuation of in-text citations and references, mainly the bracket "[" (often fused with a period, ".[") before a reference number in academic or Wikipedia-style text. It also fires weakly on other citation pieces such as "(", superscript braces, the space before a year in author–year citations, separator dots in section or figure numbers, and words like "Figure" or "page".

15373.name: Tokens in citation or cross-reference markup that come just before a reference number or label: \ref, \cite{ / \citep, "Ref"/"Source", opening brackets and superscript markers, the commas or spaces separating numbers in citation lists like [2,3,5], and "image" in markdown image links such as (image2). The feature fires on the scaffolding of numbered references rather than on the numbers themselves.

15401.name: The opening words of a subordinate or adverbial clause, mostly right after conjunctions like "when", "if", "after", "since" and "while": the subject plus verb ("they start", "we have") or a participle or gerund ("camping with", "being heated at"). Activation peaks on the main verb, the start of the clause describing the condition or time of an event.

15423.name: Separator and delimiter tokens (spaces, hyphens, periods, slashes) placed immediately before a number or code segment inside structured strings such as DOIs, URLs, dates, file names, version numbers, and metadata like ratings or word/page counts, where a name or word gives way to digits.

Separator tokens, mostly hyphens and bare spaces, that link two alphanumeric segments in URLs, slugs, dates, IDs, product codes and metadata strings. They usually come right before a number, e.g. "Words 3 Pages" or "line 32". A few weak activations fall on ordinary words in prose.

1546.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across the continuation of an ongoing phrase, clause, or list. It marks the middle and tail tokens that elaborate or complete a structure begun earlier: the remaining list items, argument fields in code, the rest of a purpose or relative clause. It appears in prose, code, citations and dates alike. Activation usually builds toward the end of the unit and stops at sentence or line boundaries, without clear dependence on topic.

A broad, diffuse feature that fires on predictable continuations of text, especially where content repeats or follows an established pattern. It responds most strongly to copying earlier material: repeated phrases, recurring identifiers, lists and sequences (RC17 RC18…, "String #", 666…, "/ / /"), repeated code calls or tags, and formulaic structures like SQL conditions, lambda chains and key-value dicts.

155.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on content-bearing words across varied text, including code. It is strongest on the head nouns and final subword pieces of specialized or technical noun phrases, especially medical and scientific terms such as 'eye movements', 'saccades', 'syncope' and 'DBS', and on product or entity names. Function words get little activation.

A diffuse, weak feature with no single clear trigger. It fires broadly across structured or technical text (code, markdown tables and lists, math variable definitions, problem statements, garbled or noisy text). Its peaks fall on key content noun phrases or technical terms being specified or defined, such as "throwing exceptions", "Faraday rotation", "tan"/"cot", "MFA" and "Athletes' Association". Secondary activity appears on surrounding formatting tokens like pipes, newlines, brackets and whitespace runs.

15569.name: Language about self-perception, ego and status: people regarding themselves as superior, in charge or entitled, plus related notions of power, dominance, hierarchy, arrogance and ambition. The strongest cases are explicit attitude phrases such as "a superior attitude towards" and "see themselves as in charge." Weaker hits are scattered words about self-regard, confidence or how one thinks of oneself.

15583.name: Fires most strongly on backtick characters, both single inline-code backticks (e.g. around `Webhooks`, and backtick-like transliteration marks in Arabic) and triple-backtick code-fence closings. It responds weakly to other markup or formatting delimiters such as closing LaTeX math (}$, $), markdown asterisks and angle brackets. Activations on ordinary words are faint and scattered.

15677.name: Main predicates in news-style lead sentences announcing a new event or development, especially the verb phrase right after the subject (e.g. 'has begun production in', 'has launched', 'filed a lawsuit', 'have identified a', 'announced that'). Weaker activation falls on surrounding prepositions, dates and objects in these factual report or headline sentences.

News-style announcement language: the main predicate of a lead sentence reporting a new event or development, typically right after the subject (said/voted/secured/launched/has begun), often with time words (Wednesday, yesterday, this week), 'new', and the clause punctuation that follows. Strongest in press releases and news ledes.

15708.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature. It fires on subword fragments and later pieces of multi-token names, technical terms and compounds, such as surnames, mid-word pieces, list items and equation terms. It is strongest when the span repeats or copies something already seen in the context, e.g. Edward Snowden, Erez Winner, Bletchley, Plaintiff/Defendant, 4x + 3x.

15746.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across scientific and technical expository prose. It peaks on phrases describing how something works or what it does, especially biological mechanisms and causal roles (e.g., "genome-wide control of gene expression", "alter regulatory function", "play a critical role", "responsible for", "pathogens that can cause", "other physiological functions"). Function words in these explanatory clauses also fire, such as "which are", "they are", "to" and "of the".

15805.name: Promotional or descriptive text about companies, brands and products. It fires most strongly on brand or company names (Graco, Samsung, ADATA, Philips, Goodrich) and on the words right after them that describe the company, such as "is known for its commitment", "is an awful brand", "from top brands like", "created the" and "Based in… is proud to". It also fires weakly on general marketing or press-release wording.

Mentions of companies, brands, manufacturers and makers (e.g., Patagonia, Nissan, LEGO, Google/Asus, Les Baer Custom, Avid Carp), plus the surrounding text describing what they make, design or do, especially promotional or company self-descriptions ("we produces/designs", "designed by ... built by").

1587.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature. It fires mostly on structural and formatting tokens at line or section boundaries: newlines after headers, HTML/LaTeX markup (e.g. '<table>' followed by a newline, '\begin{align*}'), separators, ellipses and code braces. It also fires on highly predictable words inside boilerplate or formulaic phrases, such as 'stay tuned', 'be sure', 'every reasonable effort to ensure', 'hello there and welcome', 'Received:' and 'Subscription'.

15899.name: Tokens about the final or positional part of a number or string, such as digits, units, place value, endings and suffixes. Common forms are "last digit", "end in", "endswith", file extension and rhyme, plus modulo operations like "% 10" and "mod" that extract the final digit. Activation is strongest on "digit(s)".

1593.name: A diffuse feature that fires weakly across ordinary prose on function words and parts of fixed multiword phrases, collocations and formulaic constructions (e.g. "is just one of the", "nowhere to be found", "may play a role", "managed to", "seconds away", "did the world a favor"). It peaks on the predictable middle or continuation tokens of these set expressions, typically modifiers, quantifiers, light verbs and prepositions, rather than on content-heavy nouns.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires on ordinary function words and clause-continuation tokens (auxiliaries such as do/does/did/is/are, and words like 'that', 'the', 'in', 'if', 'best', 'final') in the middle of fluent explanatory or instructional prose, especially assistant-style answers, tutorials and code comments. The strongest activations fall on predictable multi-word phrase continuations ('in place at', 'if they are', 'can't seem to stay', 'you want information') rather than on content-specific words.

15977.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly in code, HTML tables and structured text. It peaks on the token that finishes a name, identifier or field value right before a delimiter or closing element. Typical hits are closing tags such as and , the ends of variable or ID names (_USER, ATIONS, relay, Cause), and closing quotes or commas around string keys. In prose it fires on scattered nouns or punctuation that end a term or clause.

16061.name: Language about technological or scientific progress and advancement, such as words like "advancements", "progress", "new technologies", "cutting-edge", "high-tech", "improved" and "modern", plus phrases like "progress has been made in recent years". Activation is strongest on explicit progress/advancement nouns and their following "in [field] technology" phrases.

1607.name: Marks plural noun phrases that refer to sets of several items (representatives, witnesses, presentations, books, museums, disorders, games, models), along with the words tied to them: quantifiers and counts (all, both, five, three, "of these"), plural pronouns (they, them, their, these) and plural verbs (are). Activation often extends to the following comma or period, or to list-ending brackets in code.
