16079.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature on discourse pivot points: clause or sentence boundaries (commas, periods, question marks, line breaks) and the words just after them that introduce contrast, debate, criticism or differing viewpoints. Typical triggers are "However, its use has also been criticized", "open to debate", "Experts debate", "some leading experts" and rhetorical questions. It fires most strongly when text shifts toward controversy or evaluation.

Weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly at clause and sentence boundaries, such as periods, paragraph breaks, and the opening words of the next sentence. It is strongest at discourse pivots that introduce a contrast or shift, like "but come up against", "although not without controversy" and "there is debate". It also fires lightly on function words and auxiliaries (has, been, the, ’t) in running prose.

16161.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature that fires on content-bearing noun-phrase tokens (often the start or subword pieces of rare, technical, or proper-noun terms) such as place and organization names, product codes, scientific and technical vocabulary, and the head nouns of the topic being discussed, typically right after a determiner, preposition, or verb.

16175.name: The word "County"/"county" (and "counties"), especially as the final part of a place name like "Lake County" or "Orange County". Weaker activation on other words or word-endings that complete a geographic or institutional name, such as River, Creek, Township, district, Province, City and University.

16209.name: Discourse transitions right after a statement ends, especially after an enumerated list ("A, B and C"). Activation falls on the closing period or line break and the opening words of the next sentence or clause, such as "The", "It", "This", "For example," or "Out of these three". These openers often refer back to or elaborate on what came before. Activation is weak and diffuse.

16219.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly within narrative clauses about motion, travel or journeys. Typical contexts are going along a way, road or route, walking past, heading somewhere, reaching an altitude or destination, and objects popping out or being carried along. It also fires on related nouns such as roads, vehicles, paths and streams, and on the clause connectors or commas inside these event descriptions. The strongest hits are phrases like "on the way I said to" and "driving down a rural road at".

16258.name: A diffuse feature with weak activation on many ordinary mid-sequence tokens, such as function words, list items, dates and phone-number digits. It fires most strongly inside arithmetic or mathematical expressions, peaking on operators like ÷ and minus, parentheses and numeric operands (e.g., "÷ 2 - ( 8 - 6 )", "+(-3)", "C/360").

16298.name: Structural and formatting punctuation in document scaffolding. It fires most on periods in abbreviations and section numbers ("Fig.", "Jan.", "1. Introduction", "12.1.1") and on commas between citation numbers ("[7, 8]", "{1,2}"). It also fires on bullet-list leading spaces, section headers ("Abstract", "INTRODUCTION", "Index Terms"), superscript markup and boilerplate like "advertisement" or "navigation".

16439.name: Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences: repeated numbers, symbols, separators and code lines (e.g., 30, 31, 30…; -*-*; ~~88~~88; repeated '; ' lines; 16x16x16). The token itself repeats an earlier element in the same run, and activation is strongest in highly regular, predictable repetition. Weak, scattered activation on ordinary words elsewhere.

1644.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that spans ordinary running prose, especially the predicate parts of clauses: verb phrases, their complements, and descriptive or evaluative modifiers ('can present a few extra problems', 'revolve around instant gratification'). Activation rises somewhat in emotionally weighted or reflective statements ('can no longer face the tragedy', 'could signify that'). It largely skips names, numbers and technical labels.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across running clauses in explanatory, instructional, or assistant-style prose (code comments, math, Q&A, narrative). It tends to activate on function and content words in the middle of elaborating or qualifying phrases (e.g., "not sure about the value", "mind playing tricks", "claimed to have", "very broad from just"), rather than on any specific token type. Activation peaks inside hedging, reasoning, or descriptive continuations.

1648.name: Line-break tokens (newline, often merged with the preceding punctuation such as period, semicolon, brace, colon or quote) that end a line, sentence, heading or code statement, across prose, lists, metadata, LaTeX and code. A single newline tends to activate more strongly than a double newline.

Line-break tokens, often merged with preceding end-of-line punctuation (periods, colons, brackets, backticks, spaces), that end a line of text, code, or a list item. Single newlines fire most strongly, while multiple newlines fire a bit less.

16494.name: Final tokens of the content words in image captions, photo credits and alt-text descriptions, such as places, names, dates and the objects shown. The text often sits just before a line break, a credit like AP or Getty, or the start of an article. Activation is strongest at the end of caption phrases describing location and date, e.g. 'airport in Thailand', 'Festival in France in 2012', 'Oct. 5, 2020'.

Content words in photo-caption-style descriptions of a scene, especially where the event, location (venue, city, country) and date are given (e.g. "speaks at the funeral of… in Tokyo on Saturday"). The strongest activations fall on place names, venue nouns and date tokens in these captions.

1654.name: The first subword fragment (often one or two letters) of a word that the tokenizer splits into multiple pieces, most often rare proper nouns, names, acronyms or unusual words (e.g. "M"+"ikhailov", "Qu"+"inoa", "D"+"CLC"). It fires most strongly on capitalized name or acronym starts.

1657.name: Content nouns and noun phrases (often multiword compounds or technical/domain terms) that name the key topic entity or concept in a clause, typically the head noun after a preposition or determiner, e.g. object-of-preposition or subject noun phrases. Function words are rarely marked.

Content-word nouns (and noun-modifier compounds) that name the topic, object, or entity being talked about, often the head of a noun phrase after a preposition or determiner (e.g. "the polygon", "chord chart", "team names", "error message"). This shows up across prose, math, and noisy or garbled code and multilingual text, and activation is weak and diffuse.

16764.name: Language tied to to-do lists, checklists and task management: lists, items, tasks, things to do, prioritizing, getting work done, pending items, check marks and checkbox brackets. It fires most strongly on "to-do" and an empty checkbox "[ ]".

16786.name: Dashes (em/en dashes, hyphens, double hyphens) used mid-sentence after a complete clause to introduce an elaboration, aside, or continuation. Occasionally semicolons, colons, or ellipses serve the same role, and the word right after the dash (when, but, from, albeit) is sometimes included.

16830.name: Double-backtick tokens (``), mostly the opening part of Markdown code fences (```) or inline code delimiters, and also LaTeX-style opening quotation marks (``). Activation is strongest at the start of a code block or quoted span. Weak activations appear on other opening delimiters such as „ and $$.

16894.name: Tokens inside loop and conditional control flow, mostly in code: the closing parenthesis, brace, colon, or indentation right after a while/if/else/except condition, and the loop body that follows (continue, break, increments, join, print, endl). Prose matches are weaker and come from analogous conditional or repetition phrasing, such as the comma after an "if" clause or words like "twice", "retry a total of 5 times", "every single", and "keeps".

16910.name: Tokens in code (and technical prose) that name or declare handles and pointers to system resources, such as file pointers and descriptors (FILE *fp, FileDescriptor, FreeFile), thread and window handles (m_hThread, hwnd, Hdl hdl) and the word "handle" itself. Activation is strongest on pointer-or-handle prefixes and type markers. Weaker activations fall on generic type and identifier fragments in variable declarations.

16963.name: Weak, diffuse activation on biology and biochemistry vocabulary, mainly words and word pieces about organisms producing or secreting chemical compounds and their biological roles (metabolites, pheromones, antibiotics, signaling, pigments, acids, hydrocarbons). The strongest activations fall on 'secondary metabolites', pheromones and microbial production. Scattered activations on name and word fragments in scientific text are low.

16995.name: Language about buildings, facilities and physical structures being built, extended, renovated, destroyed or replaced. It fires most strongly on parts and additions of structures (wings, extensions, new parts) and on words like "new", "building" and "renovations", plus the function words and punctuation near these descriptions.

17181.name: Words for defense (defense/defence, defensive, defender, defending, the D in D-line), strongest in team sports, especially American football and basketball (defensive coordinator, defensive tackle, a team's defense). Weaker for defensive meanings in military, gaming, biology or workplace contexts.

Words built on the root "defen-" (defense/defence, defensive, defending, defender, defensively, defenseman), mainly in sports contexts describing a team's defensive unit, positions, or play. Activation peaks on "defensive" used as a modifier for football positions or team units (defensive lineman/end/back/line/front) and on team defenses, is weaker for soccer "defence," "defending champion," and non-sport or psychological uses.

17239.name: Phrases in scientific or academic writing that introduce the authors' own work and its contributions, such as "Here we", "In this study,", "We show", "this paper", "the present work", and "herein". The signal is strongest on "Here", "we", "study" and "show", especially where an abstract turns from background to what the authors did.

17246.name: Head nouns, or the final subword of a noun, naming a technical device, instrument, component or functional unit, often an agent noun ending in -er/-or/-ator/-iter. Examples include modulator, saturator, mixer, switch, amplifier, limiter, controller, telescope and balancer. Activation is strongest on the suffix that marks the word as a device.

17252.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires in mostly technical or instructional text about storing, passing, embedding or protecting data and information (secrets, input, URLs, strings, keys, text fields). It picks out the words for the data item, the container or location, or the method of conveying it (e.g. "carry it on-board as", "save data using", "in brackets", "as input").

17257.name: Separators and numbers in academic citation references marking the transition from volume/issue to page numbers: the colon, space, or parenthesis after a volume/issue number, the first page number, and the dash in page ranges (e.g. "243:646–648", "82, 65-82").

17269.name: Speech-attribution phrases for quoted or reported statements: verbs of saying or thinking (said, says, explained, claims, admits, added, continues) and the speaker reference attached to them (pronoun, name ending, 'according to X', interview speaker labels). Activation is strongest right after a closing quote, as in “...,” she says.

17298.name: Concessive hedging: modal verbs (especially "may be"/"might") and "while/though" clauses that grant something as possibly true before a contrasting "but". Activation is strongest on the concession itself ("may be X,") and on the comma just before "but".

1733.name: The final word or token of a short noun phrase that ends a parenthetical, appositive, or list item, i.e. the token immediately before a closing parenthesis, comma, dash, or period, such as "(the loop)", "(3.6 m)", "Google Chrome," or "de facto standard,". It marks the completion of an inserted or clarifying phrase.

17385.name: Tokens in passages describing the past or history, such as historical eras, events, dates and past figures (World War One, the Nixon administration, 1984, Sept. 11, Truman/Eisenhower), childhood memories, and origins or first occurrences. The strongest activations fall on named historical periods and events that anchor a 'back then' timeframe.

174.name: A diffuse, weakly firing pattern on content words that complete a phrase, mostly head nouns serving as the object of a verb or preposition (e.g. "raising money", "pet stores", "on walls"). It also fires on some predicate adjectives and participles and on following commas or conjunctions at phrase boundaries. There is no single topic, so it looks like a general marker of a phrase's main noun or argument completion.

Content-bearing words that complete a phrase or clause, mostly the head noun of a noun phrase (often after "the", "a" or a preposition) naming the object of discussion, such as question, code, input, variable, file, help. The text is mostly technical, programming or assistant-style. Weaker activations fall on verbs or participles that end a clause, like done, failed, provided and help.

17413.name: The day number in a written calendar date, usually right after a month name (e.g. "On April 3,"), often with an ordinal suffix like st/th. It fires most strongly in sentence-opening "On [Month] [day]" phrases introducing an event. Where the day comes first ("13 May", "19th November"), the month name is marked instead.
The day-of-month number in a date that follows a month name or numeric month, usually in narrative phrases like "On [Month] [day]" that introduce when an event happened.

17490.name: In code, the indentation whitespace and closing braces (or else/dedent lines) that come right after a block ends with return, break or pass, i.e. the dedent where nested scopes close. It fires most strongly on leading spaces/tabs before '}' and on following 'else'/'return' lines. There are weak, sporadic hits on line breaks and structural tokens in non-code text.

17525.name: Software installation and filesystem terms, especially names of directories, folders and file types where programs get installed or stored (e.g. /sbin, /bin, install, binaries, executables, dll, runtime, dev files, scripts, tmp, Applications, program_files). Activation is strongest on path segments and install targets in build or setup instructions. Weak, scattered activations also appear on list punctuation and structural tokens.

Category/type words that classify a resource or component, chiefly in software and computing contexts: directory names in file paths (template, Bin, usr, var, headers, init.d), and modifiers naming a kind of file, code or build element (DLL files, system apps, read-only sections, compile dependency, library path, classpath). It fires more weakly on similar classifier nouns elsewhere (staff, books, assets, parking, stationery).

17540.name: The digit "3" as a standalone number token in numeric, mathematical, code, or tabular contexts (coefficients, decimals, operands, list items). It fires most strongly when 3 is a coefficient or term in an algebraic expression. It rarely fires on the word "three".

17543.name: Junctures in procedural or technical text (instructions, API docs, code) where one action or step ends and its result or the next step follows: sentence and clause boundaries after an action, step numbers, "and"/"will" connectives, and especially the hand-off to a response or output (e.g. "Response from the API:", closing parentheses or braces after a call).

Tokens in process or step-by-step descriptions at the point where an action has been performed and its outcome or next stage follows. Typical cues are waiting, a response or feedback, results, success or failure (e.g. 'If your request fails', 'sit back and wait a few minutes', 'a call succeeded') and sentence or step boundaries leading into the next step.

17567.name: Abbreviated honorifics and titles placed before a person's name, such as Dr, Prof, Mr, Mrs, Ms, Sen, Rep, Gov, Gen and Lt, usually followed by a period. 'Dr' fires most strongly, especially when it introduces a named expert after verbs like 'said', 'by' or 'contact'. Weak activations also appear on other short abbreviations, such as 'St' for saint and 'Re'.

17693.name: Nouns or phrases that name a limit, boundary or capacity that something reaches, runs out of or goes past. These usually follow words like "beyond the", "more than", "greater than the", "end of the", "edge of the", "out of", "exceeds" or "run down the". Typical targets are edge, radius, battery, number of items, maximum allowed, duration and limit; code examples mark the bound variables (lim, $late, payload length).

A limit, capacity, or available amount that something exceeds, drains, or overruns, usually right after words like "exceed", "more than", "greater than", "over the", "off the", "drain the" or "<=". Examples include battery, budget, quota, max, available space, capacity, size of the volume, and .length. Activation is strongest on code bound checks (e.g. ".length" in a length comparison) and on "available" or "capacity of".

17707.name: The verb "issue" in all its forms (issued, issuing, issuance, Japanese 発行), meaning to officially put out or distribute a document, statement, warning, certificate or product. It often extends to the following article (a/an), and fires more weakly on synonyms like "released" or "uttering" and on the look-alike "ISS".

Forms of the verb "issue" (issued, issuing, issuance, issuers), meaning to officially release or distribute something such as statements, warnings, documents, cards, currency, or stamps. A following "a" or "of" is sometimes included. Other tokens show only weak, sporadic activation.

17738.name: A diffuse feature for forward-looking or prospective content: tokens within statements about future events, plans, predictions or possibilities, such as modals (will, would, may, could, should), 'future', 'expected', 'possible', 'longer term', 'lasting implications' and upcoming-time phrases ('this summer', 'for the weekend'). It often fires on the sentence boundary or conjunction that introduces such a clause, and activations are mostly weak and scattered.

17741.name: Tokens in the middle of a multi-token word, name, or fixed phrase (word fragments like 'un|sc|athed', 'Nan|op|ore', 'Aix|-M|arseille', or function words in set expressions like 'point of view', 'piece of paper', 'all the time', 'up to date', 'U.S.'), where the following token is highly predictable. Activation is often strongest when the phrase repeats earlier text.

Tokens in the middle of a fixed collocation, name, or split word whose continuation is highly predictable: word fragments and first pieces of multi-token words (Obi-W|an, LOS AN|GELES, U|.S., 4 p|.m.), and connecting words in set phrases (more or less, all of a sudden, first of all, exactly the same, shapes and sizes).

17748.name: Digit chunks in the middle of long multi-digit numbers, mostly after a decimal point or the first few digits (decimal expansions, conversion constants, IDs, DOIs, ISBNs, phone numbers). The strongest cases are long mathematical or physical constants and precise decimals.

17756.name: Diffuse, low-intensity activation at syntactic boundaries: where a phrase or clause completes and the next constituent begins. Typical spots are the end of a subject noun phrase or the verb right after it ("builder remain liable", "division reported", "Edward is"), and commas closing introductory or subordinate clauses. Sentence-final periods and question marks also fire, as do connectives such as because, and, as, when and that. The same behavior appears in Japanese at topic and clause particles (は, が、).

17779.name: File extension tokens for structured data/config formats (mainly .json, .xml, .yaml; weaker for .csv, .txt, .html) attached to filenames, strongest for config/manifest files like package.json, config.json, AndroidManifest.xml. Also fires weakly on format names alone (xml, Json) and on .json method calls.

17833.name: The first word or two right after an opening article (mostly "The", sometimes "A") at the start of a title, heading or sentence. These are usually the head noun or modifier of a noun phrase, often in a "The X of Y" construction (e.g. Importance, Art, Essence, history).

The first content word (noun or modifier) right after a determiner like "The", "An" or "This", most often at the start of a title, headline or sentence. It marks the head of the opening noun phrase, e.g. "The Power of…", "The film…", "The syndrome…".

17885.name: Words inside the condition or triggering circumstance of a rule, contract, law or policy (after 'if', 'in the event that', 'when', 'during any period', 'would be counted as'), i.e. the hypothetical event or situation under which a provision applies. It peaks in legal and contractual conditionals such as 'In the event that the vessel…', 'or has violated…' and 'when medical proof is given', with weak scattered activation elsewhere.

18041.name: Separator tokens (commas, 'and', 'while', 'with', newlines, semicolons, opening parentheses, periods) that occur between entries in a list of people, mostly cast or credit lists. They usually fall just after one person/role description and right before the next person's name, so they predict that a new proper name is coming.

18055.name: Present-tense speech/reporting verbs (especially "says"/"say") attributing statements or claims to a source, e.g. "he says", "researchers say", "results show", typically introducing or interrupting a quotation or reported clause; strongest for "says" after a named person in news-style attribution.

18059.name: Fires on a partial-word token, usually the first or a middle subword piece of a word split into several tokens. These are mostly rare proper nouns such as surnames, places and institutions ('Beck'→man, 'Urb'→ana, 'Wat'→ertown, 'Lie'→berman, 'Id'→so), plus technical terms and URL or path fragments. The fragment leaves the word incomplete, so the next token is a predictable completion. Occasionally it fires on whole words that commonly begin a fixed compound or phrase (e.g., 'partial' → fulfillment).

18067.name: Fires on the token right after a number, mostly a percent sign fused with following punctuation ("%)", "%,", "%.", " percent"). It is strongest on "%)" closing a parenthetical statistic, as in "(13%)". It also fires weakly on closing parentheses or other punctuation that end a parenthetical aside or measurement.

18104.name: Subword tokens inside non-English words or phrases (Spanish, German, French, Danish, Bosnian, Lithuanian, transliterated Russian) that appear within English text, often as translations, titles, or parenthetical glosses. Activation is strongest on the continuation pieces of foreign words, such as German terms in philosophy or a Spanish translated abstract title, and weak on odd fragments in URLs or rare English words.

18130.name: Unit words that follow a number to state a size, mostly in digital and computing settings. The strongest are "-bit" and "bit" in phrases like 32-bit or 8-bit. Weaker hits include bits, bytes, digit, character, pin, syllable, note, hour and ounces, typically in compound measure phrases such as "N-unit".

Unit or measure words placed directly after a number, typically as compound modifiers like "32-bit", "4-digit", "15-pin", "140 characters", "Gigabit". It is strongest for "bit"/"bits" in computing contexts (bit width, encryption strength) and weaker for digits, pins, ounces, characters and similar units.

18262.name: Nouns, usually the final token of a proper name, for geographic places and political entities (countries, states, cities, regions) and, less strongly, organizations or groups tied to them. Typical contexts are locative ones like "in X", "from X", "around the world" and "abroad". Country names that stand for a national government or actor activate most strongly.

18267.name: On the right-hand side of an assignment (mostly in code, sometimes math), a variable name that repeats the name being assigned on the left, as in self-referential updates like `x = x + 1`, `cur = cur->next`, `df = df[...]`, or `n = n;`. The token that completes the repeated identifier (e.g. "ref", "_max", "1") is what is marked. The signal is strongest when the right-hand reference exactly matches the assigned variable, and weaker for near-matches like `tVal = trueVal` or `num = int(num)`.

18276.name: The final token that completes a clause or sentence, typically just before punctuation or a boundary. These are often predictable phrase-closing words: sentence-final adverbs and particles ("too", "though", "respectively", "rn", "eh"), tag-question pronouns ("shall we", "aren't you") and fixed-phrase endings ("for example", "as follows", "over time"). It also fires on clause-final verb or particle endings in other languages, such as German verb-final suffixes ("-ellt", "-legt", "haben") and Chinese/Japanese sentence-final markers (了, 吗, です). These non-English endings activate most strongly.

1829.name: Locations and spatial descriptions: place names (cities, regions, states, countries, landmarks), street addresses, and prepositional phrases describing where something is ("in the valley", "down the block from", "to the north of"). Activation is strongest on proper geographic names and spatial-relation words inside location phrases.

18296.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no clear semantic theme. It shows up on varied structural or boundary tokens, most strongly on delimiters in code, markup and lists: closing quotes, comma or semicolon followed by a newline, colon plus line breaks, and units like "px". It also fires faintly on function words and connectors mid-phrase (of, the, and, who, on, "(").

1831.name: A diffuse feature firing on content words (mostly nouns, plus some verbs and adjectives) that head a new phrase. These are typically the first meaningful word after a determiner, sentence start or list bullet. The strongest cases are abstract or relational head nouns followed by 'of' (shape of, graph of, effects of, limits of, timing of, interior) and participles opening a clause (Planted, Holding, identified, observed).

A diffuse feature that fires on content words (mostly abstract or generic nouns, plus some verbs and adjectives), typically right after a determiner, preposition or line break. Examples are 'values', 'reception', 'medium', 'concentration' and 'pairs'. It activates sparsely across many tokens in ordinary, and often garbled or spammy, prose. The strongest activations come on nouns that head a noun phrase, such as 'The ___ of' or 'a ___'.

18327.name: The word "artist" and its variants (artists, artiste, artistic, artistry), meaning creative practitioners such as painters, musicians or performers. Activation is strongest on the noun "artist(s)" and weaker on the adjective forms and on related creator words like author, comedian or creative.

18356.name: Verbs and determiners in calls to submit or send something to someone, such as a comment, message, question, email, or information (e.g. "Leave a", "Send us an email with", "submit questions", "register your"). The phrases often appear in reader-engagement or contact prompts, and the feature fires most strongly on the verb and the following article or possessive, just before the item being sent.

Verbs and following determiners in requests or calls to action asking the reader to provide, send, or contribute something (leave a comment, send photos, email, submit your, bring a, give me your), typically after "please", "you can", or "by".

18405.name: Tokens tied to hyperlinks and web markup: URL and path pieces (://, ../, /, .html, .md, domain fragments), Markdown link syntax (](, [), HTML tags and attributes (<thead, alt, quote marks), and boilerplate link or navigation text such as 'see more' in several languages (Ver mais, Zobacz więcej), 'view all', 'click here to' and 'for more information'. Stray whitespace tokens in scraped page layouts also fire.

18407.name: Diffuse, weak activation across expository scientific/technical prose, strongest in dense biomedical text describing how entities (hormones, cytokines, genes, factors) function or relate. It fires on subject nouns, linking verbs and connective phrases that state a mechanism or causal role, such as "is associated with", "promote … by the respective activation of", ", leading to the induction of" and "are the main … subtype", along with nearby commas and periods.

18446.name: The start of an explanatory annotation, chiefly code comment markers (//, #, ', bullets) at the beginning of a comment, plus the first few words after them. Weaker hits fall on verbs and function words inside descriptive or explanatory prose, such as captions, documentation and technical explanations.

18506.name: Function words and phrase content within adverbial or prepositional phrases that set the temporal or circumstantial backdrop for the main event (e.g. 'at a time when…', 'as the national debate shifts from…', 'on the eve of an election', 'during', 'after', 'following a', 'due to the', 'delayed by a fire drill'). Activation is strongest on extended 'when/as…' context clauses describing ongoing situations.

18513.name: A weak, diffuse signal in lofty, idealistic or inspirational passages about purpose, virtue, God, country, humanity, democracy, the earth or the world. It fires on function words and nouns within these grand statements rather than on any single token type. The strongest activations are on phrases expressing a higher calling or universal scope, such as "God. What would the world", "put on this earth to be", "Country, we advocate" and "activist on the planet".

18539.name: First-person pronouns (mainly "we", plus "We", "our", "us", "I") used by authors to introduce their own work in scientific or technical writing, such as abstracts and papers. They usually begin a clause stating what the authors did, propose, or present, and often follow framing phrases like "In this study,", "Herein,", or "To address this,".

1857.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across content-bearing spans in ordinary prose, mainly noun phrases and predicates naming the specific subject, setting or domain of the passage (places, organizations, products, technical or medical terms). Activation peaks on the key topic nouns, such as 'quantum dots', 'Boquete', 'carcinoma' and 'Academic Decathlon', and stays weak on function words and generic connectives.

Diffuse, weak activation over multi-word descriptive noun phrases and their prepositional complements (often following 'the', 'of', 'in'), spanning entity/domain descriptions such as places, organizations, technical items, and groups of people. It peaks on content head nouns and compound modifiers (e.g., 'network security', 'automobile industry', 'stores', 'places'), and on code it fires loosely on identifiers and paths.

18573.name: Words for letting someone or something go, leave or return from custody or an institution, such as being released, discharged, paroled, sent or taken home, or leaving hospital. The strongest cases involve people released from custody or discharged from hospital or the army. Weaker activations cover related ideas of release, issuance or approval.

1859.name: Mostly weak, diffuse activations on words about errors, failures and problems. The strongest are on "error" and related terms (error messages, error handling, error reports, errors, crash, failed, alerts, rejection, misconduct, caution/emergency). The feature also fires faintly on error-reporting code and system-message contexts such as print statements and log-like text.

18610.name: Fires on the first fragment of a word that the tokenizer splits into several subword pieces, usually a word-initial piece (often capitalized), and mostly for rarer words, proper nouns and technical terms. It tends to appear after a quote mark or within a title or name.

18612.name: The subword token "yst" (including "myst"/"syst") inside a longer word, e.g. crystalline, polycystic, systolic, mystic/mystique, demystify, cholecystectomy. Activation is highest in medical and biochemical words (polycystic, cholecystectomy, homocysteine).

18619.name: Tokens inside dense structured or symbolic content, chiefly operands, operators, brackets and function names within math equations (the strongest is \sin^2 in a LaTeX formula), plus dot-leader runs in tables of contents and fragments of chemical names and formulas. It also fires weakly on odd, out-of-place words in garbled or unusual prose.

18683.name: Words describing a bad fate that befalls someone, especially punishment, capture and loss of freedom (arrested, prison, sentenced to death, banishment, detained, imprisoned), plus related misfortunes such as being trapped, chased, evicted or laid off, foreclosure, or injury. Arrest and imprisonment terms activate most strongly.

18684.name: The final token of a noun phrase (often the object of a prepositional or modifier phrase: a place, specimen, tissue, cell type, or title) that closes off a constituent, marking the boundary right before the sentence continues with a verb, comma, conjunction, closing parenthesis or period.

18713.name: Tokens of the word "large" and its forms (larger, largest, enlarge, Large), marking great size, scale or quantity. Activation is strongest for the base form "large" used as a plain adjective (e.g. "a large number", "large-scale") and weaker for comparative and superlative forms.

18730.name: The comma that separates a city name from its following state, region or country in a location or address (e.g. "St. Louis, MO", "Copenhagen, Denmark"). It is most common in academic affiliations, supplier credits and citations, and is strongest in manufacturer parentheticals such as "(Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO)". It occasionally fires weakly on similar connectors like "in" after an institution name.

1880.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across many genres (prose, code, technical, legal, recipes) on content-bearing tokens, mainly nouns and noun phrases naming key entities, technical terms, proper names and list items, together with the punctuation or line breaks that close those items. It seems to track salient topic or entity spans rather than any single word or meaning.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no sharp semantic focus. It fires on scattered tokens in structured, often synthetic-looking or slightly garbled text such as code, CSS, math and calculations, tables, lists and logic puzzles. It tends to land on key nouns or terms (identifiers, units, named entities like 'root beer', 'MJD', 'container') and on line-ending punctuation or newline/whitespace tokens that close a clause or list item.

1887.name: Opening parenthesis tokens (" (", "(", "[(", ">(", "(('") that start a parenthetical, such as an abbreviation, citation year, clarification, enumeration, count, or math/code argument. Activation is often highest when the parenthesis begins a line or opens a standalone aside.

18935.name: Words that refer to a person's or group's positions, beliefs, views, policies, stances or commitments, often political, plus verbs and phrases of expressing or committing to them (said, signed on to, committed to, vote for). The strongest cases are nouns such as 'stances', 'policies', 'beliefs', 'comments' and 'commitments'.

18955.name: Word pieces containing "add"/"addle" (often preceded by s), the strongest being "saddle", "sadd" in saddened/saddled, "Saddle River", and "saddle thrombus". Weaker on similar pieces such as straddle, swaddle, paddle, cradle, madden and Saddam, and on other horse-riding or straddling terms (stirrup, astride, bridle).

Word pieces containing the letter sequence "add"/"addle", strongest for "saddle"/"saddled"/"saddening" (also Saddam, Saddleworth, straddle, swaddle, paddle, maddening). Weak activation on similar-sounding fragments like astride, buckle, ashtray.

19006.name: A diffuse, weak feature tied to document structure in encyclopedic or wiki-style text. It fires most strongly on wiki boilerplate and lead-sentence phrasing ("From The … Wiki⏎⏎The", "Not to be confused with", "also known as", "Jump to navigation / search"). More commonly it fires weakly on transitions between sections: sentence-final periods followed by paragraph breaks, header and title boundaries, and the first token after a heading.

1902.name: Fires on the first token of a document and, most strongly, on the first break after the opening title or header line: the newline, comma or space that ends a headline, file header or shebang. It also fires on tokens whose next token is nearly certain, such as " don" before 't, "201" or "200" before a year digit, " able" before "to", " such" before "as", "Figure " or "Chapter " before a number, and "utf-" before "8".

A position-based latent with no consistent meaning. It fires moderately on the very first token of a text and peaks on one token shortly afterward, usually within the first several tokens. That peak token is typically a function token such as a period, comma, newline, space or "the", regardless of content or language.

1922.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires at the end of a multi-token term or name, such as the head noun of a compound phrase after a rare or technical modifier ("schedule", "Environment", "framework", "effect", "option") or the final subword of a split word ("ging", "escence"). It also fires on the punctuation, parentheses or newlines that close that phrase. In short, it marks phrase-boundary completion rather than any particular meaning.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature active on garbled, incoherent or degenerate text, such as mixed-language fragments, nonsense pseudo-code, repetitive token loops and broken markup. It fires weakly across many tokens. The strongest activations tend to fall on punctuation, delimiters, colons, closing brackets and line breaks that end a fragment.

1929.name: A weak, diffuse feature spread across ordinary running prose. It shows no single lexical trigger and mostly fires on function words, clause boundaries (commas, periods, "but", "however", "that", "which"), and the content words that continue a clause. It is strongest mid-sentence in expository or narrative text, where the next phrase elaborates, contrasts, or adds a result (e.g., "result in", "contribute to", "downside of").

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across long runs of ordinary tokens (function words, nouns, punctuation, code) rather than on any specific word. It is strongest in rambling, semantically incoherent or machine-generated-sounding text, where sentences are grammatical but lose meaning (for example "outcomes befall as a result of human-cetera interaction"). It also appears on garbled code and mixed-language snippets.

19364.name: Tokens marking the start of a new question, problem, or list item, typically after a line break or numbering. These are numerals and their following period or colon, bullets, and the first words of a question or problem statement (e.g., "What/Which/How/Is", "A", "If", "Consider"), common in quiz, homework and Q&A text.

The opening token of a new item, entry, or segment, typically right after a paragraph break, a list/question number ("2.", "Problem 2.", "Q:") or another separator. It fires most strongly at the start of numbered questions, exercises and problems ("A person travels...", "You are shrunk...") and on the numbering itself. The activating words are mostly function words or sentence-starters such as The, A, How, There and I.

19396.name: Tokens that close off a formatting or separator element, often fused with a newline: the final dashes, hashes, quotes or comment markers of a divider, banner or header line (e.g. -----, ####, //, ''', -->), and line breaks after such lines. This fires mostly in code comments, markdown and tables. Weak, scattered activations also appear on stray tokens in prose.

19434.name: Tokens immediately after a newly introduced term, name, or acronym (often technical, quoted, or parenthesized), at the point where its definition or description begins. Typical spots are a closing parenthesis or quote, a relative pronoun like "which"/"who", or a copula such as "is a"/"are".

19562.name: Weak, diffuse activation on phrases that describe what something can do or enables: its capabilities, advantages, uses, or functional properties. Typical cases are "can slow down... and sort on any field", "capable of reaching an enormous amount of users", "the ability to manage", "which let you control" and "starts up from rest". Activation is strongest on verbs and prepositions of capability or action and their objects, often in lists of benefits or features.

19631.name: The base quantity or denominator in a rate or ratio expression, typically a round number (100, 1,000, 10,000, 1) or unit word (dollar, thousand, kW) following "per", "for every", "each", or "/". Strongest on "100" in phrases like "for every 100 people" or "per 100 grams".

1969.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature on formatting and separator tokens rather than words. It fires mostly on the space before a number ("January 1995", "n = 3"), decimal points and digit chunks inside numbers, DOIs and IDs, and on paragraph breaks or punctuation at section boundaries. The strongest activations are in numeric tables, equations and headings.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires most clearly in numeric contexts. It peaks on the space token before a number (e.g. 'last 26', 'the 762'), on hyphens in scores and vote tallies (53-46, 3-0), and on thousands-separator commas (26,616). It also fires sporadically and weakly on unrelated tokens.

19721.name: Bodily functions and their disorders, chiefly digestion and elimination: bowel, constipation, fiber, bloating, digestive tract, bladder, insomnia, secretion and congestion. Strongest on constipation, fiber and bowel. It also fires weakly on related ideas of flow, blockage or release in non-medical settings, such as clogging drains, stagnant energy and releasing tension.

Words about digestion and bowel function, firing most on constipation and laxatives, then on intestines, bowel habits, digestive disturbances and urination. Weaker activation on other bodily-function or body-care terms involving blockage, release or clearing, such as flossing, exfoliation, clogging, cleansing, cramping and stiffness.

1976.name: Abstract, purpose- or benefit-oriented phrasing typical of mission statements, marketing, and formal expository prose. It is strongest on extended clauses describing goals, capabilities, and outcomes, such as "to help you…", "enabling X to deliver…", "emphasize the importance of…", or lists of verbs like "manage costs, mitigate risks, and maintain…". Activation is spread across whole clauses rather than single words.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that spans whole stretches of generic, abstract, buzzword-heavy explanatory or corporate prose, such as mission statements, lists of services, benefits, processes and goals (e.g. 'create safer cars', 'protection of… promotion of…', 'Planning, Budgeting, and Project Execution'). It peaks on polished, formulaic phrasing and fires weakly on scattered tokens in incoherent, mixed-language or garbled synthetic text.

19762.name: A diffuse feature active across source code and technical/mathematical text, peaking in machine-learning and statistics code and prose (building or returning a model, activation functions like sigmoid, loss and likelihood functions, logistic regression, fitting and predicting). It fires mostly on structural tokens: indentation whitespace, line breaks, closing parens or braces, "=" assignments, "def"/"self", and variable names. Elsewhere it shows only weak, scattered activation on ordinary words.

19764.name: Connectors placed between personal names in author lists and citations, mostly "and"/"&" (also commas) right after a surname and before the next author's name. Activation is strongest in in-text academic citations such as "(Xiong and Kupski, 1999)" or "Lavidor and Ellis".

19770.name: Restrictive or exclusive focus words, mainly "only" (strongest when "Only" starts a sentence, e.g. "Only those" or "Only now"). They also fire on the determiner or quantifier that follows, such as "only the" or "only a few". Activation is weaker on related limiting or exceptive words like "except", "unless", "not until", "even" and "anything but".

The restrictive/limiting focus word "only" (strongest when it starts a clause, e.g. "Only then" or "only the"), plus the tokens right after it. Weaker hits fall on similar limiting words ("just", "merely", "not every", "even") and on the word following "only" or "just".

19786.name: The word "future" and its variants (futures, futurist, futuristic, Tomorrow), including capitalized names. Activation is strongest on financial "futures" and "futurist", and weaker on everyday uses such as "sustainable future" or "future-proof".

19914.name: The word "cell" (also cells/cellular, "Cell" capitalized, or as a fragment like sub-cell-ular) in biological contexts. It is strongest when "cell" acts as a noun modifier in compounds such as cell death, cell division, cell contact, cell cycle and cell viability. Related biological units (neuronal, plant, brain, particle) activate weakly.

The word "cell" (usually singular, lowercase), strongest in biological contexts, especially as a modifier in compounds like cell death, cell growth, cell culture, cell function and cell biology. It fires weakly on "cells", on non-biological senses (cell phone, prison cell, the place name Cellardyke), and on a few other nouns that modify a following noun, such as "plant growth" and "company voluntary".

19927.name: Sentence-ending punctuation fused with line breaks (".⏎⏎", ".⏎", "?⏎⏎") and bare paragraph breaks, firing most strongly at abrupt boundaries in spammy, incoherent or auto-generated web text where the next line begins an unrelated heading, ad or topic.

Sentence- and paragraph-ending boundaries (periods, newlines, especially ".

" and "

") in low-quality, spammy or incoherent web text (SEO/casino/pharma spam, machine-generated gibberish), firing where the text abruptly switches to an unrelated sentence, heading, or boilerplate. Strongest after nonsensical sentences.

Sentence- or line-ending punctuation and newline breaks (especially ".\n\n") that close off a segment in incoherent, spammy or keyword-stuffed web text (SEO spam, casino ads, gibberish), right before an abrupt shift to an unrelated topic or heading. Weaker activations land on other boundary tokens such as runs of spaces, closing brackets, and menu or boilerplate words.

19993.name: Word-internal subword fragments, usually mid-word pieces right after the first token, in rare or unfamiliar words split into several tokens: proper names, foreign-language words, technical terms, acronyms and misspellings. The word's identity is not yet determined at that point.

20012.name: Scientific and technical process descriptions, mainly physical or chemical, that involve supplying, moving or treating substances. It responds most to phrases about introducing gases, reagents or particles into a system, such as feeding a hydrocarbon gas or admitting gases. It also responds to related process vocabulary like temperature, transport, solutions, baths, material removed from surfaces and dissolving agents.

2002.name: Later items in enumerated lists or series (comma/and/or-separated, or run-on menus and tags): the final items, the separators and conjunctions leading up to them, and the closing element of the enumeration. Activation rises toward the end of the list.

20032.name: Separators and connectives that come right after a negative or lower-bound number and lead into the next value. These include range words such as "to" and "and", commas, semicolons, inequality signs, and LaTeX integral bound markers like "}^{". Activation is strongest for range expressions running from a negative number to a positive one, e.g. "-5° to 36°" or "-1,1".

20047.name: Opening delimiters that begin a value right after a key or assignment, e.g. an opening quote following '=' or ':' in code, config and JSON/YAML (sometimes '{' or '['), and opening <td>/<th> tags that start an HTML table cell.

20089.name: Words for soft, moldable, kneadable substances, chiefly "dough" (including "dough" within doughnut, sourdough, and the name Dougherty), along with batter, crust, clay, slurry, pulp, papier-mâché and paste. The "kne" token of knead/kneel also activates. Activation is strongest on "dough" in baking contexts.

20095.name: Punctuation or spacing immediately following a weekday name in date headers/timestamps (the comma after "Monday", "Friday", etc., or the space after "Tuesday,"), typically right before the day/month in blog or article dateline metadata; weakly also "Posted on"/"Updated:" lead-ins to dates.

20149.name: Negation tokens ("not", "n't", "neither", "non", "no longer", "un-") and, more weakly, the verb or condition word where a state is being checked or failing. These usually fall in descriptions of conditions or outcomes such as a file not being linked, something that wouldn't fit or work, "if not given", or "check whether X is".

20223.name: Contexts about layoffs, job cuts and cost-cutting (e.g., 'pink slips to employees', 'laid-off workers', '1,000 employees… affected', reducing waste). Activation peaks on words in these workforce-reduction phrases, such as employees, workers and slips, and on the surrounding function words. Elsewhere there are weak, diffuse activations on ordinary function words in news or expository prose.

20232.name: Positive aesthetic or admiring adjectives (and related nouns/adverbs) such as "wonderful", "beautiful", "lovely", "delightful", "marvellous" and "beauty". The strongest activations are on "wonderful"/"wonderfully", weaker on "beautiful"/"lovely", and weakest on "beauty" used as a product or category noun.

Positive aesthetic/admiring words, chiefly "wonderful" (strongest), "beautiful", "beauty", and "lovely", plus similar terms like "delightful", "amazing", and "magical", used in any context to praise or describe something pleasing.

2025.name: Relational/classifying adjectives (often ending in -al, -ic, -ical, -ological) placed before a noun to specify its domain or type (e.g., financial, legal, optical, emotional, medicinal, political), including word-piece suffixes that complete such adjectives.

2028.name: The preposition "of" (including capitalized "Of" and fused forms like "numberOf"), mostly in noun-phrase constructions that link a head noun to its complement, such as possessive, part-whole, attribute or title relations ("President of", "benefits of", "squares of"). Activation is highest when "of" follows a specific, technical or title-like noun.

The preposition "of" (and its equivalents such as "Of", "-of", or Chinese "的"). It fires most often where "of" links a head noun to its complement ("the Sword of", "a table of", "the odds of"), and also on the "Of" in "Of course".

20314.name: Structural tokens at the start or end of a line that open or close a block or list entry: closing braces and HTML tags in code, indentation before numbered list items, section/chapter headers, and labels preceding a colon. The common thread is boundaries in structured text, where the token marks a transition between elements.

20317.name: Legal entity suffixes that end company names, chiefly "LLC" (strongest, especially after a comma or in copyright, applicant and manufacturer lines). "GmbH" and other forms such as L.L.C., PLLC and PLLP activate more weakly.

20351.name: The first word of a message string, most strongly when that message is an error, warning, or status report. This shows up in program output and code string literals (print, log, and raise calls), and in log or error lines just after a colon. The strongest cases are error-description words right after an error prefix, like "Specified driver could not be loaded", "Unrecognized", "No suitable", and "No issue". Weaker activations land on sentence-initial words of notices or list items.

20352.name: Word-internal subword fragments in unusual or rare words, such as names, URLs, domain names, code identifiers, acronyms and technical terms. The fragment usually sits mid-word, where tokenization splits the word at an unnatural point that is not a morpheme boundary, and the word continues after it. Examples include 'pag' in pagelines, 'ib' in Unibet and 'fs' in rsfsocialfinance.

2044.name: Fires on unnatural, low-quality or garbled text. It is strongest in spun, machine-generated word salad and essay-mill prose, where it covers long runs of incoherent phrasing. It fires weakly on isolated anomalies such as typos, wrong word forms ("critical acclaimed", "filling to", "there me"), odd fragments and artifacts like "[email protected]" or mojibake.

Fires on incoherent, garbled or machine-spun text (word salad, SEO spam, gibberish identifiers), marking tokens that don't fit their context semantically or grammatically. It is strongest on long runs of fluent-sounding but nonsensical prose.

20458.name: Words in decision, approval or voting actions, especially verbs like approved, voted, signed into law, allow or permission and the prepositions or "to" that follow them, right before the object of the decision. Activation peaks on official approval by a governing body ("commission approved to").

Words describing a decision or official action by an authority, board, council, court or voters, especially "approved", along with words like "voted to", "decided to", "consider", "reject", "support", "grants" and the prepositions or articles that introduce the thing being acted on (a measure, budget, plan, project).

20517.name: Opening punctuation or markup tokens (quotes, brackets, asterisks, #, parentheses, HTML tags) placed right before the first word of a title, heading, quotation, or other delimited span. These usually appear at the start of a line or after a colon or label.

20563.name: Object pronouns (him, them, me, us, you, it, herself), and occasionally nouns that refer back to one, placed right after a verb or preposition. They point to a previously mentioned person or entity, usually one receiving the action (e.g., "given to us", "betray him").

20613.name: Placeholder or toy values in code, math, and examples. These are typically the first in a sequence: single-letter variable names (a, x, A), sample literals (1, 'a', "hello", 'bob'), and first elements of arrays or tuples. They appear in demo code, function parameters, and abstract statements ('state A', 'if A ⊢ B').

20628.name: Function words and punctuation that come right after a topic's subject or title is introduced, usually at the start of a definition or description ("X is a…", "X refers to…", "X has…", a comma or period closing the first descriptive clause). It fires on the verbs, relative pronouns, commas and periods that build an expository opening sentence about a named entity or term, often one just given as a heading.

Function words and punctuation immediately following a just-introduced topic or entity name (usually right after a title or heading), especially the copula/verb that begins its definition or description ("X is a…", "X has…", "X (also known as …) is"). It also fires on the commas and periods that end such introductory, encyclopedic statements.

20631.name: Volume numbers in bibliographic or serial citations: the word "volume"/"Vol." and especially the number (plus surrounding period, space, comma) that follows it. Weaker activation for similar part, season, issue, edition, or book numbers in a sequence, and for the word "volume" meaning a book.

20653.name: A weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on discourse connectives and formulaic multi-word phrases that link clauses, such as "on the other hand," "moreover," "however," "then," "in such a way that," "at the time of" and "further I will." It is strongest at the completing word of a fixed expression, for example "hand" in "on the other hand." It appears especially in SEO-style, promotional or non-native web English. It also fires on transliterated Hindi/Urdu words and scattered sentence-ending punctuation.

Markers of Indian/South Asian English: characteristic phrasings and non-native constructions (e.g. 'on basis of', 'keeping in view', 'as per your requirement', 'till date', 'as compared to', 'since…, so', redundant 'then' after 'if', 'etc'). It also fires on South Asian names, terms and contexts (Singh, Jhabak, garam masala, Rs., Sri Lanka, Delhi '011' phone codes).

20657.name: Words or symbols that link two quantities in a rate or ratio, mostly "per" (miles per hour, cost per click). It also fires on "/", "to" (debt to EBITDA), "vs", "in", "on" (return on investment) and "Per" in identifiers like samplesPer. Activation is strongest for "per" following a measured quantity.

20814.name: Units of measurement and quantity labels that come right after numbers, especially scientific or technical units (mol, mL, A, J, GB, g, oz, rpm). Activation is strongest on the unit token and often carries onto the slash or "per" of a compound rate unit (mol/m², mL/min, flops/MB). Weaker activations fall on counted nouns after numbers and on parts of ratio or fraction expressions in math and code.

20924.name: Terms for health and well-being outcome measures, peaking on "quality of life" (especially "life") and its abbreviation QoL. It also fires on related outcome constructs and instruments (disability, health perceptions, EQ-5D, QALY, VAS), on parts of similar acronyms like QoS/QoE, and weakly on scattered other tokens.

21011.name: Nouns for a gathered group or assortment of items, chiefly "collection"/"collections", plus related words such as selection, compilation, catalog, archive, library, range, variety, collector, treasure, and curated. Activation is strongest for "collection" itself, especially for museum, library or artist collections and in the phrase "collection of".

Collective nouns for a group of gathered or owned items, chiefly "collection" (strongest, especially a personal or museum collection), plus near-synonyms such as selection, set, line, range, fleet, library, archive, stash and assortment, often followed by "of" plus the items.

21022.name: Diffuse, weak activation across technical/scientific and product-description prose about devices, materials, light and energy. It fires mostly on function words and descriptive tokens in phrases that characterize a device's or material's properties and performance, such as high brightness, low power consumption, long-lived, perfectly sinusoidal output, and does not suffer from. It is strongest in LED/lighting and efficiency descriptions.

21037.name: Weak, diffuse feature that mostly fires on prepositions linking a noun or verb to what follows, especially Latin/Romance-like "p"-words (par, por, per, pers, prom, porcelain) and also by, through, of, for. It is strongest on French "par" and Spanish "por" meaning "by/via". There are occasional weak hits on word fragments and paragraph breaks.

21065.name: The determiner (mostly "the") right after a role or affiliation phrase like "director of", "member of", "spokesman for" or "scientist at", introducing the organization, institution or group a person belongs to or leads. It fires most strongly in "head of the" and "co-chair of the" titles.

Determiners (mostly "the", sometimes "a" or possessive "'s") that introduce an organization, institution, group or body after a role or membership phrase, e.g. "president of the", "member of the", "spokesman for the", "head of the". Activation is strongest after leadership or role titles followed by "of".

21066.name: Tokens describing or attaching to institutions and organizations (especially universities). The strongest activations fall on clauses, parentheticals and prepositional phrases that add affiliation, location or descriptive detail about an institution, such as "which has affiliation with", "(formerly", "located in", acronyms in parentheses, campus suffixes, and URL or email domain parts. Activation is weak on generic function words elsewhere.

21114.name: Fires on the predicate words of a clause about the remaining or alternative part of something previously described, such as "the rest", "others", "the balance", "otherwise" or "additional components". These clauses contrast that part with the main case. Activation is strongest right after such remainder subjects (e.g., "the rest failed", "others is called insolence", "the balance could be taken from", "other problems simply seemed to be exaggerated") and weak elsewhere.

21151.name: Clause-boundary punctuation and connectives (commas, periods, dashes, parentheses, semicolons, 'which', 'and', 'It') placed right after a complete statement or noun phrase, where the text is about to continue with an elaboration, explanation, or example of what was just said.

21166.name: The final token of a function, method, command or operator name right before its arguments are applied, usually the last subword of an identifier right before an opening parenthesis (e.g. make_feed_request(, url_for(, add(). This also covers math functions and operators acting on operands (f(x), ReLU(x), \div, ->, *().

21199.name: Tokens at the start of, or linking to, a second parallel element that mirrors an earlier phrase with a variation, such as an alternate in parentheses, the second item of a pair or list, a repeated field label, or code lines repeating a prior pattern. The feature anticipates the text echoing a previous structure ("old and my new", "Min… ⏎Volume Range Max", "(maybe Ie7)", "die… open(").

A diffuse feature with no single topic. It fires on function words, connectives (and, to, for, unless, plus) and sentence or line-break punctuation at clause boundaries. It is strongest where the text sets up a parallel, contrastive or repeated structure that echoes earlier wording, such as 'origin and destination', 'not my favorite books', 'carrier sheet', 'compare them to the same edges' and 'second-to-last dimension'.

21288.name: Closing delimiter tokens that end a nested or paired span, most strongly doubled closing braces "}}" in LaTeX subscripts, \text{}, \frac, \sqrt and template expressions. It fires more weakly on other closers: markdown bold "**", closing quotes, generic-type ">>" or ">", ")}", "})" and HTML closing tags.

21291.name: Function words that come right before a name, label, description or quotation is applied to something, most strongly "as"/"as a" after verbs of naming or describing (referred to as, known as, describing it as, called). Also covers similar connectors such as "called", "a" after calls/calling, and the colons, commas and opening quotes that introduce quoted characterizations.

21295.name: Weak, diffuse activation in tense or alarming narrative contexts, peaking on words describing fear, panic, worry or desperation (e.g. 'Panicking I began to try', 'heart dropped as she', 'feared', 'desperate') and on the reaction clauses around them. Elsewhere it fires faintly on function words, commas and verbs in emergencies, illness or death, urgent waiting or rushing.

21374.name: The word "email" (also "e-mail", "Email", "inbox") and related contact or identifier terms such as phone, IP, ZIP and username. It fires most strongly on "email" in form or contact contexts like "your email address", sign-up prompts and registration fields.

21439.name: Nouns and verbs for things a person says, records or produces that can be held against them or used as evidence, such as statements, confessions, testimony, remarks, recorded conversations, communications, photos/images and fingerprints. Contexts are often legal, investigative or reputational. The strongest activations are on confession, statement and self-incriminating phrases like 'incriminate herself'.

21458.name: The start of a second predicate in a coordinated clause: the verb, participle or predicative adjective (often with its preposition, e.g. "consists of", "works as", "ranged from") that comes right after "and", "but" or an auxiliary ("and is", "and was") and continues talking about the same subject without restating it.

The verb, or start of the predicate, in a second coordinated clause whose subject is omitted and carried over from earlier, usually right after "and" (sometimes "and is", "but", or "then"). Examples include "and resides on", "and hosted", and "and is teeming".

2162.name: Numbers in running text, whether written as digits or words (cardinal or ordinal), that give a count, quantity, amount, percentage or ranking. The leading number of a phrase activates most, and statistics such as sports tallies activate strongest.

Cardinal numbers (digits or spelled-out words) used as quantities or counts in running text, especially the first number of a phrase. Activation is strongest for sports statistics and tallies such as scores, vote counts, sacks, touchdowns and saves.

21714.name:
Tokens that close an opening tag or block header and add a line break (e.g. "> ", ""> ", "{ "). They mostly follow HTML opening tags such as , ,
and

, and mark the point where nested child content is about to start.

21723.name: Binary operators (+, -, =, ==, /, ·) in math formulas or code, usually right after a product term or closing parenthesis, e.g. xy + ..., ps-qr, f(z))/. A few weak activations land on other separator tokens such as bullets, periods and commas.

21753.name: Error and failure messages, especially software, system, or network error output such as "failed", "connection refused", "error", "could not be loaded", or "too many arguments", along with error codes and the punctuation inside them. It fires weakly on nearby tokens about things breaking, being rejected, or not working.

21825.name: Nouns naming the features, functions or capabilities something offers, most often a product, software, app or system (e.g. "features", "functionality", "functions", "capabilities", "properties"). Activation peaks on "features"/"functionality" and sometimes carries onto a following "that", "of" or "are".

21836.name: Words and phrases describing conduct, behavior or the manner and course of action: how someone acts, lives or behaves. Examples include the actions people take or avoid, ways or approaches of doing something, staying within or transgressing bounds, and doing right or wrong. Typical cases are 'act and behave', 'walk in the', 'how they live', 'doing nothing wrong', 'in such a way that', 'strategies' and 'trying to be'.

21846.name: Tokens that close a unit, typically right after an enumerated list or series of items: final punctuation, closing brackets/quotes/braces, line breaks, or the word right after the list ends. Activation is weak and diffuse, peaking where a list or bracketed/quoted group closes (")", "\"]", " }").

The token right after a list or enumeration of items ends (closing parentheses or brackets, periods, commas, dashes, quotes, newlines, or a connecting word like 'to', 'as', 'and'), marking where the series closes and the main sentence or structure resumes.

21928.name: Short value-like content tokens in math, code and structured data, such as numbers, single-letter variables, string literals and dictionary keys. They often sit right after =, (, quotes or currency symbols. Many repeat or are determined by earlier context (e.g. a repeated bid amount, a variable or answer value), though there is a weak scattering of ordinary words too.

21945.name: Whitespace tokens (spaces, trailing spaces, newlines and paragraph breaks) that come right after sentence-ending punctuation and mark the boundary before a new sentence, paragraph, heading or list item.

21981.name: Line-break and line-continuation tokens that fall mid-sentence: newlines (and following comment markers like ///, *, //, or indentation) that hard-wrap a sentence before it is finished, often right after a word that needs a continuation (articles, prepositions, adjectives, 'and', 'the'). Strongest when the newline splits a grammatical phrase.

22047.name: Expressions of quantitative comparison or relative magnitude, especially in technical and scientific text. Typical forms are "comparable to", "larger than", "much greater than", "of the same order of magnitude" and "≫". The words "than" and "to" in these comparisons are usually the strongest tokens. Weaker activations fall on nearby size, scale and quantity terms such as widths, intensities and velocities.

22129.name: Templated, machine-generated boilerplate text (citation headers, metadata records, product/listing pages, database-generated sentences), firing on the fixed scaffolding between variable slots: newlines and punctuation that end a filled-in field (name, place, date, number) and the stock template words that follow, such as "She was born", "and arrive at", "followed by", "is".

22201.name: Fires at the end of a sentence's subject noun phrase (often a proper name or organization, especially in headlines and opening sentences) and on the verb or auxiliary that immediately follows it (has, is, are, warns, gives, appears to), i.e. the subject–predicate boundary.

22257.name: Separators (mostly semicolons, also commas, periods, newlines, braces and bullets) that end one field of a document's metadata and begin the next. The strongest cases are the semicolons in academic article history lines ("Received …; Revised …; Accepted …"), especially right after the year of the revised date. Weaker cases mark field boundaries in citation records, copyright/license notices, credit lines and similar boilerplate.

2233.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single trigger word. It fires on the core content of explanatory or defining phrases: the words that say what something is, what it does, or how it works. These phrases typically follow a setup cue such as "i.e.", "that is,", "occurs when", "By that I mean", "governs", "are the", "need to" or "built for". Examples include "an elastic material deforms through a small opening", "how long your armour lasts when" and "do not accommodate naturally the notion of a secret key". Activation is strongest in the middle of such a functional or definitional description, especially on its main noun or verb.

Tokens inside clarifying or definitional phrases that restate or explain what something means or does, typically right after "i.e.,", a colon, an opening parenthesis, or a relative pronoun ("that", "where", "who"). Examples include "relationship is actually linear", "modify the original list" and "how far the object is from the axis". Activation is highest on the core predicate of the explanation, mostly in technical or instructional text.

2239.name: Temporal-perspective words that relate a thing's state to a different point in time than the one being narrated, usually the present or a later moment. The strongest is "now", especially in "what is now" and appositive "now a ...". Weaker ones include "today", "to this day", "later", "eventual", "will become", "still", "current", "future" and "retroactively named".

22433.name: Nouns for external threats or unwanted agents that something defends against, removes or fights off (enemies, invaders, attackers, predators, pests, viruses, disease, asteroids, dust, toxins), usually the object of verbs or prepositions like "against", "combat", "protect from", "remove" or "filter out". It is weaker on other things a system takes in or acts on (food, glucose, sauces, the environment).

Nouns naming the threat, enemy or harmful agent that something defends against, fights, or is protected from (invaders, predators, viruses, foreign substances, enemies, attacks, disease, danger), usually the object of verbs like protect from, stop, fight, kill or intercept. Weak activations appear on unrelated object nouns.

22443.name: Prepositions (mostly "of", "in", "to", "for", "on", "about") that come right after a noun, adjective or verb and introduce a prepositional phrase. Strongest when the phrase ties a head word to a following noun phrase ("members of", "efforts in", "to all"), and it often extends onto a following "the".

22495.name: Boundary tokens that close a title, name, or header-like field in structured or semi-structured text. These are mostly newlines (often double) right after a page/article/namespace/class title or metadata value. Closing HTML tags, quotes, braces, file extensions/domains, and the ' on' after an author name in code headers also fire. The activation marks the end of a label just before new content begins.

22574.name: Tokens right after a 'Returns'/'Output'/'@return'/'Value'/'Result' label in docstrings, API docs, and problem statements, i.e. the colon, newline, indentation, bullet or opening words ('the', 'A', 'Print the single number') that begin the description of what is returned or output. It also fires weakly on commas after sentence-initial words like 'Finally' or 'Eventually' and on similar section-heading punctuation.

22618.name: Tokens that mark conditioning, i.e. what something is computed or evaluated relative to. This covers the conditional bar in probability notation like P(A|B), which activates most strongly, plus similar bars and separators in math or code (restriction, set-builder, random-effect bars, ~). It also covers words like "given (the)", "assuming", "subject to", "constrained", "considering", "based on" and "from".

22756.name: Postal address unit designators that come right before a number, most strongly "PO Box" and its variants (P.O. Box, BP, C.P., GPO Box, CP), plus the following space. Weaker activations occur on similar address labels such as Suite, Room, Apt, #, Street/Highway, and UMR.

22761.name: Language about change or development over time, especially present-perfect phrasing describing how things have shifted, grown, evolved or been transformed since some earlier point. Typical forms are "has changed since", "have grown", "evolved over the years", "huge changes have begun" and "in the meantime". The strongest activations come from explicit descriptions of change since a past reference point. Weaker activations land on scattered nouns and verbs nearby.

22766.name: The "public" access modifier at the start of a top-level type declaration (usually "public class"), typically in Java, placed right after imports, comments or annotations. It is strongest when unindented at the start of a line and weaker for indented C# declarations inside namespaces or "public" inside URLs.

22794.name: Parameter/key names in key=value syntax, mostly keyword arguments in code function calls (e.g. delimiter=, encoding=, fontsize=, cls=) and also BibTeX fields (author=, title=) and URL query keys. Activation peaks on the argument name right before '=', especially after a comma or opening parenthesis.

22854.name: Statement-terminating tokens in code, typically closing parentheses, semicolons or brackets fused with a newline (");⏎", ";⏎", "))⏎"). They most often end the last statement inside a block, right before a closing brace or dedent (e.g., after error handling, throw/exit/fail calls). Weaker activations appear on similar line endings in HTML tables and Python.

22856.name: Words that name a particular time point when something happens, mainly "day" (also night, year, hour, date, holiday names like Christmas Eve or Thanksgiving), typically in phrases like "the same day", "that day", "launch day" or "the night before" that anchor an event to a specific occasion.

Words naming a specific day or point in time, mostly "day" (strongest in "same day", "first day", "that day", "Christmas day"), plus related time units and occasions such as night, morning, week, year, date, today, and holidays. It also fires on date fragments like ordinal suffixes and day numbers, usually within time-reference phrases such as "on the ___ of".

22878.name: Tokens in academic, scientific, or technical prose that mark scholarly discourse: research and expertise vocabulary (theory, method, study, explanation, foundations, perspectives, expertise), researcher actions (we prove, argue, uncovered, solve this problem), and citation or reference formatting such as titles in quotes, journal abbreviations, and citation counts.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in technical, academic or methodological contexts, such as text about research, engineering, models, theory, scientific methods and expert explanations. It tends to activate near words like 'models', 'sciences', 'theory', 'engineers', 'research', 'technical' and 'proof and simulation', and on function words inside those passages. It is driven by the expert or scholarly register of the surrounding text rather than by any specific word.

2289.name: Words expressing attempt, effort, ability or goal toward an action, most often the infinitive "to" after verbs like try, able/unable, managed, working, aim, along with "can", "if you can", and "as ... as possible". The common thread is striving or capacity to accomplish something.

22978.name: Punctuation and connectors inside taxonomic author citations that follow scientific species names, such as the comma or space before the year, the closing parenthesis or period after an abbreviated author name, and joiners like '&', 'et', or 'ex'. It fires weakly on similar separators in ordinary author-year literature citations.

23033.name: Words inside natural-language explanations embedded in technical or code contexts, firing most strongly within code comments (e.g. after //, /*, #, <!--) and descriptive identifiers such as test method names. Activation is weak and diffuse in ordinary prose.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single token trigger. It fires on scattered mid-sentence words, mostly content words and function words inside explanatory or instructional prose. The text is typically technical documentation, code comments, recipes, how-to steps, notes and forms, and the tokens usually fall within phrases describing what something does or what to do.

23058.name: Tokens at the start of a new sentence or clause, mostly the opening words of a statement such as "There are", "Most of us", "While", "Although you may", "As" and "In the case of". These framing phrases set up a general claim or the next point in expository prose, often right after a period or paragraph break.

2308.name: Symbolic operators and connector symbols, especially arrows and relational tokens (=>, ->, \to, \rightarrow, >, >=, ±, ×, \circ), along with other special symbols like ©, ####, and emoji. These are tokens linking two operands or marking structure, mostly in code, math/LaTeX, and formatted text; arrows activate most strongly.

23148.name: Relative pronouns (mostly "where", also "which"/"whom") that open a non-restrictive relative clause right after a named place or institution (school, university, city, company). The strongest cases follow educational or employer names, as in biographical text.

2322.name: Nouns (or noun modifiers in compounds) naming the functional role, purpose, use, or domain/sector of something, often following phrases like “used as a”, “as a”, “for”, or “in the”.
