Examples include “tool”, “laboratory”, “food source”, “investment”, “medical applications”, “drinking water”, “training aircraft”, “entertainment world”, and “side dish”.

23262.name: Tokens that come right after a newly introduced named entity, usually a product, system, method, species or acronym, and begin describing it. These are mostly commas, closing parentheses or periods, and verbs like "is"/"was" or relative pronouns like "which"/"that"/"a" that open an appositive or definitional clause. Activation is strongest on the comma or parenthesis right after the name.

23280.name: Line breaks and trailing punctuation (e.g. ".", "!", ")", ";" followed by newlines, and occasionally markers like "###" or "<td") at a boundary where one document, section or list item ends and an unrelated one begins, typically just before a new title, headline or heading.

23415.name: Leading/partial tokens of variable or identifier names in code, especially at the beginning of a line or statement where a previously defined variable is being reassigned or used (e.g., the first subword of a multi-token identifier like "waiting_time", "test_files", "cleanArticleID").

23463.name: Standalone punctuation or symbol tokens, often combined with newlines (e.g. "---", "…", ":", "/", ".", "{"), that act as separators or filler at section and document boundaries. They typically appear where one text segment ends and an unrelated one (a new heading, a scraped fragment, a code block) begins.

235.name: Word-initial fragments, usually capitalized or space-prefixed, that begin a longer word split across tokens, such as name parts (Ver, Char, Mel), abbreviations (Rev., prof., Std) and truncated stems (Ex, dist, rep, def, Comp). Activation sits on the first piece, which predicts the rest of the word; full short words like obj, err and Pro also fire.

Word-initial fragment tokens: the first subword piece of a longer word that is split across multiple tokens (e.g. "param"-etric, "Rec"-all, "Lib"-elle, "Met"-roid, "dir"). They also include truncated identifiers and abbreviations in code (len, int, del, _prod). The feature seems to mark an incomplete word stem that predicts a continuation, and it shows up most in noisy, technical, or garbled text.

23533.name: Punctuation that ends a clause or sentence (periods, commas, question/exclamation marks, colons, dashes, Chinese 。, line breaks). It fires most strongly in non-English text such as German, Dutch, Catalan, Hindi and Portuguese, and at boundaries where the next clause or sentence begins.

23561.name: Statistical labels inside parenthetical results in scientific writing, mainly 'n =', 'P/p =' or 'p <', 'r =', 'OR', 'CI', 'AUC', plus the following '=' or '<' and sometimes the leading '0' of the value. The label letter is the strongest part; weaker hits fall on other labels placed right before a number (level, Km, Rs., table <td> cells).

23582.name: Words that introduce the result or product of a transformation, conversion, reaction or formation: prepositions and verbs such as "into", "to", "to form", "produce", "yielding" and "create" placed right before the resulting substance or form (e.g., "converting X into", "react to form", "reduced to"). Activation is strongest for chemical and physical reaction contexts like "react to form" and "decays to form". Weaker activation falls on list conjunctions joining multiple products.

Words marking the result or output of a transformation, conversion or production process. Most often "into" after verbs like turn, convert, transform or change, but also "to", "as", "produce", "generate", "release" and "get". The word links a source to what it becomes or yields.

2363.name: The negation word "not" (sometimes "Not" or, weakly, similar words like "never", "even", "without") when it stands without an auxiliary verb and negates a phrase, clause, or contrast. Typical cases are "not only…but also", "but not X", "not just", "not least", and sentence-initial "Not". Activation is strongest at the start of sentences or clauses, and weak when "not" simply follows "is" or "has".

23731.name: The word "victim" and its forms (victims, victimhood, Victim No.), usually as a noun for a person or thing harmed by crime, disaster, attack, disease, hacking or predation. A following "of" gets weaker activation. Related roles like prey, survivors, sufferers, casualties, perpetrators and beneficiary activate weakly, as does the name fragment "Vict" (Victor).

23737.name: Technical terms for operations, transformations or mappings applied to something (function, operation, unitary transformation, map, gate, transition probabilities, update, applying), strongest in math notation defining a function "f: X \to Y"; weak elsewhere in technical/code text.

23738.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on mid-phrase continuation tokens such as prepositions, verbs after a subject, the second word of a compound noun, word-suffix pieces, and code or LaTeX syntax fragments. These appear mostly in technical, code, math or documentation text. The strongest activation is on the second word of a short label inside code ("Front End" in a print call).

23762.name: Place names, mostly cities, towns and neighborhoods. Activation falls on the token that completes the name, often a suffix fragment such as "ington", "ville", "ley" or "burg", or the second word of a multiword name like Santa Barbara or Orland Park. These names usually appear in addresses, datelines or institutional affiliations.

Place names, mostly cities and towns (often US college or mid-sized towns), with activation landing on the token that completes the name, such as the final subword or the second word of a multi-word name (e.g. "ston" in Evanston, "Haven" in New Haven). Activation is strongest in locative contexts like "in X" or "based in X". It occasionally also fires on venue names, university domains and person names.

23827.name: Administrative boilerplate covering access, permissions, contact details and usage terms: tokens in instructions about whom to contact, how to obtain or use material (accounts, licenses, membership, availability, restrictions), and disclaimers or correspondence notes. Activation is strongest on directive phrases like "are required to contact" or "are urged to consult".

Words in formal boilerplate or notice-style text about access, availability, permission, restrictions and contact procedures (e.g. 'available from', 'contact … by writing to', 'requires a special permit', 'may not be copied', 'with permission'). They are mostly function words and predicates that link a resource to how, where or under what conditions it can be obtained or used.

23851.name: Words for travelling to, visiting, attending or staying at a place or event, such as visit/visiting, trip, journey, travel, stay, attend and "you're in [place]". It fires most strongly on "visiting" and attendance or stay phrases. It also fires weakly on related activity nouns like purchase, sale, ride and experience.

23896.name: Opening punctuation that starts a citation or source attribution right after a quoted or stated claim, mostly " (" before author/page/verse/source references, plus "[" for numbered footnotes, "Source:" colons, and numbering periods or braces in reference lists.

23943.name: Separators that come right after a URI scheme or resource prefix, mostly "://" (http, https, ftp, s3, postgresql, res, gs). Also fires on related prefix delimiters: ":" in jdbc:/dbi:/jar:/steam:, "mailto:", and "\\" or "//" at the start of a path. Activation is strongest for less common schemes such as postgresql, res, ftp and s3, and weaker for ordinary http/https.

23998.name: Hyphen/minus/dash characters and tokens naming them, usually as literal symbols in code strings, math, identifiers or separators (e.g. '-', "--", -*-, minus sign). The strongest hits are words for such punctuation ("hyphens", "hyphenated", "underscores"), with weaker hits on related naming conventions like snake_case and camelCase.

24029.name: The comma (or semicolon) right after a surname in inverted "Surname, Given-name" form, as in author lists, citations and bibliographies. It also fires weakly on other separators after a leading name or term ("Place, Region", "Term, qualifier").

Commas placed right after a surname (often an unusual or foreign one) in "Lastname, Firstname" inverted order, as in author lists, citations, bibliographies and obituaries. Sometimes the following initial or first-name token fires instead, and weakly the comma after a place name or other proper noun.

24051.name: Fires on text about visual formatting and layout of web pages and documents: CSS properties such as font-size and px values, HTML header and h1 tags placed at the top of a page, colors, typography size and image dimensions. The strongest activations come from descriptions of where or how titles and headers are styled or positioned. Weaker, scattered activations fall on markup and code syntax and on assorted function words.

24139.name: A standalone space token that sits right before a number (a year, address number, ID, count, time, percentage, list index), usually following a comma, colon, dash, slash or the end of a name or title. It also fires on the leading space before bullet points or list items in metadata-like text such as citations, addresses, dates and listings.

24140.name: Variable or symbol references in math expressions and code, especially a variable appearing again after it was already used (e.g. the x in “x = 0.6x”, “2x”, “self”, array indices). It fires most strongly on single-letter variables that follow a coefficient or operator. Weaker activations fall on pronouns and determiners that refer back to an earlier subject.

24345.name: The direct object (usually a noun or noun phrase) that immediately follows a transitive verb, especially gerunds and imperatives, as in UI commands and titles, e.g. 'Transfer money', 'measuring gamma rays', 'Engineering enzyme', 'cooking dinner', 'Stop leak'. The activation is on the object token(s), not on the verb.

24439.name: Words about explaining or accounting for something, giving a cause or reason for a phenomenon. "explain" is the strongest, especially after modals or hedges ("may explain", "partly explain", "would explain"). Related forms ("explanation", "explained"), "account for", "understand", "makes sense", "reason" and "why" activate more weakly.

24441.name: Binary operators that combine sets or functions, mostly set intersection: the LaTeX \cap token (strongest), the ∩ symbol, and the words "intersection" and "union". Weaker activations go to related operators such as \cup/∪, \circ (function composition), ∧, Python & between sets, and .intersection. Isolated non-math tokens (e.g. "Pages", "the") activate only faintly.

24442.name: Separator tokens (colons, equals signs, opening quotes or braces, spaces) right after a property, parameter or field name and just before its value is written, especially color values in CSS, plotting and code (e.g. 'color:', "col = '", 'background-color: #'). It also fires more weakly on the space before a number in prose.

24448.name: The final token(s) of long alphanumeric strings such as IDs, hashes, URL shortener codes, hex addresses, part/serial numbers and numeric values. The activation lands on the last chunk of these random-looking sequences, right before a delimiter like a slash, quote, newline or space.

245.name: Weak, diffuse feature on the token immediately following a number or completed noun phrase, usually a connector or separator leading to the next item: range and comparison words ("to", "and", "than", "more"), math operators (+, =, ×, )/( ), dashes, spaces, commas, newlines, and units. It is most common right after numeric values in ranges, equations, dates and measurements.

Separator or connector tokens that come right after a number (or a numeric or other item) and link it to a following value. Typical cases are hyphens, dashes, slashes, plus signs, ±, commas and line breaks in scores, records, ranges, page spans and table cells, e.g. 3-0, 15 - 10, 9st 4lb / 130lb. Weaker activations fall on short words that play the same linking role after an item (in, and, at, than, for).

24573.name: Content of formal, journalistic or official-report prose, especially clauses reporting attributed claims or findings about government, military, intelligence or security actions (e.g. sources saying an attack was intended to cause harm, that malware was used against agencies, or that officials attempted/created a program). Weaker activation is spread across function words in similar documentary/historical report text.

24647.name: Number chunks (usually three-digit tokens like "000", "130", "700") inside the suffix of DOI identifiers. They tend to fall in the middle of the article number after the journal or year prefix, not at the start or end.

24660.name: Terms for biological or physical specimens collected for testing or analysis, chiefly "blood" and "samples" (blood tests, blood work, serum, saliva samples, specimen, biopsy, tissue, swab), plus verbs of collecting or sampling. Activation is strongest on phrases like "blood samples" and "saliva samples".

24738.name: The "pom" letter sequence across words and languages: whole tokens like "pomp" (pompous), "Pom" (Pomodoro, Pompidou, pom-pom) and Czech/Slavic "pom" (pomalu, pomáhají), plus "om/ome/omer/um" pieces right after a split-off "P/p" (Pompeo, pomegranate, Pomeranz, pummeled). Activation is strongest on "Pom"/"pom" tokens.

Word-piece tokens for the sound "pom"/"om" (and similar "um"/"omm"), mostly right after a "P" (or L/G) at the start of a word. Activation is strongest for a capitalized " Pom" opening a proper noun (Pomona, Pomsky, Pompidou, Pomodoro, Pomc) and for "Pompe"/"pomp", and weaker for mid-word fragments like p-ome-granate, p-um-meled, L-om-ax and G-om-el.

24740.name: The letter pair "GL" (any casing or prefix: " GL", ",GL", "/GL") as a token, nearly always in an uppercase acronym, abbreviation or code: GLP, GLUE, GL(n) groups, GLaDOS, GLA, postcodes, IDs and random strings. It is strongest when GL begins an acronym or follows an opening parenthesis. There is weak firing on similar tokens such as "GH" and "gh".

24747.name: The subword token "uz" (and close variants such as "Suz", "Luz", "uzz", "z"), mostly found inside proper names and foreign words like surnames, place names and brands (Suzuki, Soyuz, Fuzhou, Kreuz-). Activation is strongest when it falls mid-word in an unfamiliar name.

The subword "uz" (and close variants like " Luz", " Suz", "uzz", "z", "Z", "ž", Cyrillic "з") appearing inside words, mostly proper nouns such as surnames, given names and place names (e.g. Kuznets, Guzman, Luzon, Suzie), plus slang spellings like "cuz"/"duz".

24819.name: The category noun (head of a reference class) in classifying or superlative statements like "the most common X", "one type/form of X", "X% of all X", saying where something ranks within or belongs to a class. It fires most strongly on disease terms, especially "cancer", "tumor" and "malignancy".

24849.name: Job titles and occupational roles, especially the head noun completing a position name after a modifier (e.g., editorial assistant, acquisitions officer, security guard, Audit Senior, DevOps expert), plus occasional work-related nouns or activities.

Job titles, occupations and professional roles, with activation on the head noun or final subword that completes the role (e.g. clerk, driver, designer, attorney, gunner). It also fires weakly on related work or field nouns (management, design, instruction). Activation is strongest in job-posting or hiring contexts.

2485.name: Separators and coordinating conjunctions (commas, "and", "or", "&", "/or", "such as", "including") that join items in coordinated lists or pairs of nouns, especially enumerations of proper names, platforms, or technologies. Activation is strongest late in longer lists, at the final ", and" or "and".

24887.name: A weak, diffuse feature with low activation that does not track any particular word. It fires on tokens inside clauses that express contrast, comparison, negation or evaluation, such as "but we weren't the only ones", "not even", "instead of", "more real than", "easier and more likely", "right or wrong" and "aren't". It also picks up some of the function words that carry these argumentative turns.

24898.name: Words that name an intervention or change in something's presence or level (loss, lack, knockdown, lesions, blockade, addition, overexpression, suppression, removal, deficiency). They usually take an "of" object and set up a cause-effect claim about what that manipulation does, mostly in scientific or experimental writing. The strongest are phrases like "Loss of", "knockdown in" and "blockade of".

24923.name: Subword fragments inside personal names, mostly non-English given names (especially Chinese, Korean, Thai and other Asian names) in author lists and bylines. It fires most strongly on the middle or later pieces of multi-token or hyphenated given names (e.g. "-Ki", "-Ho", "ih", "h").

24931.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on structural boundary tokens where one unit ends and a new one begins: sentence-final periods, paragraph and line breaks, stray spaces, list and line numbers, markdown and closing markup such as ** and , and code delimiters such as ```, $$ or (['. It peaks slightly in code and markup contexts, but overall reflects text-segmentation positions rather than specific meaning.

24954.name: Tokens that are a name or identifier stem immediately preceding an index-like suffix, usually a digit (e.g. value→3, decorator→1, Part→2, R→1, Profile→7), but also Roman numerals, letters or subscripts (Walker B, Science IV, Villa Wagner II, n_i). Common in code variable and function names, labels, part or section numbers and model/catalog codes. The feature anticipates an upcoming number or label.

25058.name: Words that refer back to a set of several items named earlier, often quantifiers or demonstratives such as "these/those", "both/all of which", "respectively", "the two", "each" and "the latter". The activating words are anaphoric or distributive and point to multiple entities already introduced in the text.

25132.name: Tokens inside URLs, file paths and web addresses (domains like .com/.org/.uk, github.com, path segments such as /blob/master, /uploads/2018/05, relative ../ paths), especially image/link sources in markdown or HTML. Strongest on domain names and path components. Weaker hits fall on source or credit attributions (website, publisher or organization names, e.g. 'CBC', 'Facebook', 'Survey').

25173.name: Words for entry points and ways in or through: entrance, entry, gate, door, access, portal, gateway, intake, ingress, mostly physical but also figurative. Activation peaks on "entrance", especially "the entrance (of/to)", and the following "of" or "to" also fires.

Words for entry and threshold points of a place, such as entrance, entry, gate, gateway, door, lobby, foyer, exit, front and access, plus verbs like enter. It is strongest on "entrance", especially "entrance to/of" a physical place like a mine, tunnel, station or restaurant.

25214.name: Initial tokens of proper names, chiefly Scottish/Irish "Mc" surnames and brands (strongest on "McDonald", especially the restaurant chain; also McKinsey, McLaren, McCormick). Weaker hits on other name-start pieces like "Maurit" (Mauritius/Mauritania), Kellogg, Tiffany and Suzuki, and on fast-food words.

Strongest on the name "McDonald", especially the fast-food chain McDonald's, and weaker on other "Mc"/"Mac" surnames (McConnell, McKinsey, McGuire). It also fires on related fast-food words ("fast food", Happy Meal, burger) and on brand or place names that look like surnames (Tiffany, Kellogg, Buckingham, Coventry).

25249.name: Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store"/"stores", plus "shop(s)", "retailer", "bookstore", "supermarket" and Chinese 店. They often follow a modifier naming what is sold (grocery, toy, comic book) or a brand name (Honeywell Store). Activation is strongest for "store", weaker for "shop", and also fires on the idiom "in store".

Nouns for retail establishments, mainly "store" and "shop" (plus plurals and compounds like bookstore, storefront, boutiques, in-store). They cover physical and online stores (App Store, iTunes store), and occasionally storage senses such as evidence stores, ammunition store, or the code term Store/load. Activation is strongest for "store"/"stores" in the retail sense and weaker for "shop".

25260.name: Tokens that begin a continuation line in multi-line math derivations: new display-math openers (\[, $$) or alignment characters (&, &=) and line breaks (\\) immediately after a previous equation closes, usually followed by '=', '\le', '+', or '⇒' chaining the next step.

2528.name: Binary operators and operands inside mathematical or code expressions (=, +, -, %, /, ==, <=, \times, \cap, \implies, closing braces, numbers). It fires at the point where an operation links two terms, including prose phrasing of arithmetic such as "by 2", "from 360" and "60 times".

25328.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on surprising or irregular tokens, typically glued directly onto the preceding text without the expected space. Typical cases are encoding artifacts (Â, â), typos or stray letters (your<<r>>, of<<A>>ustralians), and citation and markup symbols († ~ {{ <p). It also catches code or parameter tokens right after a colon, comma or equals sign, and odd punctuation or whitespace. It reflects broken formatting and unexpected token boundaries rather than any particular meaning.

25348.name: Separator tokens (commas, spaces, newlines, '=', ';', ':', '>' of table cells) in numeric lists, sequences, tables and citations, at the point just before the next number is expected. It fires most strongly in patterned number series such as 1978, 1987, 1996…, where the next value is predictable. Activation is weak on prose lists and other non-numeric text.

254.name: Fires on non-English text (Danish, Dutch, Russian, Greek, Bengali, Japanese, Azerbaijani, Spanish, French, German), mostly on word-continuation subword pieces, inflectional endings and short function words, and most strongly in longer foreign-language passages. It fires weakly on foreign fragments inside English text, such as names ("du Pont de Nemours", "Chateau de"), loanwords and domains, and only rarely and weakly on ordinary English tokens.

Tokens inside foreign-language (non-English) words and phrases embedded in English text, especially Romance or Latin function words and word endings in titles and names (e.g. "de la", "pour le", "come", "en el", Latin inflections). It fires weakly on unusual or all-caps English text.

25411.name: Currencies and foreign exchange, peaking on currency names (dollar, yen, USD, Sterling, Euro) and words like currency, forex, and exchange rates, especially when a currency's strength or value is discussed. Weaker activations fall on related value and conversion words (devaluation, value, converter) and on scattered unrelated tokens.

25621.name: The space (or separator like period, hyphen, "Op.", "of") right after an identifier label and just before its number, e.g. street names, "Suite", "P.O. Box", "RFC", "No.", "Proposition", "Flight", "Op." or grant and patent codes. It fires on the gap that joins a name or category to its numeric designation, mostly in addresses, citations and catalog codes.

25701.name: The boundary that closes a conditional or temporal subordinate clause (if/when/once/in that case/by default/when not needed) and opens the main clause. Most often it is the comma at that point, but it can also be the first word of the consequent, such as "then", "so", "otherwise", "it" or "the". The same pattern appears in other languages, for example Chinese 就 and 时候，. Activation is strongest when the condition has just ended and the result is about to begin.

25706.name: Words about losing a spouse, parent or loved one and the marital or family status that follows, such as widow, orphan, bereaved, mourning, grieving, divorce, single, and phrases like "lost his" or "died when". "Widow" and "orphan" activate most strongly. Weak activations also appear on look-alike fragments ("wid", "Div") and related ideas such as inheritance, succession, vacancy and remains.

25761.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single clear trigger. It mostly fires on syntactic junctures where a sentence pivots into further elaboration or consequence. These junctures include commas, relative "which" and "that", conjunctions such as "and" and "but also", colons, opening quotes and paragraph breaks. It also fires on some head nouns and verbs that introduce such continuations (failure, violation, dedication, aided, commenced). It appears often in news, legal or narrative text, frequently about wrongdoing or its effects.

25776.name: Punctuation or symbol tokens (underscore, $, @, *, /, ., -) that act as a prefix glued to the start of a following identifier, path, handle or word, as in _name, @user, $scope, .NET, /dev, -1. Most common in code, URLs and file paths, and strongest for leading underscores such as ._ and __.

25818.name: The final digit of the DOI registrant prefix (e.g. the last digit in "10.1371", "10.1109", or the "/j" after "10.1016"), i.e. the point where the publisher prefix ends and the slash begins the suffix in DOI citations.

25952.name: The "al" token in "et al." in academic author citations (e.g., "Smith et al. (2010)"). It is strongest when the citation is the grammatical subject of a sentence reporting what the authors did. Weaker activation on other citation markup such as LaTeX \citet/\cite.

25966.name: Language describing selection, qualification, or allocation rules: who or what gets chosen, ranked, or advances (top teams, largest party, most votes, minimum/maximum limits, fractions of a group, candidates picked). The strongest activations fall on ranking and qualifying phrases in electoral, competition, and admission procedures.

260.name: A dense, broadly active feature over ordinary flowing prose (and even code), firing on most content tokens but typically skipping articles and short function words like "the", "a", "and". Activation peaks around sentence and paragraph boundaries, on the opening words of a new sentence or paragraph and on key topic nouns there (e.g. "concept", "mechanism", "variation", "limitations").

A dense, nonspecific feature that fires on nearly every token across diverse text (prose, code, instructions, puzzles, multilingual and garbled text), with notable gaps on articles and short function words like "the", "a" and "of". It peaks on content nouns and verbs that open a new sentence, section or explanation (e.g. "phrase", "dominance", "breakdown", "examples", "Testing").

2602.name: A diffuse feature for generic expository or promotional prose, strongest at the start of a document's body or section (right after a title, heading, or line break) and in summary sentences that define or describe what something is or does (e.g. "X is an online retailer that offers…", "It is essential to…", "These attitudes can vary…"). Weaker activations fall on heading markers, colons, and structural tokens that introduce such content.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires broadly across runs of tokens in LLM-style or synthetic instruction/assistant text: chatbot answers, code with comments, math and word problems, task prompts, and formal explanatory prose. It does not track any particular word. It is somewhat stronger at clause boundaries, punctuation, newlines and transition words (e.g. 'However', 'To get', 'Yes'), and nearly absent in casual human writing.

26026.name: Historical and biographical narration about scientists, inventors and notable figures, with the strongest activations on scientist names and roles, dates and attribution phrases ("discovered", "invented in 1947 by", "developed by", "was first known as") that credit a person with a discovery or achievement. Weak activations are scattered over function words in nearby scholarly or historical text.

26088.name: Word-piece tokens beginning with a consonant cluster plus "re/ren" and ending in "nt" or similar, mostly in proper names and name fragments (Trent, Brent, Brett, Laurent, Trev, Bren, -rent), along with "torrent". Activation is strongest for "Trent" and "Brent".

26097.name: Whitespace and newline tokens (mostly double newlines, sometimes fused with punctuation like ",", "{", ":", "]") that close a header, metadata line, salutation or code declaration and come right before the main body text or code block. Code-fence backticks and markup tokens at the start of a block fire more weakly.

26107.name: Operations that combine or split sequences around a separator. In code this covers join and aggregation calls (.join, StringJoiner, implode, sum, collect, fold, reduce, split, sep=/delimiter=/axis= arguments); the strongest activation is on "join". In prose it covers phrases like "separated by", "separated with" and "with commas" that describe how items are delimited.

26128.name: Words marking the endpoint of a process or movement, such as the final destination, recipient, or end-use stage where something ends up or gets used (e.g., 'before installation', 'prior to utilization', 'distribution to individual people', 'end users', 'to those who need them', 'returned to their homes'). The strongest activations fall on use and consumption stages like installation, utilization and feeding.

26140.name: Words expressing fractions or proportions of a whole (third, half, quarter, fifth, tenth, percent/%), usually after quantifiers like "one", "about", "over", "less than" and followed by "of". Activation is strongest on fraction denominators such as "third" and "fifth"; multiples ("fold", "times", "dozen") fire weakly.

26231.name: Paragraph-break newline tokens (often fused with preceding punctuation like '.', ')', '-*-', '+', '#') that end a header, comment block, license notice, or boilerplate section and come right before a new section. They fire most strongly when the next part is code such as imports, includes, use statements or a function definition.

26308.name: Mostly source code, especially beginner-style or student-written programs. It fires on structural tokens such as declarations (int/String/float, def, class, struct), imports and includes, assignments ('=', '[]'), newlines, indentation and punctuation, with the strongest response on variable declarations and initializations. Weak scattered hits in prose fall on connectives like 'through', 'via' and commas.

26426.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires mostly on function words and punctuation (prepositions like of/at/in/over, articles, commas, periods) right before an upcoming noun phrase. It is strongest when the next words are a specific entity such as a title plus name (President, Gov.), a place, an acronym (HTML, NIL) or a named person. It also fires on subword pieces inside proper names (Chen, Dalberg, Hacohen).

A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single token identity. It fires mostly on function words and punctuation (the, of, to, for, in, commas, periods, 'says') at phrase or clause boundaries. These are typically the positions just before a new noun phrase or named entity, such as a person, organization, place or title, gets introduced.

26446.name: Words for stealing: "theft" (strongest, including split pieces like "the|ft" and "thefts"), "thief/thieves", and weaker hits on "stealing", "burglaries", "shoplifting" and "heist".

Words denoting stealing: chiefly "theft"/"thefts", plus "thief", "thieves", "thievery", "steal(ing)", "shoplifting", "heist", "embezzlement" and "loss" in loss prevention. Literal crimes, identity/data/copyright theft and titles like Grand Theft Auto all count. The plain noun "theft" activates most strongly; verb forms are weaker.

26499.name: Academic degree and graduation contexts, especially the tokens describing when, where, or what degree was earned (e.g., "degree in", "graduated from … in", "for the degree of"). It fires most strongly on the final digit of a graduation or award year ("B.A. degree in 1928"), and weakly on similar completion or award dates and on thesis boilerplate.

26506.name: Words naming a location or site, mostly body parts and anatomical regions (groin, thigh, neck, abdomen, pedicles, epidermal) plus bodily samples (blood, saliva, urine). Activation is strongest where the word gives the place where something is applied, inserted, taken from or felt, often after prepositions like through, from, over or around. Weaker activation appears on geographic places (rural, onshore, New Jersey).

Words naming a physical location or site, mostly body parts and anatomical regions (skin, hand, chest, nose, forehead, artery, finger), usually the object of a locative preposition saying where something is applied, inserted or taken from. Strongest on anatomical phrases in medical or procedural contexts ("the back of a patient’s hand", "transcervical access", "pars plana"). Weaker on non-body locations like a wall, coast or firewall.

26553.name: A diffuse, weak feature found in expository scientific, technical and health writing. It fires on scattered function words, punctuation, list separators and content words, most strongly within explanatory clauses that describe mechanisms, roles or effects (e.g., "nutrients may play a role", "vitamin E utilization", "filters and … technology remove").

26566.name: Scientific measurement and characterization contexts: names of analytical techniques and instruments (spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, SEM-EDS, spectra), phrases introducing how something was measured or confirmed ("carried out by", "evaluated by", "indicated by", "confirmed by"), and labels for physical/chemical property fields in data sheets (pH, density, melting point, properties).

266.name: Words tied to electricity and electromagnetism, firing hardest on "electrical" and "electro-" forms (electronegative, dielectric) and somewhat on magnetic, battery power, wire and similar physics/engineering terms. It also fires weakly and diffusely on scattered technical or scientific words and on loosely related senses such as connection, charge, voting and Magn- word pieces.

26695.name: Fires on tokens in structured data and dataset contexts, such as table markup and cells (HTML td/th, LaTeX tables), CSV filenames and column names, lists of numeric values or categories, and phrases introducing data ("were as follows:"). It is strongest on HTML table tags and cell contents like "Age" and on number sequences in tables or charts.

26728.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (periods, often merged with closing brackets/citation markers or newlines), and occasionally clause-ending commas, that close a descriptive or technical statement, especially in academic or expository writing just before a new sentence or a shift in topic.

2679.name: The attribute name "class" inside HTML/JSX tags (e.g. <div class="...">) is by far the strongest trigger. It fires weakly on related styling and selection words such as style, id, setStyleSheet and getElementsByClassName, on "class" used as a code or programming concept, and on a few scattered unrelated tokens.

26937.name: Words about remembering and honoring people or events, especially "memorial"/"Memorial" (strongest when it is a noun or part of an institution name like Memorial Hospital/Stadium/Library). Weaker on related forms such as commemorate/commemoration/commemorative, monument, remembrance, centennial and "In Memoriam".

26942.name: Tokens within formal proper names of organizations and institutions, especially academic author-affiliation lines (Department/Institute/Laboratory of …, University of …, Academy of Sciences), along with nearby author names, titles, and award or agency names, often in Chinese or East Asian contexts. Activation is strongest on the connecting words and descriptive words inside long multi-word institution names.

26958.name: Tokens that come right before a cited or listed item: opening quotation marks, colons, "like", "namely", "=", bullets, opening parentheses and list commas. They usually follow a metalinguistic or definitional cue ("the word", "the predicate", "misspelled", "Model:") and signal that a specific term, string, value or example comes next. Activation is strongest on opening quotes after "the predicate" or "the word".

Tokens that open a mention of a literal word, phrase, name or value, i.e. where the text starts quoting or citing something as a string rather than using it normally. They are mostly opening quotation marks after words like "word", "the lyrics", "named" or "searched for". Related tokens are colons, slashes, "=" and delimiters that introduce a quoted term, label or field value.

27065.name: The finite verb right after a sentence's subject, nearly always a form of "have" (has/have/had), mostly as a perfect-tense auxiliary ("has found", "have been") but also as possessive "has the right". Sometimes it is a form of "be" or a following "been". The strongest cases follow subjects like "I", "this study/research" or "the undersigned" in reporting or formal contexts.

Perfect-tense auxiliaries ("have", "has", "'ve", and the "been" that follows them) placed right after the subject, where a past participle is coming next (e.g. "we have developed", "Microsoft has released", "has been treated"). Activation is strongest for first-person "I/We have" in reporting or research statements.

Finite verbs (mostly auxiliary "have"/"has"/"'ve", also "had", "were", "been", "made") immediately after the clause subject, typically marking the present perfect or the start of the predicate in a declarative statement (often first-person "I/We have…" reporting actions or findings).

27144.name: Words about processing, transforming or cleaning data (clean, parse, convert, encode, clip, format, hash, anonymize, sanitize, translate, wrap). These appear mostly in code or technical prose, often as method names. The feature also fires weakly on code block endings such as closing braces, parentheses and newlines.

27152.name: Formatting/structural tokens that open a new labeled item in structured documents: markdown bold "**" before Proof/Example/Definition/Figure headings, HTML "<td" opening table cells (esp. in tables of contents or figure lists), list numbering punctuation before "Theorem" entries, and separators like newlines, citation brackets, or "and" right before a theorem/figure/section reference or title.

27193.name: Mostly code. Fires on the token right after a variable, field, or member name: the assignment operator (strongest, especially " =" assigning an object or value such as "= new"), or a member access or method call (.Add, .set, .Size), a colon in struct-field initializers, or a closing bracket. Prose activations are weak and sporadic.

27213.name: Tokens inside structured, list-like or quantitative content, most often numbers, variables and math operators. These include equation steps, prices, dates, units, format specifiers and answer options such as Yes/True/Never. Activation peaks at the start of a new line or item that restates or continues a calculation, e.g. "4x +" or "x > -5".

2726.name: A weak, diffuse feature on ordinary prose tokens (content words, prepositions, commas and periods) within the first sentence or clause after a paragraph break or heading. It seems to track the progression of a new paragraph's opening statement, with mild peaks at clause boundaries and key nouns or verbs rather than at any specific word.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature with no specific lexical target. It fires on ordinary tokens in running prose, mostly in news, informational and descriptive text. Activation tends to land at phrase and clause boundaries: the head noun ending a noun phrase, the preposition or conjunction linking two phrases, and the comma, period or question mark that closes a clause. It is slightly stronger on clause-final punctuation and on key words in the opening statement of a sentence.

27266.name: Short, non-word fragments forming abbreviations, symbols, or code-like identifiers: variable names (h, diff, lr_qi), chemical symbols (Cs, Pb, Ca/Al), acronyms (MF, LAR, FDA, USDT), codon strings (atc, atg), and digit pieces of numbers or dates. They often sit in parallel lists of similar items, and the strongest activations are on single-letter or very short suffixes that complete a compact code.

2727.name: Quantifiers and scope words that set how much of a group is covered, chiefly universal ones such as "all", "every", "any" and "no one". It also fires, more weakly, on other totality or extremity words like "complete", "completely", superlatives and "main"/"primary", and on the nouns they modify. Activation is strongest on "all" and "every" before a noun phrase.

27271.name: The head noun of a clause's grammatical subject, right before its verb (e.g. 'officials talk', 'Google will add', 'the FBI has been'). Activation is strongest for named organizations, institutions, governments and companies acting as agents (Supreme Court, Google, Sony, MTV, Fed, Congress). It also fires on generic subject nouns such as customers, consumers, God, money and teeth.

27302.name: A determiner (almost always "the", sometimes "this"/"an"), usually right after a preposition like "in", "within" or "of", that opens a noun phrase naming a domain, field or sphere of activity (industry, market, realm, world, field, process, area). Activation is strongest when an industry or market phrase follows.

27340.name: A diffuse, weakly firing feature found mostly in technical or scientific explanatory prose (math, physics, computing, cryptography). It lands on mid-sentence function words and connective tokens (the, and, with, of, is the, by, into) and on verbs or nouns that introduce the object of a described operation or process (takes, produce, finding, state, outcome). These tokens tend to sit just before the key object or result, as in step-by-step descriptions of how something is done or transformed.

27345.name: The first token of a multi-token proper noun, mostly place names (towns, regions, islands, institutions, businesses), especially after locative words like "in", "at" or "of the". It marks the start of a rare or foreign name that the tokenizer splits, such as the "Ge" in Geelong or the "Hal" in Halcyon.

2736.name: Fires on the later pieces of multi-token technical names, mostly biochemical ones such as hormones, growth factors, cytokines, vitamins and chemical formulas. It typically lands on a word-internal fragment (lept|in, prol|act|in, interle|uk|in) or on letters and numbers inside an acronym (TGF, HIF, BDNF, SO₄). It is strongest on growth-factor terms ("growth factor", "TGF").

Tokens within names of biochemical molecules (and some other technical terms and acronyms), strongest for inflammatory cytokines and growth factors like interleukins (IL-1, IL-6), tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and growth factors (TGF, IGF), especially the final 'factor', number or letter. It fires weakly on chemical formulas, enzymes and tech acronyms.

Inner or final subword pieces of technical names, mostly biochemical and biomedical (cytokines, drugs, chemicals, vitamins), less often acronyms and technical terms. Activation is strongest for inflammatory cytokine names, especially the 'F' in TNF and the parts of interleukin-6/IL-6.

27361.name: A diffuse, weak feature centred on literalness, identity and sameness: things taken as-is or left unchanged. It fires most strongly on phrases like "matches any literal character" and on immediate or trivial outcomes ("return 500", "starts immediately", "F = 0", "the theorem is trivial"). It also responds to equality and identity expressions ("=1", "equals unity", "the same as", "equal width", "sameRoot") and to echo or unprocessed meanings ("repeat it back", "just copy and paste", "served raw", "face value", "literal translation"). Activations appear in both prose and code or math.

27372.name: Language about collections, repositories and access to stored information or content (archives, libraries, databases, digital records, scanned documents, PDFs, images, datasets), especially phrases describing what a resource contains, provides, or makes available ("access to", "including", "collection of", "available for").

Words about information resources, records and collections and how people access them, such as archives, library items, digital images, documents, files, content and reports, along with verbs like view, access, borrow and redistribute. It is strongest in archival and library contexts (e.g. "free access to high resolution images", "Collection, ARS-0003").

27469.name: Separator tokens (commas, spaces, dashes, pipes, bullets, newlines, tabs, table tags) that sit between items in a list or sequence, such as numbers, names, table cells or list entries. Activation is strongest in long, regular numeric sequences, often toward the middle or later part of the series before the next item.

27490.name:
Formatting and markup tokens that mark a paragraph or section break between sentences, such as HTML tags (

,
,

, ), LaTeX commands (indent, skip), escaped newlines (\r\n, \n), {np} markers, invisible characters and odd whitespace. They usually come right after a sentence ends and before new text starts. Repeated page boilerplate ending a header line (e.g., 'On Air Stations') also fires weakly.

27515.name: Punctuation and structural boundaries in news-style prose, mainly sentence ends and paragraph breaks just before a new sentence starts. By far the strongest hits are dateline punctuation, the ")" and dash after "(AP" that open a wire story. Strong activation also appears on the abbreviation period in "Sept." Weaker hits fall on the period after a quote attribution ("... said.") and on a sentence-final period followed by a blank line.

27607.name: The second quantity or item in a comparison or contrast. The strongest activations fall on numbers, units and amounts that come after words like 'than', 'compared to/with', 'against', 'while', 'vs', 'as opposed to' or 'from…to' (e.g., '$758 million', 'five hours per week', '2mg/dl'). Weaker activations hit other non-numeric terms in that contrasted position.

27638.name: Fires mainly on live code lines that come directly after commented-out code, especially when the active line repeats or replaces the commented version, as in '#filepath2 = …' followed by 'filepath1 = …' or a '//QGridLayout' line followed by 'QVBoxLayout *layout = new …'. Activation peaks on the identifier, assignment and declaration tokens at the start of such lines. Elsewhere there are only weak, scattered activations on miscellaneous code and prose tokens.

27651.name: Placeholder or redacted content standing in for missing, unknown or user-supplied information, such as "YOUR_API_KEY", "<username>", "N/A", "No Data", "TBD", "xxxx", "##", blanks, ellipses, masked digits or censored words.

27656.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear topic. It fires mid-sentence on tokens that complete a predictable collocation, fixed term or multi-token word, such as "threat status", "goals of care", "anticholinergic burden", "Care Programme", "down-grade", "Ghibellines" and "emeritus". These tokens are often the head noun of a phrase or a word-final subword piece. It also fires on some function words in formulaic phrasing like "so that it is" and "want to".

27667.name: Separator tokens immediately preceding a number in structured numeric data, mostly the colon or period between hour and minute in timestamps, plus the space before page numbers in tables of contents, before dates and times, or after an HTML tag that comes right before a number.

27683.name: Words about cost, price and money: "cost", "costs", "-cost", "cost-effective", "price", "cheaper", "inexpensive", "budget", "cash", "profit", "investment". Activation is strongest on "cost" itself, especially in "cost-effective", "reduce the cost of" and "Cost:" labels. Weaker activations come from economic or affordability language and spending idioms such as "break the bank", "bottom line" and "spend on gas".

27778.name: The final digit (or decade-ending 's') of a four-digit year written in pre-2000 form (mostly 19xx, especially 1980s–1990s), completing the year after a tokenized prefix like "199" or "198".

The last digit of four-digit years from the late 20th century (mostly 1980s–1990s, sometimes 1890s), coming right after a "198"/"199" prefix token. It also fires on the "s" of decades like "1980s"/"1990s" and on "90" in "'90s".

27857.name: Leading indentation whitespace (spaces/tabs) at the start of a code line that continues a block of sequential statements at the same nesting level, typically before a new statement; weaker on paragraph/line breaks between items in prose or lists.

27864.name: The speaker in a dialogue attribution: a pronoun or name (often its last subword) right after a closing quotation mark or quoted speech, naming who said the line (e.g. '"...," he said').

27886.name: The demonstrative "this"/"This" used as a determiner or pronoun referring back to, or pointing at, the current document, entity, or previously mentioned item ("this paper/section/state/issue"), typically at the start of a sentence or clause. Weaker activation appears on similar deictic determiners ("the", "your", "present", "here") and on the boilerplate word "Forgot" in "Forgot your password?"

Demonstrative determiners, mostly "this"/"This" (occasionally "these", "your", "our", "his"), placed before a noun to point to the current document, entity or situation (this paper, this invention, this action, this article, this correspondent). It is often sentence-initial or follows a preposition, and is strongest where it refers self-referentially to the text or its author.

Demonstrative determiners (mostly "this", also "these"/"that") that begin a noun phrase pointing back to an entity or context already established, especially sentence-initial "This" and "this" referring to the current document, court, country or institution. Repeated boilerplate like "Forgot your password" also fires weakly.

27935.name: Tokens inside proper names, especially the final or distinctive piece of a multi-word named entity (places, organizations, institutions, products) that comes right before a generic head noun such as University, Group, Park, Bed, Tower, Cluster or Committee. The token is often a subword completing a name (Mon-roe, Yuk-on, McBurn-ey) or the modifier word of the entity name.

27996.name: Words introducing the second (or remaining) member of a contrastive or enumerated pair/partition after an earlier member was mentioned, such as "the other", "another", "the latter", "the second approach", "others", "the rest", "some", "one" or a parallel number ("four ... and four"). These usually come right after "and", "while" or a comma and mark the complementary part of a split.

Words that start the second or later item in a parallel or contrastive enumeration, pointing back to a set already introduced. Examples are "the other", "another", "others", "one", "the second/third", "the latter", "some", "those" and repeated numbers, as in "one…, the other…" or "some…, others…". Activation is strongest on "other" and "another" in "one X, the other Y" constructions.

28066.name: Binary operators and connectives (+, −, →, ×, or) that come right after a closed parenthesis or bracketed group in math or code, joining it to the next expression. The feature also fires weakly and constantly on "content" in the web boilerplate "Skip to main content".

28142.name: Tokens that open a new top-level structural unit, most often after a preamble of imports, attributes, namespaces or doc comments. The strongest cases are code declaration keywords such as struct, func, fn, enum, class, public/internal, def and opening braces. The same role shows up as markdown heading or bullet markers (#, ##, ###, *), math-block delimiters ($$), docstring openers and paragraph-break newlines or indentation. A weaker, noisier variant fires on function words (the, and, a, of, with) that introduce a new clause or phrase in prose.

28265.name: Sentence-ending punctuation (mostly a period, often fused with paragraph breaks '.⏎⏎') that closes an opening or lead sentence of a news, press-release or abstract-style text, right before the next sentence elaborates on it. Strongest after news-lead statements with attribution (e.g., 'officials said Friday', 'announced Tuesday').

28347.name: The end of a loop header (mostly while, also for/loop) in code: the closing condition token, the colon or brace plus newline that opens the loop body, and the indentation that starts the body's first line. Strongest for while loops, especially where the condition ends with a comparison against 0 or True.

28365.name: Components of file system paths, directory names, URLs and hostnames (e.g. /usr, /local, Program Files\, GOPATH, localhost:, github.com), with the strongest activation on path segments and separators in shell, config and code snippets. Weak activation also appears on ordinary words in prose.

28404.name: Tokens within bibliographic citations and reference strings, especially author name lists (name parts, initials, separating commas/periods), the boundary after a title (closing quotes, periods, "by", "vs."), and publication years. Strongest in "To cite this version:" author lists.

28430.name: Tokens that follow verbs such as "make/made" in fixed phrases about a first appearance, arrival, or milestone ("made his debut", "make their way", "made landfall", "his first", "maiden"). The possessive pronoun after "make" activates most strongly, especially when the phrase is about a debut or breakthrough.

28493.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires on words carrying an informal, conversational or expressive tone. These include interjections and discourse markers ("Oh", "Yes,", "I guess", "Just curious", "sorry,", "Naturally!"), and colloquial or idiomatic phrasing ("good stuff", "magic touch", "sped things up"). It also covers rhetorical questions and asides ("what is it?", "(again)", "Lies... Lies"). The common thread is a shift from neutral, technical text into a chatty, emotive voice, and this holds in code comments and Chinese text too.

28503.name: Subword tokens inside a word, typically a vowel plus "l" plus "d" (eld, ild, old, feld, Mold, Eld) and similar consonant clusters, found mostly in proper names (surnames, place names, taxa) and sometimes in rare words like feldspar or dildo. Activation is highest for "eld" (Sheldrake, Meldrum, Elder).

Word-piece tokens containing an 'l' followed by 'd' (mostly 'eld', 'ild', 'old', 'Feld', 'Eld', 'Mold'), usually in the middle of rare proper names or uncommon words that are split into subword pieces.

28611.name: A diffuse, low-level context feature for technical computing text, especially networking, internet, web-browser and security topics (TCP, sockets, SSL, Tor, VPN, packets, scripts) and source code. It fires weakly on scattered tokens rather than on any single word type: function words, verbs, punctuation, and code indentation or closing braces. It is somewhat stronger on phrases about whether connections or functions work or fail (e.g., "seems to work ok", "loose some packets", "even when i allow").

28644.name: Scientific and technical terms for measured responses or signals, especially physiological and neural ones. It fires on words like 'responses', 'signal', 'activity', 'movements', 'reflex', 'arrival times' and 'effects', usually in the context of recording or measuring how a system reacts to a stimulus (EEG, MEG, fMRI, seismic, acoustic). Activation is weak and is strongest on 'response(s)' and on the parts of measurement-technique names, such as '-encephalography'.

28648.name: The subject-specific middle word in the names of government or regulatory agencies, above all "Drug" in "Food and/& Drug Administration" (FDA). "Disease" in "Centers for Disease Control" activates moderately, and similar words in other agency names (Safety, Wildlife, Criminal) only weakly. Generic lowercase "drug" also activates weakly.

28765.name: The word "poor" (and variants poorly/poorest), firing most strongly when it means low quality or inadequacy (poor judgment, poor nutrition, poor attempt) and somewhat less for poverty or pity. Weak activation on similar-sounding "pale"/"Pale" (e.g., Paleolithic).

The word "poor" and its variants (poorly, poorest), covering low quality, poverty, and pity ("poor woman"). It fires weakly on related negative adjectives (weak, inadequate, badly) and on look-alike tokens such as "pale" and "po".

28794.name: Words naming the method, technique or approach used to carry out a procedure, chiefly in medicine and surgery (minimally invasive, laparoscopy/arthroscopy, robotic, laser, open, orthotopic, epidural). It fires most strongly on 'invasive'/'vasive' and also responds weakly to technique modifiers in other technical fields (batch, no-till, gel-free, RF discharge).

28813.name: Words right after temporal modifiers that place something earlier (or occasionally later) in time, such as "previous", "previously", "earlier", "past", "last", "at first", "traditional" or "future". The feature fires on the modified noun or verb (version, ones, thought, described, identified, week, emotions, approaches) and on the clause that follows, often past-tense verbs like "were" or "had" in sentences contrasting an earlier state with the present.

28840.name: The token right before a year, mostly the space, "(", or ":" separating the year from preceding text, plus sometimes the year's first digits (e.g. "199", "201"). It is strongest in citations and publication data such as author/publisher lists and dates.

28896.name: Code operations that remove or extract elements from a data structure, especially stack/queue/heap pops (.pop, heappop) and also .remove, delete, shift, take. Activation is strongest on pop and weaker on related mutating operations such as reverse, clear, /= and >>=, which modify a container or value in place.

28897.name: Month tokens within specific dates (full names, abbreviations, or numeric month fields), usually followed by a day number. Activation is strongest for a month that begins a standalone date line, such as a timestamp or byline at the start of a line.

28903.name: Tokens right before or at the start of a specific factual detail, most often a number. Typical cases are the bare space or year prefix before a year (e.g. '200', '199'), dates, quantities and measurements, version numbers, and DOI/citation digits. It also fires on separators within such numbers (periods, hyphens, slashes) and occasionally on words that lead into a named source or reference, such as 'published in' or 'report from'.

28961.name: Long runs of repeated filler characters (dots, underscores, dashes, hashes, pluses), with the feature active on the middle or later chunks of the run instead of its start. Most cases are dot leaders in tables of contents running up to a page number. Others are blank fill-in lines on forms and signature lines, markdown table separators, and decorative separator lines.

28977.name: The separator between a date and the time that follows it in a timestamp, usually a single space but also an ISO 'T' or an '@'. It fires right before the hour digits in post dates, email headers and log metadata.

28996.name: Names of TV, radio and media programs, along with talk-show hosts and broadcasters (e.g. Oprah, Tucker Carlson, Matt Lauer, Trevor Noah, Wendy Williams Show). It fires mostly on the final or distinguishing word of the title or name, and on generic media words like "show", "program", "podcast" and "programme".

29041.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mainly in code and technical text on tokens that complete a reference to a named software entity. These include the final piece of identifiers or class names (LoginActivity.class, Fragment1, TicTacToe, VerticalSlider), file and program names (.html, .jsp, binary, -server) and generic nouns like 'function', 'method', 'dialog' and 'services'. It fires most strongly on '.class' and numbered class names. Occasional low activations on punctuation and list items are noise.

29057.name: Scientific/natural-history text about organisms, firing most strongly on Latin species names of disease vectors (Aedes aegypti, Ixodes ricinus, ixodid ticks) and the relative clauses describing what they carry, transmit or infest (e.g. “—which can carry”, “that infest”). Weak, diffuse activation spreads across function words in other biology and ecology passages.

29199.name: Words marking the outcome or resolution of a described process or sequence of events (match results, final scores, trend changes, solutions obtained), e.g. 'to wind up', 'run out comfortable winners eventually', 'and finally pass', 'took her result', 'we obtain', 'is returned as'. Activation concentrates on connectives and verbs that introduce how things ended up, and is strongest in sports and competition results.

29243.name: Fires on the token right after the last item of a list or enumeration (e.g. "A, B, and C"), usually the closing period, comma, bracket or quote, and sometimes a word like "who"/"and"/"are". It marks where the enumerated sequence of names, places, elements or numbers ends.

29272.name: Lists of alternative choices or candidate answers, strongest on multiple-choice answer options (lettered labels such as A./B., a)/b), the options themselves, True/False, "It is impossible to tell"). It also fires weakly on informal sets of alternatives, like "X or Y", questions guessing a series of options ("Germany? The United States?"), and enumerated items with their separators.

29332.name: Phrases giving the location of a residence or other setting, usually right after verbs like lived, home, moved or rented. It fires mostly on locative prepositions (in, on, near, outside, next to, on the outskirts of) and on the place names or place nouns that follow (home, street, town, state names).

29444.name: Separator tokens (commas, newlines, spaces, tabs, dashes, semicolons, HTML tag boundaries) between items in long repetitive lists or sequences, such as number lists, names, table cells and code lines. Activation is strongest deep inside the list, where the next item is predictable from the established pattern.

29454.name: Minute and second digits in clock times within timestamps (the number after "HH:"), typically in post, revision or log metadata. It also fires weakly on nearby timestamp parts such as time zones, the final digit of a year, and trailing "by" or "ago" in edit and post metadata.

The minute and second digits of clock times in timestamps (the numbers following a colon after the hour, e.g. in "22:14:26"), typically in metadata such as post dates, revision logs and email headers. Seconds often activate more strongly than minutes. Weaker activation appears on the final digits of years and other trailing timestamp parts.
Two-digit minute and second numbers following a colon in timestamps (HH:MM or HH:MM:SS), often in post, revision, or log metadata. Activation is strongest on the final seconds field.

29470.name: Plural quantifier and determiner words (many, several, multiple, numerous, various, some, few, more, a number/lot/couple/bunch of, a dozen or so) that introduce an indefinite plurality of items. The strongest activations fall on the quantifier itself, and on the "of" in phrases like "a number of".

2949.name: Opening brackets, parentheses and similar delimiters ("(", "[", "{", "\(", "$", often fused with an operator like "/(", "*(", "^{", "_{", "%(") that begin a grouped sub-expression in math, code, or chemical notation. Activation is strongest when the bracket directly follows a division, multiplication, or function sign, as in "/(", "*(", or "log_b (".

29520.name: Prepositions, articles and partitive phrases that place an item within a larger sequence, collection or whole, e.g. after ordinals or position words like first, latest, last, part, chapter, beginning or end. The strongest cases are "in a series of", "of a", "of the" and "in the".

29521.name: The token "nod" and its forms (nod, nods, nodded, nodal, nodule/nodular), whether a head gesture, a figurative "nod to" (homage), "nod off", or the technical senses (nodal points, nodules). The strongest activations are on medical "nodules/nodular" and on "nodal". Related head gestures such as "shook her head" and stray "NOD"/"Nod" fragments activate weakly.

29554.name: A diffuse, low-level feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires weakly across very different contexts: prose, math/LaTeX, code, URLs and timestamps. The activating tokens tend to sit at structurally predictable points. These include word-completing subword pieces ("ounding", "isions", "iness", "ival", "ators", "oman") and formatting or connective symbols ("://", ":", " =", "-", ")", commas).

29562.name: The final token(s) of a key, parameter, attribute or field name that comes right before its assigned value. This shows up in key=value pairs (function keyword arguments, URL query parameters, XML/HTML attributes, config entries) and in 'Label: value' metadata or measurement names (e.g., 'Email Address:', 'heart rate 133'). Activation is strongest on the closing subword of compound identifiers.

29653.name: Fires mainly on the Chinese negation character 不 inside compounds and phrases (不过, 不断, 不同, 不可行, 搜不到). It responds more weakly to English negations (not, n't) and to the Korean verb stem 하. It also fires on a space that directly precedes CJK text after a colon or bullet in mixed-language code or docs.

29720.name: Names of media companies, TV channels, streaming platforms, studios and publishers that air or produce content (e.g., Netflix, HBO, Starz, ITV, A&E, BBC 4, Warner Bros. Pictures). Activation peaks on the final or distinguishing token of the name, often after 'on the', 'by' or before a possessive 's. There is weaker activation on other organization acronyms such as NASDAQ, DARPA and NASA.

29747.name: The last token of a multi-token proper name or technical term, mostly organization, institution and company names (suffixes like Inc, Ltd, LLC, University, Hospital, Committee), but also places, people and chemical names. It fires where the full name ends, which is often right before a comma, parenthetical acronym or the following clause.

29757.name: Small numeric quantities, mostly the digits of an uncertainty or error margin right after ± (e.g. the '0.1' in '7.4 ± 0.1'). It also fires on small percentages, the upper bound of a range, small dimensions and short durations ('in 3 days'). Weaker activations appear on words meaning a small amount, such as 'slightly' or 'only'.

29772.name: A diffuse, low-activation feature that fires on function words and verbs in news-like narration of events, especially sports, competitions and organizations participating in, joining or withdrawing from something over a span of time (e.g. teams, seasons, races, 'for five years', 'from 1992 to 2011', 'during the war'). It is strongest on phrases about a team or company leaving or entering a competition, such as 'would be pulling out of Formula One and selling its F1 team' and 'this season's'.

299.name: A diffuse, low-level feature spread across ordinary expository or narrative prose. It peaks at discourse transitions, especially sentence-initial contrast or shift connectives ("However", "Yet", "Indeed", "Whilst", "Cue", ", but"), and also fires more weakly on sentence and paragraph boundaries and on the phrases that continue a clause after a pause.

A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires on everyday natural-language prose rather than on code or math, often across whole stretches of fluent, human-sounding text. It peaks on stock, formulaic phrasing typical of forum help requests, personal anecdotes and promotional or job-ad copy, such as "grateful if someone could clarify", "get the chance to", "value for money" and "Key Responsibilities".

29918.name: The element name inside a closing markup tag: HTML/XML (, , ), BBCode ([/size], [/i]) and LaTeX \end{table}/\end{figure}. It fires on the word right after the closing slash or \end{, marking the end of a block. Weak, scattered activations also occur on other end-of-segment tokens such as code fences, closing brackets and line breaks.

29988.name: Inner subword pieces of technical chemical, drug, toxin and biochemical names (e.g. colchicine, trichothecene, puromycin, digitalis), with the strongest activation on fragments of compounds, antibiotics and toxins in scientific contexts. A few weak hits land on related whole words like "antibiotics".

30010.name: Words right after a preposition or verb that give the circumstantial details of a cited statement, report or event: its date, venue, publication, speaker or medium (e.g. "said in court papers", "says … in March 1927", "published April 14 by", "told the specialist newspaper"). Activation is strongest on dates (months and years) in such source attributions.

Words inside adverbial or prepositional phrases that situate a statement or event by its source, occasion, time or setting, typically in news-style attribution (e.g. "in a post on the…", "writing in the … this week", "after a private meeting with the nominee", "with reporters after Sunday's race", "a few weeks ago", "that night"). Activation peaks on the time or occasion nouns and the determiners or prepositions leading to them.

30057.name: Identifier-completing subword tokens in code and structured or technical text, such as variable-name suffixes (_cat, _true, _number), type parameters (Rust's <Self in generics, the strongest), member accesses (.ErrorMessage, .epsilon), parameter names, and labels in data, metadata or table layouts (Views, DOCUMENT, SYN, °F). They usually finish a compound name or field label rather than ordinary prose.

30073.name: Fires weakly and diffusely at points where the main text is interrupted by inserted annotation or markup, usually right after a noun or phrase. Examples include bracketed tags and footnote markers ([VIDEO], [2], [NA], [citation needed]), citations (\cite, n.), and markup or link syntax (](, <sup>, http, ][). Trademark marks ((TM), (R)), stray artifacts (IMG, \e, Email) and odd spacing also trigger it. The strongest activations are on opening brackets of such bracketed insertions.

30092.name: Whitespace separator tokens preceding a number in structured metadata: mainly the space before the year in dates (e.g., "Submitted on 10 Feb 2015", "June 16, 2006"), and the leading space before "1." at the start of a numbered list. Year-prefix digits like "197"/"198" also fire weakly.

30097.name: Words naming an institution, organizational unit, program, service or facility (e.g. Extension, Institute, Department, Lab, Centre, office, programs, services), often the head noun or acronym tail of an organization's name, plus nearby text describing what the organization offers or does.

30164.name: Weak and diffuse activations on words tied to continuation over time toward an eventual end point or outcome, such as processes going on until something stops or disappears ('went on until', 'sooner or later', 'will soon', 'end of the month', 'died out', 'ad infinitum', 'continue', 'wait much longer', 'still owe'). The strongest hit is 'until' in the gradual-erosion example. Many other activations are low-level noise on function words and punctuation.

30233.name: Election and electoral-geography concepts, especially the US Electoral College, electoral votes, swing/key states, and election results by state or district. It responds most strongly to "Electoral College", "electoral votes", and phrases like "key states like Pennsylvania". Weaker activation appears on related political-unit words such as states, counties, borough, electorate, voters and ballot.

30246.name: Clause- or sentence-ending boundary tokens (periods, commas, 'and', semicolons, closing brackets/quotes, newlines) placed right after a completed noun phrase, most strongly when that phrase is a proper name of a person, organization, or work (e.g., 'described by Gerlof Fokko Mees.' or 'produced by DICE and EA,'). The feature marks the point where an informational statement about an entity wraps up and the text moves on.

Clause- or sentence-ending punctuation (mostly periods, also commas, paragraph breaks, or connective 'and'/'is') right after a noun phrase that completes a statement, especially one naming a person, organization or entity in an identifying role (e.g. 'led by X', 'produced by X', 'the judge was X'). It marks the boundary where that statement ends and the next begins.

30307.name: Spread thinly across news-style prose, mostly on attribution and sourcing language: speech or reporting verbs (said, mentioned, suggested, reportedly), "according to", source nouns (expert, sources, studies, police, professor), and the punctuation and sentence boundaries around quotes and claims.

30383.name: Fires on the separator or boundary token right after a person's name, in signatures, bylines, author lists and credits, where the name gives way to a title, role, affiliation, footnote marker or handle (e.g., a newline, space, dash, parenthesis or padding before 'Chief of Police', 'Secretary', 'Blogger', a department name, or '@handle'). There are some noisy formatting and punctuation hits elsewhere.

30392.name: Words built on the root "susp-" (suspend, suspended, suspending, suspension(s), suspense, suspicion), firing most strongly on the initial "susp" token. It covers every sense: halting or banning (flights, sales, users, dividends), hanging or particles dispersed in a fluid, vehicle suspension, and narrative suspense. The suspend/suspension senses fire more strongly than "suspense". Weak activations appear on similar-looking fragments in other languages.

30399.name: Degree/magnitude modifiers qualifying a comparison or change, above all "significantly"/"(statistically) significant" in scientific findings (e.g. "significantly higher/decreased", "significant effect"). Weaker on other intensifiers such as slightly, substantially, considerably, sharply, marginally, and percentages placed before comparatives. Activation is highest in research-results contexts reporting measured differences.

Degree or magnitude intensifiers that quantify the size of a change or difference, most often "significantly" or "significant" (also "considerably", "substantially", "marked", "severe"), plus "percent" after numbers. They typically come right before comparatives or change words (more, less, higher, lower, increase, reduction), and activation is strongest in statistical or research-findings contexts.

30449.name: Fires on boilerplate and setup tokens in technical or structured text. The strongest activations are on code preambles such as import/package statements and their aliases ("import numpy as np", Go import blocks, \documentclass, #include). Weaker activations appear on declarations, config syntax, the variable-introducing "Let ..." in math, and formulaic document structure like tables of contents, academic affiliations and forum headers.

30469.name: The main verb (often a copula or auxiliary like is/are/was/has/would/can) that comes right after a long, complex subject noun phrase, especially one containing prepositional modifiers ("the X of the Y"). It marks where the subject ends and the predicate begins. It sometimes fires on a comma or "to" sitting at the same subject–predicate boundary.

30495.name: Tokens that fuse a leading punctuation mark or symbol (parenthesis, quote, bracket, asterisk, hyphen, slash, dollar sign, @, period) with the first letters of the next word, e.g. "(T", ""C", "[s", "-user". They mostly appear at the start of a line or a parenthetical or quoted span, where the tokenizer splits the following word oddly.

30499.name: Opening delimiters or spaces that come right before an inline value (a math variable, number, or code literal), usually after a noun that the value names (e.g. 'the complete graph on $n$', 'set to 1 inch', 'port 3333'). Strongest on the opening LaTeX '$' or '\(' of inline math; weaker on backticks, quotes, and the space before a bare number.

30518.name: Words built on the root "collaborat-" (collaboration, collaborate, collaborative, collaborator, including split pieces like "Coll|abor|ating"), covering joint work, partnerships and co-authored efforts. Near-synonyms such as "cooperate" and "team effort" fire only weakly.

30570.name: The final digit of a DOI's publisher prefix (the "10.xxxx" registrant code), right before the slash that starts the suffix, sometimes including the slash. Weak activation on similar URL path segments such as "/embed" or "/articles".

30614.name: Discourse boundaries in expository or news-style prose: sentence-ending punctuation, paragraph breaks, and the words that open a new sentence or clause ("The", "A", "In", "One of"). Activation is strongest where a report, study or source is introduced or attributed, as in "The report said", "X notes that", "which conducted the survey" and "said".

30616.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens in hard-to-predict, high-entropy text rather than on a particular word. Typical contexts are random alphanumeric strings, hashes, IDs, URLs, IP addresses and numeric lists or codes. It also fires on rare non-Latin scripts, garbled LaTeX, and incoherent spam or machine-generated prose.

30662.name: The first token of a word, name or compound that the tokenizer splits into several pieces, so the word is unfinished at that point. These are often single capital letters or short prefixes that begin acronyms, brand names, chemical or technical terms, usernames, or hyphenated compounds (e.g. E-skom, P-glycoprotein, she-wolf, Co-founder).

30695.name: Words for empathy, sympathy and compassion toward others' feelings or suffering (empathy/empathetic, sympathetic, sympathy for, pity, feel sorry for, compassion, mercy), with weaker activation on related warm attitudes (understanding, solidarity, admiration, caring) and on look-alike fragments such as 'path/athetic' in parasympathetic, apathetic and telepathy, or 'merc'.

Words for feeling for or with others, especially "sympathy"/"sympathetic", along with compassion, empathy, mercy, pity, condolences and solidarity. Weaker activations go to related emotional-attitude terms (admiration, affinity, apathy, heart, support).

30744.name: The preposition "on" (and equivalents like Dutch "op", "starting") introducing a temporal expression — a date or weekday — especially after event or publication verbs (took place, born, launched, posted, submitted). It fires more weakly on locative or platform uses of "on".

30774.name: Words about creative authorship and composing, especially writing and composing music and songs (songwriter, composer, writing music, song-writing), plus related terms for writers, playwrights, designers, and creators. Activation is strongest for music and song writing.

30828.name: Fires on "thereby" (strongest) and related consequence/means connectives that introduce a resulting action or the mechanism of a preceding clause: "whereby", "hereby", "thus", "thereupon", and the Chinese "从而". Activation is highest when "thereby" is followed by a participle describing the result ("thereby increasing…").
