30930.name: Coordinating conjunctions (mostly "and", also "or", occasionally a comma or slash) that join two nouns or adjectives into a coordinated phrase, especially right after a noun or modifier, where another item of the same kind is about to follow (e.g., "pain and dysfunction", "wires or cords").

30945.name: The second item in a coordinated pair of descriptors, usually after "and"/"&": a further role, profession, or title given to the same person or thing (e.g. "actor and director", "historian and author", "singer and songwriter"). It also fires weakly on other second-coordinate nouns or adjectives.

Role, title, or descriptive nouns (e.g., owner, CEO, chairman of, author, host of, former…) that follow a conjunction like "and" in a coordinated description of one person or entity, the second item in an appositive list of roles or attributes, usually just before the person's name.

30966.name: Adjectives and participles describing something left in an unfinished, unresolved, unaddressed or not-yet-acted-upon state, most often un- words (unanswered, unchecked, untreated, untapped, unexplored, unborn, unknown), plus related ideas like outstanding, open problems, loose ends, missed, pent-up and undercooked.

31039.name: Pieces of abbreviations, acronyms and initialisms (e.g. TFA, CTA, IMHO, OOP, PO Box, B/L, VoIP, RTL), typically the token right after the first letter of an uppercase acronym, plus some shorthand fragments such as 'vols', 'thx', '24/7' and 'ra'.

31048.name: Weak, diffuse activation across text discussing proposed solutions, policies, plans or approaches to problems, often political or argumentative commentary. The strongest hits are on nouns and phrases naming the proposal or its proposer (e.g. "policy proposals", "proposed by the", "Solutions", "Experts"). Function words and punctuation around such claims also fire at lower levels.

A diffuse feature in news and political or policy writing, firing on words in clauses about government plans, proposals, bills, initiatives and ideologies, and on how they are announced, compared, supported or debated. Typical spans include 'suggesting the administration has yet to decide on a final plan', 'Trump's plan… compares with', 'With Labour having committed to' and 'the plan also'. It also fires weakly on clause boundaries, such as periods and commas, within such discussion.

A weak, diffuse feature in expository news, policy, and argumentative prose. It fires most on nouns for proposals, policies, plans, or ideas (package, compromise, framework, plan, bill, ideas, demands, Solution, concepts) and on the tokens that open the claim about them: predicate starts like "is/has been/was a", relative "which", reporting verbs like "stated that it" or "experts note", and the punctuation or sentence boundary that begins a new assertion.

31120.name: Punctuation or function word right after a citation or reference to a source (patent number, paper [1], author et al., journal, institution, URL, date), marking the boundary where the citation ends and the text goes on to describe what that work did. Strongest on the comma or period directly after a patent or reference (e.g. 'JP20033078A,' and 'incorporated by reference herein in its entirety. In').

31149.name: Verbs and nouns for making, creating or preparing something (cook, make, build, prepare, bake, mix, craft, grow, manufacture), plus the words right after them such as the object or a following article/preposition. Activation is strongest for food and drink preparation (cooking dinner, making applesauce, preparing dishes, homemade cookies).

Verbs and words about making, creating or preparing something, especially food (cook, make a meal, cooking, kitchen skills, blend). Tokens like create, make, build, grow, produce, and 'your own' usually come after 'to' or 'can'. Activation is strongest for cooking and meal preparation.

Verbs and nouns about making, building or preparing something oneself (create, make, build, compile, cook, DIY, crafts, homemade). Activation is strongest for hands-on, do-it-yourself production such as cooking, DIY projects and compiling code yourself.

31220.name: Promotional, corporate or marketing-style language about benefits and value, such as verbs like help, enhance, deliver, streamline, reduce and drive, and phrases like achieve business goals, productivity, performance, customer satisfaction or reduced costs. Activation is strongest in value-proposition phrases describing what a product, service or technology enables users to achieve.

31254.name: Ranges, most often year or date spans like 1945-1948 or 1830 and 1860. It fires on the separator (hyphen, en dash, "to") and the end-point number that closes the span. It is strongest on dash-joined year ranges, and weaker on page or chapter ranges, times, and decades such as 1950s.

31273.name: The name "Roger" and similar-sounding name fragments. The first name "Roger" fires most strongly, especially before a surname or initial. The surname "Rogers"/"Rodgers" and fragments like "Rog" or "ogers" fire moderately. Weaker activations appear on phonetically similar name pieces such as Peggy/Peg, Siegel/Nigel ("-igel") and Berger.

31316.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no single clear trigger. It fires mostly on tokens that complete a content-word noun or compound term, especially in technical, scientific or product-description text. These include head nouns of technical noun phrases (processor, algorithm, ions, timezone, holder) and final subword pieces of longer words (-etry, -osity, -iddle, -urg, -fish). It also fires occasionally on nearby connectors or closing parentheses inside such terms.

31402.name: Encyclopedic or travel-guide passages about the history of buildings and landmarks (churches, chapels, temples, cathedrals, palaces, statues, terminals). It fires on the building nouns and the historical narration around them, such as construction, dates, past locations, renovation or replacement, and later use, for example "was built in 1851 at the", "replaced a previous version", "redesigned", "(now the".

31412.name: Tokens that open an anonymous function or closure definition in code: Python "lambda", Rust closure pipes "|" / "(|" (often after .map), C++ lambda "[]", JS/R/PHP inline "function", arrow-function parameter parentheses, and Fn/Function types. Strongest for lambda passed as an argument or assigned to a variable. Weak hits on math function names like f/F.

31421.name: The first word of a new sentence or line, mostly after a period or line break, that opens a new section or instruction. It is strongest for "For" (especially "For more information" and "For other purposes") in boilerplate such as repository notices, copyright statements, and contact or reference lines. Other openers like "To", "See", "Other", "On" and "In" activate more weakly.

31460.name: Code statement boundaries where an object, widget, or variable is being instantiated or assigned. The strongest activations fall on the closing parenthesis, semicolon and newline (");\n") that end constructor calls such as new X(...) or Widget::new(...). Weaker activations fall on the class names and variable names involved in these creation and assignment lines, especially for GUI components like labels, toolbars, shells and boxes.

31463.name: A diffuse feature found mostly in scientific and technical prose. It fires on words inside clauses that describe processes, changes of state, or goals: reaching a steady state, finding or obtaining solutions, transforming, distinguishing, varying over time. Activations usually fall on the verb or object right after purpose or result phrases such as "to", "leads to" and "in order to".

31518.name: The last token of a person's name, most often the surname after a first name or title, strongest for well-known political leaders (President Obama/Trump/Biden, Roosevelt). When the surname is split into pieces, the final subword fires (e.g. Gorbache-v, Hickenlo-oper), usually where the name is the subject about to say or do something.

31630.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires mainly inside technical and procedural text. It is strongest on statement-level code inside loop or conditional bodies, especially variable assignments and updates (e.g. "resA = *it1", "v = Vec::new(); for", "flips += 1") and the indentation tokens before them. It fires weakly on operators and expressions in math, and on scattered content words and phrases in explanatory prose describing methods or steps, which appear to be noise.

31674.name: The final token(s) of a product or model name, especially vehicles (Toyota Supra/Prius/Corolla, Laguna, BMW R24) but also gadgets, planes, guns and spacecraft. Activation lands on the name suffix or model number that completes the name after the brand. Generic vehicle-type nouns (van, sedan, wagon, minivan) also activate, with car names strongest.

31693.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature in scientific and technical prose. It fires on the key terms of technical noun phrases and method descriptions, such as model parameters, processes and components. It is strongest where items are paired, coordinated or contrasted, as in "X and Y", "both … as well as", "horizontal/vertical" and "possibility/impossibility".

31843.name: The integer part of a decimal number, i.e. the digits just before a decimal point (prices, measurements, percentages, coordinates), especially when a similar number appeared earlier in the context. It occasionally fires on plain integers.

31865.name: A diffuse, weak feature centered on normative or value-laden phrasing about what is best, right or beneficial for someone, such as "do what's best for your story", "the best fit for their team", "seek their greatest happiness" and "what is right". It also fires faintly on surrounding advisory or concessive language ("but", "take your time", "there is no").

31869.name: Expressions of equality, sameness or comparison: equals signs and == operators, words like "equal", "equality", "identical", "same", "agreement", "equivalences" and "resemblance", and equality-test functions such as Assert.Equal and cmp. Activation is strongest on explicit equality terms like "equal sign", "==", "identical" and "equality".

Words and symbols expressing equality, sameness, matching or comparison: "same", "equal", "equality", "identical", "match", "agreement", "unity", "unchanged", and the "="/"==" operators in code and math. Weaker activations land on comparison-linking words like "with", "to", "like", and on fragments of such concepts in other languages (ÉGALITÉ, 平).

31889.name: Anaphoric determiners that point back to something already mentioned, chiefly "said" used in the formal/legal sense of "the aforementioned" (e.g. "the said drawings", "aforesaid"), along with Chinese 该/該 ("this/the said") and "aforementioned". Activation is strongest in legal or archaic "the said X" constructions. Weaker hits come from other uses of "said/Said" (speech verb, the surname).

31904.name: Abstract head words in formal or literary multiword phrases, especially nouns heading an "of" construction ("the point of", "the part of", "the consequences of", "the close of the year", "the number of"). It also fires on intensifying or degree modifiers (full, utmost, total, very much, precisely) and time or quantity expressions (some time, just before, at three). Activation is broad and weak, peaking on "the point" and "the part".

3191.name: Word-internal and word-final subword fragments (suffixes, inflectional endings, continuation pieces) of words split across multiple tokens, mostly in non-English or uncommon words (Latin, Slavic, Icelandic, German, Portuguese, Arabic, transliterations, rare names). The strongest activations fall on inflectional endings of heavily inflected languages.

31929.name: The double-slash token "//" in any role: code comments, integer division, URL and path separators, XPath, and decorative separators in bylines or headers. Activation peaks where it joins a URL or template placeholder (e.g. "{{site.github}}//") or appears as a quoted string literal. Weak activations also land on unrelated tokens.

31933.name: Output/print statements in code across many languages (print, println, printf, cout <<, Console.WriteLine, echo, System.out.println, warn), firing on the print function name and its accompanying syntax such as the opening paren/quote, format specifiers (%d, {0}, \n), stream operators/endl and the closing paren/semicolon. Weakly fires on a few output-like prose words.

32.name: Mainly code: the identifier that begins a called expression, usually right after '=' or 'return' or at the start of a statement, such as a module, class or function name preceding '.method(' or '(' (json.dumps, numpy.array, plt.gcf, Activator.CreateInstance, Ray::new, substractWords). Elsewhere, in prose, math, URLs and LaTeX, activation is weak and scattered.

32005.name: Weak, sparse feature for anomalous or obfuscated text. It fires mostly on single Cyrillic look-alike letters swapped into Latin or Greek words (e.g. a Cyrillic 'с' in 'topic' or 'confirmo'). It also fires on spaces just before words written in homoglyph scripts. Other weak hits are odd tokens in spun or garbled text (misplaced 'often', 'simply just') and leading list numbers like '1.'. Text written entirely in a foreign script mostly does not trigger it.

32015.name: The token "ID" (also " ID", "-ID", "IDs", occasionally "I.D"/"iD"), the identifier abbreviation, most often as a suffix to a noun naming an identifier field or label (Job ID, Patient ID, polygonID), and usually followed by a number or colon.

32050.name: The word-start subword token "rhe"/"Rhe" (as in rheumatoid, rheumatism, rheology, rheometer, Rhein). It fires most strongly in "rheumatoid arthritis" medical contexts. Weaker activations occur on "he"/"whe"/"hes" fragments after an h-cluster letter (diarrhea, wheeled, wheezing, rhesus, Phe).

32084.name: The token that comes right after a noun for a table or other structured display (table, chart, figure, diagram, template, box, list, tree, field, Table class), most often in tabular contexts. Usually this is a function word or punctuation continuing the phrase (to, for, in, are, be, comma, colon), or the markup that follows a table opening tag: '>' plus newline after <table, or ']' and '\' after \begin{table}. LaTeX table environments activate most strongly.

3209.name: Mostly weak activations on scientific and technical writing about modeling and analysis. The strongest are on names of approximations, frameworks and analytical methods (e.g. "within the Bogoliubov approximation", "framework of MCT", "Approximate Evaluation", "quasi-linear", "asymptotic techniques"), and on words describing simplifying assumptions or idealized models such as linear, classical, continuum, assumption of independence, simplified and predictable.

32142.name: The word "elite" and its plural "elites", both as a noun for a privileged ruling group and as an adjective meaning top-tier (elite squad, elite performers, elite colleges). Weaker matches are related ideas of exclusivity and high status, such as aristocracy, ruling class, exclusive, select, inner circle and esteemed.

3215.name: Coordinating conjunctions (mostly "and", also "or", "as well as", and occasionally a comma) that follow a completed noun phrase or clause, marking where a second coordinated item or predicate is about to be joined. The conjunction is sometimes paired with the next word ("and the", "or your", "and especially").

32190.name: Tokens that end in a backslash (often fused with preceding punctuation like :\ .\ }\ '\), which begin an escape sequence, LaTeX command or file path (e.g. \n, \033, \t, \label). They fire most strongly in code string literals just before newline or ANSI escapes.

32440.name: The main-clause subject and its first verb, coming right after an introductory modifier phrase (participial, adjectival, or prepositional, e.g. "Born in Chile," or "Due to its simplicity,"). These are often pronouns (he, they, it, we, I) or short noun phrases. Activation is strongest when the subject is the entity the fronted phrase describes.

The subject (and often its main verb) of a main clause that comes right after an introductory phrase, usually a participial, prepositional or appositive phrase set off by a comma, e.g. "Recently painted, this home offers" or "A native of Winnipeg, Jeremy". It also fires on the main verb that follows a long subject noun phrase. Names and nouns like "game" or "it" get the strongest weight.

32458.name: Imperative instructions or prompts aimed at a user, as in UI/form text, input() prompts, button labels and directions (enter, select, input, submit, add, press, specify, "please …"). They appear across many languages, e.g. 'Digite', '请输入', 'зарегистрируйтесь'. The strongest signal is on the verb that starts a prompt string requesting user input.

32541.name: Boilerplate legal or policy text such as disclaimers, copyright notices and terms. It fires on the subject entity (organization, publisher, author) and the verb phrase that follows, stating its responsibility, rights or obligations. It is strongest on disclaiming phrases like "does not", "will not be responsible", "assumes no" and "offers no warranties".

32561.name: Words that open a slot for an upcoming object or complement: transitive verbs (exploit, achieve, destroy, count, display, automate) and relational prepositions or nouns (of, to, on, with, for, near the, quality of) that come right before the noun phrase or pronoun they govern. That following argument is often 'the …', 'them', 'it' or 'that …', frequently pointing back to something mentioned earlier. The strongest activations fall on longer predicate spans, such as 'to recover the original color of', 'assigned to' and '(or'.

32562.name: The final digit of a year marking the end of a lifespan or period, usually a death year in a birth–death range like "(1921–1981)" or after "died in/on". It also fires weakly on other death-related words such as "died", "passed away", "d." and "dies at".

3259.name: The final element of a location or postal address, typically a country name (or a state/region abbreviation or the end of a postal code) that closes a comma-separated address string. It fires most strongly in academic affiliation and contact-address lines.

32609.name: Words that come just before a noun for a person or group of people (trainer, team, professionals, staff, specialists, artists, users). These are mostly prepositions and determiners such as "by", "with", "of", "our", "a" and "the", plus descriptive adjectives such as "skilled", "experienced", "talented", "licensed" and "medical". The phrases often name the people doing, helping with or collaborating on an action, e.g. "guided by a local", "consultation with a licensed", "team of skilled".

32689.name: Final tokens or subwords that complete a multi-token proper name, especially titles of games, films, albums, products or series. These are often sequel numbers or subtitles ("2", "VI", "Fallen Kingdom", "Jr"), and the model predicts them once the name's opening is recognized.

3269.name: Nouns (and their preceding prepositions) naming the recipient entity that some agent acts on, lives in, or interacts with, especially biological hosts or targets such as a host plant, host cell, cell line or test animal. The strongest case is a pathogen's host ('in interaction with rubber tree'). Weaker activations fall on general targets, substrates or locations ('onto a building', 'into the gut', 'invasion of the Soviet Union').

3280.name: Function, method, class and library identifiers in code, especially the name being called or imported (often right after a dot or ::, before an opening parenthesis), e.g. .get, .write_all, sprintf, WriteLine, Mutex, info. Weaker activation on similar call-like tokens such as LaTeX commands (eqnarray, limsup), shell commands (curl) and URL domain parts (.com, .org).

32836.name: A weak, diffuse feature about limits, thresholds and repeated occurrences: quantities, frequencies, durations or patterns of activity being capped, measured or restricted. It fires on words like limits, period, times, years, consecutive, streak, bursts, peak demand, chatter and bounce. It also fires on rate-limit and anti-abuse contexts, such as spam filtering, reporting requirements, chasing losses and repeated identical samples.

32842.name: First element of a coordinate pair or tuple, plus the comma after it, mostly in code and math (e.g. Point(50f, 50f), [0, 1], (3, 4)), with the x-coordinate activating most strongly. Weaker activation appears on other index or coordinate tokens inside arrays and point lists.

33074.name: The punctuation that ends a news dateline or source credit and comes right before the article body begins. It is most often the closing parenthesis after an agency name, as in "(AP)" or "(Reuters)", and fires most strongly there. It also fires weakly on other dateline separators such as dashes, colons, brackets, periods and line breaks that follow a location, date or byline.

The punctuation that closes a news dateline or wire-service credit at the start of an article, just before the story body begins. Typical cases are the closing parenthesis after an agency name such as (AP), (Reuters) or (UPI), the period of a state abbreviation (N.H., Calif.), and the following dash, slash, colon or line break. Activation is strongest on the ")" after a wire-service name.

33106.name: Grammatical particles, case endings and inflectional suffixes in non-English text, especially Japanese particles (に, と), Korean postpositions (에, 로, 으로) and case or verb endings in agglutinative and inflected languages (Azerbaijani, Turkish, Russian, Latin). Activation is strongest on Japanese に and Korean 에.

3311.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires at positions where a number is about to follow, especially the standalone space token before a numeral. It is strongest in ranges, dates, years and numbered sequences ("to 90.0", "November 2019", "1997 to 1999", list indices). It also fires more weakly on separators and first digits within such numeric patterns, such as dashes, periods, "%", commas and "or".

33136.name: Website boilerplate headers for comment, answer, review or result sections (e.g. "4 thoughts on", "8 Responses to", "Leave a Reply", "0 comentarii", "1 Answer", "Results 1-1 of"). The feature fires on the word just after the count/label, usually a preposition like "on", "to" or "for" that introduces the post title, or a plural ending. It is strongest for "N thoughts on “Title”".

33158.name: Tokens at the start of repeated import/include lines in source code (Python "import"/"from", C/C++ "#include <" or "\"", Rust "use"/"::", C# "using"), firing on the keyword or delimiter that opens each successive dependency path. The strongest activations are on the "<" after #include. There is weak, sparse activation on other repetitive list-like structure, such as category separators, bullets, and repeated command flags.

33188.name: Words naming infrastructure, utilities, public services and institutions that serve a locality or community (government services, post/mail, courthouses, police, hospitals, railways, wastewater, outlets, area codes, banks and companies operating in a town), plus phrases describing what connects to or supplies a place (e.g., 'railway reached Putney', 'blood supply from the artery'). Activation is strongest in local-geography or civic-amenity contexts.

33193.name: Fires in birth-date contexts, mainly on the space token right before the day or year number that follows "born", "b.", "born on", or a month name in a birthday entry. It also fires on the word "born" itself in parenthetical "(born YEAR)" notes. Occasional weak hits appear on unrelated tokens.

33254.name: Practical travel‑guide and consumer‑advice prose: tips about transport, journey times, fares, prices and costs, and conditional advice ("depending on", "unless", "check", "buy a SIM card", "use local bus/taxi"). Activation peaks on concrete logistics details such as durations and prices.

33270.name: Indefinite or narrative time expressions, especially the noun completing a phrase like "one day", "next day/time", "someday", "ever", "once", "in the middle of the night". Activation peaks strongly on "day" in "one day" used to introduce a story event or an unspecified future time.

Time-unit nouns (especially "day", also night, time, morning, week) completing indefinite or narrative temporal phrases, strongest for "one day" introducing a past anecdote or a hoped-for future ("one day I…", "the other night", "on a Friday morning").

33299.name: Tokens containing the dollar sign "$" in any role: currency amounts, LaTeX math delimiters, shell prompts, and variable sigils in code (PHP, Perl, R, Rust macros, template ${...}). Activation runs highest for code and shell uses such as R's "\$" accessor, Perl comments, terminal prompts and PHP variables, and is weaker for plain currency and math.

33396.name: A diffuse feature found in expository, advisory or policy-style prose about practices and processes, such as healthcare, management, public engagement and wellbeing. It fires on words that name means or approaches for achieving an outcome: nouns like methods, measures, steps, ways, tool, factors, involvement, engagement and communication, and action verbs like help, create, streamline, enhance, implementing and focusing. It also fires on nearby function words like "to", "in" and commas within those purpose and benefit statements. Activations are strongest on terms for participation and engagement and on tools.

33421.name: The preposition (mostly "of", sometimes "in"/"the") right after purpose-type nouns such as aim, goal, objective, purpose or focus, in phrases like "The aim of this study is to...". It is strongest in academic or research statements of intent.

33443.name: Function words and nouns in website navigation and boilerplate text that invites users to search, find, browse or look up information or resources (e.g. "search for", "find something about", "list of", "reviews", "archive", "websites"). The strongest activations come on the prepositions and objects in these search-and-find calls to action.

33528.name: Names of data serialization/parsing formats and libraries in code (pickle, json, csv, XML, serde_json, XmlSerializer, struct, DataStream), strongest for 'pickle' and 'json' as Python import targets; weaker for other type/parse names (Integer, int.Parse).

33541.name: Tokens inside proper names of institutions, especially hospitals, medical centers, universities and research institutes. Activation falls on the name-continuing words or word pieces after the first word (e.g., 'Hospital', 'Medical Center', 'Health', 'Museum', or the rest of a split name) and is strongest for hospital and medical-center names.

33546.name: Function words and verbs in descriptions of how something was made, assembled, decorated, or equipped: materials, added components, and methods (e.g., "made out of", "with a", "and added", "attached to"). Activation is strongest on crafting narratives that list added elements ("added a piece of ribbon and lace to").

33820.name: Fires on the verb, gerund or claim noun (often with a following "that", "to" or "of") that names an action, statement or belief whose rightness is being judged. Typical frames are "was right in revealing", "correctly found", "wrongly stated that", "justified in refusing to", "mistaken if you believe", "rejected her argument that" and "determination that". The judged acts are usually assertions, decisions or stances.

Verbs or action nouns naming a specific act, statement or decision that the surrounding text judges as right, wrong, mistaken, controversial or justified (e.g. 'right in asserting', 'mistake of quoting', 'correct that', 'decision to hire'). Activation sits on the act being evaluated, often a speech or decision verb, or a 'that'/'to' introducing the evaluated claim.

33852.name: The leading number in a quantity expression (digits or spelled-out words, often the part before a comma, decimal, or unit) that gives an amount, duration, price, or measurement. It fires most strongly on prison sentences and other durations ("sentenced to 15 months", "70 lashes") and on dollar amounts.

The leading digits or number word of a numeric quantity in running text. It fires on the number that is about to be followed by a unit, scale word or counted noun (million, years, percent, days, ,000, -foot), often after $, "up to" or "to". Activation is strongest for durations and sentence lengths, e.g. "six years in prison", "six months", "seven years".

34025.name: The noun "point"/"points" (and similar discrete-location nouns like "dots", "node" 点), especially in the geometric/mathematical sense of a location or data element (each point, a single point, data point, at point A). It is strongest in technical contexts and weaker for score points or other senses.

The noun "point"/"points" (incl. midpoint, timepoints, -point), mostly meaning a location or position, as in geometric, data, or physical points in space, also other senses like point guard, decimal point, stock points. Weak firing on similar nouns (dots, pin, notes). Strongest in mathematical/geometric contexts ("another such point", "about a point").

3419.name: Words about creating or initializing something, strongest on programming object lifecycle terms (constructor, destructor, initialization, created, setter). It also fires weakly on sign-up and registration wording and scattered tokens in technical text.

Object-creation vocabulary, mostly in programming: by far the strongest on "constructor(s)", and weaker on related terms like create/creating, instance, instantiate, builder, factory and copy. Faint, noisy activations also appear on unrelated words, such as section headers and "Commentary".

34205.name: Clause and sentence boundaries in expository, documentation- or tutorial-style prose. It fires on transition points such as punctuation and paragraph breaks, and on clause openers that set up an explanation ("You can", "To access", "If", "Whether you are", "As a", "The syntax of… is"). These tokens mark where the text moves from stating a topic to explaining how something works or what the reader can do.

Clause and sentence boundaries in explanatory, technical or instructional prose. It fires most on periods, commas and line breaks that end one statement, and on the words that open the next one ("This is", "In this case", "If", "A", "You", "However"). It also fires on linking verbs and connectives inside definitional or descriptive statements ("are called", "is", "will", "that", "to").

3437.name: Word-initial fragments beginning with a vowel plus p/b (mostly "hyp"/"Hyp", with weaker "imp", "hip" and "yp"), firing on the first subword of words like hypotension, hypertrophic, hyperspectral, impressive and impacts. "hyp" fragments activate most strongly; whole words and unrelated tokens activate only weakly.

34577.name: Words describing fullness, crowding, or capacity: something being packed, clogged, congested, cluttered, flooded, overstretched, backed up, busy, filled to the brim, or in high demand (and occasionally its opposite, emptiness or lack of space).

Words about capacity, fullness, and limits: being full, filled, crowded, empty, sold out, maxed out, capped, overloaded, limited, or taken. The feature fires on adjectives, verbs, and particles that describe how much something is occupied or saturated, with the strongest activations on words like 'full', 'sold out', and 'capped'.

34778.name: Tokens where arguments or inputs are being specified. Activation is strongest inside function and method signatures and parameter lists, such as C, C#, Java and Perl prototypes. It peaks on opening parentheses, parameter types and names, and the commas or newline indentation between parameters. It fires more weakly on usage-syntax option brackets. It also fires weakly in procedural instructions where the user is told what to supply or choose ("choose the", "fill in the", "add the recipient", numbered step markers, bullets).

Tokens marking a slot where an input, argument, or parameter is expected next. The strongest cases are function signatures and parameter lists ("=function(e", "open(", "(enum mode, uint", "(int"). The pattern also covers API descriptions such as "expects an", "takes a" and "given by the arg". It appears in UI instructions to supply a value ("Enter your", "enter a name", "type in a number for", "Choose a") and in form field labels followed by a colon or asterisk.

34799.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens, often mid-word subword fragments or function words, in text that is non-English (French, German, Spanish, Romanian, Polish, Korean, Persian, Greek, Welsh, Russian) or unusual and nonstandard English (archaic or Scots spelling, Shakespearean contractions, ungrammatical or machine-translated phrasing). It seems to respond to language or orthography that departs from ordinary modern English rather than to any particular meaning.

A diffuse feature that fires on tokens where the English is unexpected or non-standard, often right after a verb or preposition. This covers misspellings and odd word splits (sup-r-ised, b-ing, anounce), awkward machine-translated, non-native or spun text ("tour to Odisha", "I am purchase the Find"), and foreign-language words. It also fires on stiff, formal announcement or notification phrasing ("has the honor to enclose", "I inform the House", "glad to announce you, that").

34875.name: Website navigation and boilerplate UI text, such as links for Previous/Next post or page, Home, Return/Back to, page-number lists (1 2 3…), arrows and separators, skip-to-content and table-of-contents links. These typically sit between or after main content.

Website navigation and boilerplate text, such as "Home", "Previous", "Next", "Back to Gallery", "Page X of Y", "«", "Jump to", and "You are here". These usually appear at line starts between scraped page content and the main text. It also fires on similar words like "Previous" or "Home" in ordinary prose at the same positions.

3497.name: Opening markup tag names and commands, mostly HTML table cell tags (<td, <th) plus <p, <strong, <br, <sub and LaTeX commands like \frac, \caption and \textsuperscript, marking the start of a formatted element just before its content.

3501.name: Separator tokens that sit between two paired or listed values: commas between coordinates, function arguments, or list items; hyphens in ranges; ' x' in resolutions; slashes and colons in ratios; 'and', 'to', or 'of' joining two terms. Most often numbers, especially in code and technical text. It is weak, firing a little more on commas inside coordinate or argument pairs.

3558.name: Code annotations, attributes and decorators that modify following declarations, such as Java @Subscribe (strongest), Rust #[derive(...)], #[allow], #[test], Blade @if and mentions of decorators. Weaker activations fall on boilerplate page and document metadata labels, e.g. 'Skip to content/navigation', 'Corresponding author', 'Open Access', 'Opinion' and 'Location', plus similar header or structural tokens in code.

3565.name: Weak, diffuse activations on nouns and short phrases that name ready-made, reusable things provided for others to adopt or build on: templates, libraries, building blocks, predefined sets, reference implementations or architectures, guidelines, protocols, and product solutions or offerings. Nearby enabling phrases like "helps you to", "enable you to", "to choose from" and "to use" also activate, with the strongest responses in software and technical descriptions.

Weak, diffuse feature in technical/assistant-style text (mostly programming and instructions). It fires on nouns and phrases for generic tools, templates, examples or artifacts being offered or used, such as code, sample, example, prompt, framework, template, placeholder, dataset and Material UI/Tailwind CSS. It also catches nearby helper verbs like provide, craft, use and help. It is strongest on terms for sample or ready-made code and resources.

358.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single clear meaning. It fires mostly on the opening piece of multi-token names or unusual terms (e.g. the first fragment of a rare word, place name or software name) and on label-like tokens in structured or boilerplate text, such as citations ("et al.", "eds", PMCID), affiliations, photo credits, numbered list entries, and code or notebook markers.

3583.name: Quantitative statistics and tallies, especially numbers paired with units or counted items (yards, runs, passes, homers, calories, percent, deaths), and the connectives that chain several such figures into a list ("and", commas, "for", "in", "with"). Activation peaks on sports stat lines like "38 passes for 441 yards and three touchdowns" or "92 runs in 92 balls".

35842.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires on mid-phrase tokens, often function words or predictable continuations, in boilerplate, SEO or promotional web text. It peaks inside title- or heading-like phrases such as “1Win Casino INDIA Offers free spin”, “21 Days Challenge to Shifting from Anxious to Calm” and “How to set up…”, and in garbled or broken sentences.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on many ordinary tokens (function words, punctuation, nouns) across running text. It is strongest in promotional or commercial copy, such as product listings, ads, hotel and real-estate blurbs, and calls to action like "contact us for your T shirts" or "Check out our other bundles".

3591.name: Mainly the word 'deliver' and its forms (deliver, delivering, delivery), along with related ideas of conveying or transferring something: ship, shipping, arrival, arrive, hand, receive, present, distribution. Weaker activations come from tokens that share its opening letters, such as 'del' word-starts and the names Daniel, Dan, Del and Danny.

3609.name: Words built on the root "activ-" (active, activity, activities, activate, actively, activists, inactive), plus weaker hits on related words for being lively, busy or in operation (alive, busy, restless, vibrant, running, fire up, back to life).

3625.name: Names of organizations and institutions, mostly government agencies, departments, and official bodies (e.g., USDA, NASA, Centers for Disease Control, Bureau of Land Management, police, ministry, commissioner), including acronym pieces and the final words of multi-word agency names. Activation is strongest on the head or last word of the agency name.

3630.name: Fires on nouns tied to riding, mounting or wheeled transport, such as bicycle, horses, 'ride the bull', rider, wheelchair, wheel, brakes, sledges, Honda and electric vehicles, and is strongest on 'bicycle'. It also gives weak, scattered activations on other product, gear or device names and on word fragments.

Fires on words tied to motorcycles, riding and motor vehicles. The strongest hits are "motorcycle," "ride helmet(less)," "rode," "RIDE," "boda boda," "Hyosung" and "four wheeler." Weaker hits include motorhome, Motor racing, car model names, carts and rides. Activation is very weak (around 1) on assorted brand/name subword pieces and casual lifestyle or travel nouns.

365.name: A diffuse, low-specificity feature that fires across stretches of fluent English prose rather than on any particular word. Activation spreads over whole multi-word clauses and phrases, usually after the opening word. It is strongest in continuous descriptive or personal sentences, such as definitions, reviews and narrated feelings or actions. It is weak and scattered on boilerplate, headings, code and metadata.

A diffuse feature firing on spans of generic, filler-like prose, typical of synthetic, SEO-spam, or subtly incoherent web text (e.g. fabricated facts, boilerplate explanations, marketing blurbs). It is not tied to specific words. It is strongest on fluent explanatory or opinion clauses such as "how much better blend tastes using these methods" or "I definitely have challenges with".

36543.name: Nouns (and some nearby words) naming concrete amenities, fixtures, equipment, appliances, furnishings, or provided facilities, typically items within an enumerated list describing what a home, venue, or product has or offers. The strongest activations come from descriptions of property and amenities such as kitchen countertops, cabinetry, appliances, gyms, games rooms and retailers.

Concrete items listed as amenities, furnishings, supplies or provisions in descriptive or listing contexts. It fires most strongly on appliances and fixtures in hotel rooms, kitchens and homes (microwave, mini-fridge, stainless steel appliances, A/C, Nespresso machine), and more weakly on food items and other provided goods.

3657.name: A weak, diffuse feature whose strongest activations fall on phrases about inspecting, examining or verifying something: "do your research, visit the sites, double check", "click and look closely", "open", "checks the tag", "get a better look", "explore", "request documentation / conduct on-site reviews" and "further evaluation demonstrates". It also fires faintly on many scattered function words and nouns with no clear pattern.

36591.name: Expletive (dummy) subject constructions, chiefly "it" or "there" followed by a copula or auxiliary ("it is", "it's", "there will", "it was", "it can be"). The verb carries the strongest signal, especially in impersonal phrasing that introduces an evaluative or extraposed clause ("it is necessary/possible/important to…", "it is believed that…").

Expletive/dummy-subject constructions: the copula (is/was/’s) right after a non-referential "it" or "there" (and sometimes the pronoun itself), as in "it is necessary/possible to…", "it was found that…", "there is…". Activation is strongest on "is" in impersonal "it is + adjective/participle" frames.

36600.name: Nouns, mostly mass or substance terms (lead, dust, paint, energy, text), that follow a quantity or partitive phrase such as "amount of", "piece of", "levels of" or "strip of". The noun names the material or stuff being measured.

Head nouns (mostly mass or plural) naming the substance or thing being quantified, typically right after a quantity or measure expression like "a lot of", "pair of", "100 grams of", "how much", "more" or a number.

3665.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single trigger. It fires on continuation tokens inside multi-word titles, terms and set phrases, mostly the connecting words and word endings. The clearest cases are paper or article titles, including their URL-slug forms: "of", "for", "in", "-of", and suffixes like "ulsion", "ICS" and "ATION". It also fires on the final pieces of fixed compounds and collocations, such as Ku Klux "Klan", word "processing", risk "factors" and "frictionless". Occasional weak hits appear on code, math notation and non-English text.

3710.name: Field-label or key tokens in structured or boilerplate web text (form fields, HTML attributes like name/alt/port, metadata labels like Name/DATE/TITLE/ID/doi, "Skip to main content", colons after labels). They mark the point right before a value or the main content follows.

Field labels and the separators that come right after them, where a name, title, value or identifier is about to follow. Examples include header and metadata fields ("Title:", "Company name", "Topic:", "Q"), words like "titled", "headline" and "addressed", key-value markers in code, JSON and HTML ("title\":", "id", "src", " ="), and URL query parameters ("?q", "?id", "?p").

3730.name: Fires weakly on short, predictable filler in templated or metadata text, mainly the digit after a decimal point in version numbers, ratings and measurements ("v1.0", "4.53 of 5", "pH 7.4"), and the last digit of years. It also hits boilerplate tokens such as bullet points, "times" in view counts, "Original language English" and separators in web page chrome.

Digits in version numbers and ratings, chiefly the part after a decimal point (the "0" in "1.0", "3.0", "v4.2.3") and scores like "4.8/5" or "3/5". Activation is strongest on version strings in URLs and licenses. It also fires weakly on values following a metadata field label (e.g. "Gender: Male", "GMT").

37405.name: A diffuse feature of news-style journalistic prose. It fires weakly on scattered content words and phrases in factual reporting and fires most strongly on longer spans that give the substance of a reported statement, claim, ruling or official directive. Typical examples are text following 'said', or clauses like 'ensure the implementation of Corona SOPs…' and 'the 16 cows that died is worth over N5m'.

A diffuse feature firing across formal news-report prose, especially politics, government, and public affairs. It is strongest on long spans of indirect reported speech or official statements, such as what officials said about problems, authorities, or government actions. These spans often come from South Asian or international news. Elsewhere it fires weakly on scattered content words and numbers like dates, durations, and counts.

37453.name: The second word of short website boilerplate and UI navigation phrases (e.g. "Skip to content", "Search form", "Menu Close", "bottom of page", "Connect with us", "Scroll To Top", "Forgot password"). These are fragments from scraped web page chrome such as menus, buttons and form labels. Activation is usually weak, with the strongest on "form" in "Search form".

Second word of web-page boilerplate UI labels scraped from site navigation, firing most strongly on "form" in "Search form" at the start of a page. It responds weakly to other interface element words such as contact form, submitting this form, menu, login, Log in, Footer, and Header.

37611.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on hard-to-predict, information-bearing slot fillers: proper names (people, places, organizations), numbers in dates, versions and figures, and specific technical nouns. These usually appear right after a preposition, conjunction or label that sets up the slot. It often fires on the first subword of a rare name. No single semantic theme ties the examples together.

Weak, diffuse feature on the first token (or subword piece) of a content word that begins a new noun phrase, most often a proper noun such as a person, place, organization, product or month. It typically appears right after a preposition, article or verb, in the slot where the object or name is introduced. Numbers, titles (Ms, Mr) and some common nouns in the same position also activate it.

37629.name: Tokens inside formal or symbolic notation, mostly LaTeX math expressions (variables, subscripts, superscripts, fractions, sums, limits), plus code such as loop headers, assignments and function calls. Activation is strongest in the middle of long math formulas. There are weak sporadic hits on other text, such as boilerplate like 'Scroll to Top'.

Tokens inside mathematical notation, formulas and code, especially variable names, operators, numbers and LaTeX commands (e.g. \frac, \sin, ^\circ, \mathbb R, x^2). It is strongest in dense inline math expressions and weak on stray tokens in ordinary prose.

Mathematical and quantitative content: tokens inside math expressions, LaTeX formulas, variables, numbers and technical terms (integrals, functions, sets, units, chemistry names, code variables). Activation is strongest in dense formula or problem statements (e.g., integrands, function definitions) and weak on scattered numeric or technical words in ordinary prose.

37770.name: Words that express generality, breadth or non-specificity, most often "general" and what follows it ("general terms", "in general", "general sense/information/knowledge", "general-purpose", "generic terms"). Weaker hits are broad or diffuse qualifiers such as "global", "overall", "uniformly", "widely", "high level", "neutral" and "dull ache".

Words marking generality or broad, non-specific scope, most strongly "general" (also universal, abstract, broad, plain, basic, all, public), typically modifying nouns like questions, area or health and often set against something specific. Weak, scattered activations also occur on unrelated words and punctuation.

3785.name: Marks the output or return type of a function or operation. The strongest cases are the type written right after "->" in Rust and Python signatures (u32, Self, String, int, RustIdent). It fires more weakly on nouns that name what something returns, yields or produces ("returns the column... permutation vector", "yields the indices of", "resultant percent value", "status codes").

37870.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on tokens at the start of a span that repeats or completes something predictable from earlier context, i.e. copying/induction-like positions. This is clearest in code, where it marks the first piece of a previously used identifier or argument (e.g., "(folder"Path, "sent"ryTraceHeader, "#n"FileNum, "${var.aws"). In prose it falls on function words just before a repeated name or phrase ("to" Thornaby, "the" curve) and on separators like ":" or "://" in structured fields.

The first token of an argument or complement right after a verb, preposition or function name, where the object is about to follow. It is strongest in recipe instructions ("melt the", "warm the", "bake at", "into the prepared") and on the opening parenthesis plus first argument of code calls ("setuid (pw", "(temp", "(kernel"). It also fires weakly on similar continuation points in ordinary prose.

3834.name: Boundaries between clauses, sentences or code blocks: sentence-ending periods, closing brackets/semicolons, newlines and markdown fences, plus the first word or two of the next sentence or clause (The, This, If you, When you, For). Activation is highest where a statement or code block ends and a new one begins.

38462.name: Words about size, fit and suitability: sizes, dimensions, measurements and capacity, plus things made or chosen to suit a person or need (fit properly, custom-made, left-handed, levels, different options). It peaks on "size"/"sizes" and fit-related words.

Words about size, fit and measurement, especially for clothing and products: "size/sizes/sizing", size labels (S, M, L, XL, cup letters, shoe numbers), "fit/fitted/fitting", measures, inches, mm. Strongest on explicit size terms in shopping/product listings; weaker on loosely related product-spec and adjustment words.

3856.name: Words that set up a comparison, resemblance or perceived impression, mainly perception and seeming verbs (sounds, looks, feels, seems, appears, comes across as) and comparison markers (like, as if, than, equivalent of, more X than Y). Activation is strongest on 'like' and the verb right after it, and covers the words that begin the description of what something resembles or seems to be.

38689.name: A diffuse, weak feature that fires at syntactic boundaries where one clause or phrase ends and the next begins. It peaks on sentence-final punctuation (often followed by newlines), on commas, and on the final noun of a phrase just before a new clause or a connective such as 'or that', 'as', 'if', 'when' or 'that'.

Diffuse, weak activation at clause and sentence boundaries: the last word of a clause, the punctuation that ends it (commas, periods, colons, paragraph breaks), and the connectors or first words that open the next clause (because, if, that, but, The). The feature tracks points where one syntactic unit closes and another begins.

38850.name: Punctuation (mostly commas, occasionally "and", a dash, or "in") that comes right after a complete clause or statement and marks the boundary before a continuation. The continuation usually adds a contrast ("but"), a consequence ("so", "and"), an elaboration or a qualification to the same sentence.

Commas (and occasionally other mid-sentence punctuation like semicolons or ellipses) that end a complete clause or phrase and introduce a continuation, often a contrast, qualification, or follow-up clause ("..., but", "..., not just", "..., so").

38859.name: Words that introduce or refer to questions, prompts, tasks, or items given to respondents (e.g., "questions", "asked to", "assignment", "surveys", "this question"). The strongest activations come in survey, questionnaire, and test contexts, especially where participants or students are being asked something.

Words about asking questions, mainly the nouns "question(s)" and the verb "ask/asked", in contexts like surveys, interviews, polls, quizzes and exams. The strongest cases are questions put to respondents ("questions asked the subjects to", "ask complicated questions"). Weaker activations fall on related words such as answers, polls, surveys, variables and assignments.

3907.name: Mentions of official positions, titles, and institutional bodies. It fires most strongly on government or organizational role words (Minister, Secretary, President, director, Coordinator, Ministry, Council) and the surrounding appositive or role phrases that introduce named officials or authorities. Activation is weaker for generic group or organization nouns.

392.name: Spans of promotional, engaging, marketing- or PR-style prose (blog intros, listicle hooks, mission statements, event and product pitches) that address or excite the reader. Activation is spread across whole phrases rather than single words, and is strongest on calls to action and enthusiastic hooks like "get ready to unwind" or "you've come to the right place". Dry technical or tabular text barely activates.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires on generic, formulaic phrasing typical of synthetic or LLM-generated text, such as task directives ("compute", "calculate", "explore and provide"), upbeat or motivational slogans ("Team up for success", "help you find information"), and dramatic concluding narrative lines. It often appears in noisy or garbled text and peaks on catchy, cliché-like phrases.

3923.name: Tokens inside repetitive or patterned sequences, where the next token is predictable from earlier repetition: repeated phrases ("Loading...", "Final Four", "Sacred Valley"), number runs, list separators, whitespace or newline padding, HTML table tags, and repeated characters or symbols. Activations are generally weak and scattered, strongest on spaces and numbers in counting sequences.

Tokens inside highly repetitive, looping sequences where the same token or short pattern (words, symbols, newlines, quotes, table dividers, numbered markup) repeats many times. Activation is strongest for long runs of a single repeated token and weaker for loosely repeating or noisy patterns.

39279.name: Mass nouns for transferable or stored content, chiefly "data" and also "information", "text", "files", "content", "code" and "ideas". They usually appear as objects of verbs of transfer, storage, processing or protection (send, transmit, exchange, store, encode, transform). Activation is strongest when the context describes data moving between systems.

Nouns for stored or transmitted digital content, chiefly "data" and also "information", "files", "content", "text" and "images". They usually appear as the object of verbs like store, access, transmit, restore or copy. Activation is strongest for "data" in technical computing and storage contexts, with weak firing on other abstract quantities such as payments and earnings.

3942.name: Weak, diffuse activation on structural boundary tokens in formatted or code-like text: line breaks, closing brackets/braces followed by newlines, indentation whitespace, list numbering periods, table row tags, and the first token starting a new line, field, or list item. It marks the point where one structural unit ends and the next begins.

39454.name: Final words of web UI link/button text that end a truncated snippet or point to further content, mainly "more" in "Read more", "(More)", "Show more", plus similar labels like "Read Next", "Click for Answer", "Apply Here", "full list", "Impact Factor", and ellipsis or back-link (↩) markers.

Words in link text placed after a truncated excerpt or teaser that lead to the full content, especially the "More" in "Read More", plus "reading" in "Continue reading", "Review", "Profile", ellipsis markers like "[…]", and "here"/"enlarge" in "click here".

4013.name: Diffuse, weak activation on boilerplate and metadata text such as site disclaimers, license and copyright notices, "X is a question and answer site" blurbs, citation and legal references, and web page navigation or help notes. It fires on scattered function words, numbers and punctuation within these formulaic passages rather than on any single token type.

4026.name: Weak, diffuse activations in formal academic, institutional, or project-description text, such as paper titles, abstracts, theses, affiliations, and initiative announcements. It fires mostly on structural or transitional tokens: sentence breaks, paragraph newlines, discourse openers like 'However' or 'Moreover', and phrases framing the research or project ('This research originates from', 'within the Top Institute', 'Project Director', 'Doctoral thesis').

40343.name: Function words and clause-opening phrases in instructional, tech-support or how-to prose aimed at the reader, especially conditional or advisory framing such as "If you…", "Please make sure…", "You will/may…" and "For instructions on…".

Diffuse, low-level activation on function words and verb phrases in instructional, conditional or advisory text (tech help, how-to guides, terms/notices). Strongest on hedged or conditional clauses addressed to the reader, such as 'if you do not have', 'you don't need to', 'this method requires you to' and 'a problem which may be cleared', with modals, 'to' and clause boundaries.

4053.name: Mostly weak, diffuse activation on technical and code text. It is strongest on CPU/assembly instruction mnemonics such as LD BC, ADD and NOP. Weaker activations hit command names, keywords and identifier fragments in code, shell commands and technical docs (e.g. rm, ssh, let, Dim, GET).

40641.name: Punctuation and separators that come right after a source title in citation or publication metadata, mostly a journal name. They mark the shift to the year, volume, issue or pages, as in "J Med Res;", "Eng." or "Theory,". Activation is strongest on the first delimiter after an abbreviated or full journal name, and weaker on later year, volume and page pieces and on labels like "Chapter", "Published" or "Report".

Punctuation and tokens immediately following the name of a publication (journal, newspaper, news agency, book source) in citations or datelines, i.e. the separator (comma, period, colon, dash, parenthesis, newline) or volume/year/date info that comes next. Strongest on the period after abbreviated medical journal names (e.g. 'N Engl J Med.', 'Arthritis Rheum.') before the year.

4085.name: The first token of a modifier that comes before a noun, usually right after a determiner like "a", "an", "the" or a possessive. Most often this is a number or number word forming a compound modifier, such as "a six-hour", "a 20% discount", "a one-day" or "a 5 week". Other prefix-like modifiers such as all-, mid-, no-, double- and large- also appear. Activation is strongest on numbers and "one", and on the space token before digits.

Numbers (digits or number words) and similar quantity modifiers that come right after a determiner like "a", "an", "the", "this" or "his" and begin a modifier, usually a hyphenated compound such as "two-month-old", "four-door" or "eight-hour", or an ordinal or measurement. Activation is highest on spelled-out numbers before a hyphen.

409.name: A weak, diffuse latent that peaks on play-by-play descriptions of physical action in sports and fights, such as wrestling moves (lockup, knee, forearm, chop), a runner tagged at home plate, or a player fouled. Weaker activations scatter across event narration, like a currency vacillating, a swing that misses, a car going too fast, or players walking onto the pitch.

Descriptions of sports and competitive gameplay, such as scoring plays, tackles, ball distribution, race strategy, deficits to overturn, and course mistakes. Activation is strongest in play-by-play or game-recap narration (e.g., "3-point play", "attempted to tackle"). Weaker activations fall on physical actions, maneuvers or tactical phrasing in non-sports text.

4143.name: Punctuation, whitespace or newline tokens (colons, commas, line breaks, spaces, opening quotes/brackets) that come right after an unfinished phrase, often a preposition or introducing word like "is", "by", "that" or "because". They mark a break just before the expected continuation, such as a list, formula, quote, URL or name.

41517.name: Names of historical dynasties, empires, eras, peoples and ruling powers (e.g., Qing, Tang, Mongol, Tudors, Habsburg, Edo, Persia), often the token after "the" or a name fragment, strongest for Chinese/Asian dynasties and periods.

Proper-name tokens (often word fragments) for historical dynasties, empires, rulers, peoples and ancient or fictional realms (e.g., Qing, Habsburg, Hohenstaufen, Ottoman, Aztec, Goguryeo, Sith). Activation is strongest on dynasty and royal-house names and weaker on other historical or exotic place and person names.

4152.name: A weak, diffuse pattern that fires on tokens inside repetitive or parallel structures, such as list items and their separators, array indices, numbered sequences, table cells, and repeated math or code expressions. It responds most to separators (commas, brackets, operators) and to successive elements once the pattern has been established. Prose examples are rare and weak.

4173.name: Words or word pieces that name a field, sector, industry, or domain of activity, such as healthcare, retail, biotechnology, life sciences, energy, or defence. They often appear as modifiers before 'sector'/'industry' or in department and organization names. Activation is strongest on the domain noun itself, e.g. 'sciences', 'biotechnology', 'healthcare'.

4182.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sparsely on scattered tokens: verbs, nouns and punctuation in prose, and identifiers or operators in code. It is somewhat more frequent in procedural or sequential text such as instructions, steps, "then do X", lists and code. The strongest activations fall on code annotations and formula operators.

41874.name: Action/function names being invoked, mostly method or command names right after an accessor (., ->, ::) or a CLI program (connect, read, findClosest, textSearch, runString, step, flags). It also fires more weakly on action verbs after "to" or "can" in prose (ensure, convert, find, assist).

The action or operation word that directly follows an agent or object: verbs after a subject or modal ("does not endorse", "will produce", "module determines", "might block") and method or function names after an object accessor in code (".build", ".Print", "->QuerySongs", ".getPropertyValue"). It also fires on similar action or resource segments in URLs and commands ("submit", "?q", "/projects", "wpt run").

41932.name: Place names (cities, states, venues), especially ones that stand in for sports teams or organizations (e.g., Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Atlanta, Washington). Activation is strongest in sports contexts where the location acts as a team or as the site of a game.

Place names (cities, states, regions), especially when they stand for sports teams, institutions or governments (e.g. "Chicago", "Cleveland", "New York", "Washington"). Activation is strongest on the final token of the name and in sports contexts. It also fires weakly on other team or organization references ("OU", "Imperial", "team").

41958.name: The word "newspaper(s)" and synonyms such as "paper(s)", strongest for "newspaper" itself. Weaker activation goes to related news/print media terms (tabloids, publications, magazine, media, broadcaster, gazette) and to word fragments like "new|sgroups" and "new|scast".
Words referring to newspapers and print news outlets, strongest on "newspaper(s)" and also "paper", "daily", "tabloids", "gazette", "Zeitung", "periodicals", and related press or news-media terms.

4199.name: A diffuse, weak feature, densest in code. It fires on highly predictable tokens: second halves of split words (Hou-this, l-umin-osity, Countergl-omp), and identifiers, variables and arguments copied from earlier context (user.password_hash, message, average, InstallMode). It also fires on boilerplate continuations such as 'top of page' and 'Date of Birth:'.

4217.name: Diffuse, low-level activation with no clear semantic theme. It fires mostly mid-way through arbitrary character strings such as numbers in phone numbers, IDs, URLs, prices and codes, subword fragments of names and foreign words, and occasionally on function words or paragraph breaks. The strongest hits are numeric chunks inside codes or prices (e.g. "SM 1417", "$187."). Overall it reads as a generic token-continuation feature for unpredictable sequences.

Tokens in the middle of alphanumeric identifiers and codes such as model/part numbers, phone numbers, IDs, hashes, URLs, dates and timestamps, mostly digit chunks and letter fragments inside longer strings. There is also weak, scattered firing on ordinary words.

4236.name: A diffuse, weakly-activating feature with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words such as articles, prepositions and conjunctions ('a', 'the', 'of', 'and', 'for'), and on punctuation at phrase or line boundaries, where a new noun phrase or content segment is about to begin. It occasionally fires on word fragments too. The strongest isolated hit is 'buy' in 'where to buy'.

A diffuse, weakly activating pattern with no clear semantic theme. It mostly fires on function words such as prepositions ('for', 'as', 'of', 'with', 'in'), articles ('a', 'the'), conjunctions and punctuation (commas, periods, brackets). These usually sit just before the start of a new noun phrase or named entity, at phrase boundaries in ordinary web text. The strongest activations come at such transitions, for example 'for' before an object, ', a', ' (www', and 'and' in lists.

42402.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature that mostly fires on tokens inside or next to numeric and quantity expressions: number words and fractions (one, half, quarter, two, six, twenty), ordinal suffixes and words (nd, th, second), dates and weekdays (Friday, Wednesday, September of), units (pages) and comparisons (or lower, × the). It also fires on list or enumeration connectors (1, 2 or 4; x, y and z). The remaining activations are scattered punctuation and function words with no clear pattern.

Weak, diffuse feature on mostly low-content connector tokens (of, per, by, an, and, the, th) inside formulaic constructions, especially right after numbers or names in dates (“March of”, “27th of”), rates and prices (“$10 Per”, “$7.25 an hour”), measurements (“43 inches by”, “6-foot”) and lists. The token links one element to the next in a fairly predictable pattern.

42449.name: Words that name the ordinary, mortal or earthly realm, usually set against something higher, alien, supernatural or beyond. Typical hits are Earth/earthly, human (beings), our bodies, mundane, ordinary, reality and the present. Activation is strongest when humans or Earth are contrasted with aliens, the divine or paradise (e.g., "to human beings", "people of Earth", "earthly paradise", "this body is named").

Words that denote the mundane, mortal, earthly realm of human existence, often in implicit contrast to the divine, spiritual, supernatural or nonhuman: "humans", "mortal", "this life", "here", "our world", "our plane", "Earth", "material brain", "human construct". Activation is strongest where the word marks this-worldly human existence as opposed to something beyond it.

428.name: Tokens that begin with or contain the letter sequence "ab"/"AB" (e.g. abstract, abuse, ability, above, abounds, Abraham, Abass, sabre), strongest when "ab" starts the word. It also fires weakly on nearby a-initial words such as about, available, adoption and Africa.

42804.name: A diffuse feature that is strongest on smooth, formulaic, generic expository prose of the boilerplate, SEO or LLM-sounding kind. Typical sources are job ads ('strong understanding of…', 'track record of working'), tech marketing ('scalable and can quickly defend'), and bland biographies ('a force for good'). It fires across whole clichéd phrases and on the sentence-ending periods and line breaks within them. Elsewhere it gives only weak, scattered activations on punctuation, formatting and random tokens.

A diffuse, weakly-firing feature with no clear lexical trigger. It spreads across runs of ordinary function words, punctuation and repetitive tokens, often in garbled, synthetic-looking or repetitive text. It is strongest at sentence and clause boundaries: periods, paragraph breaks, and the transition words that start the next clause ("However", "Similarly", "but", "and").

4299.name: The day-of-month number in a date, plus any ordinal suffix (th, nd) or a month name that follows it. Common formats include 'May 18, 2015', '28 Feb 2024' and numeric forms like 02/26/2019 or 26.01.2018. Activation is strongest when the day follows a written month name, especially one preceded by a weekday (e.g. 'Saturday, May 11'). It is weak for purely numeric dates, timestamps and non-date numbers.

43385.name: Later digit chunks inside long multi-token numbers (after a comma, decimal point, or a prior digit group), such as trailing digits, decimal places, "000" groups and continued Roman numerals, with occasional unit words or name suffixes that directly follow a number.

Trailing digit chunks (and separators) inside long multi-token numbers: the later/final tokens of large integers or precise decimals, typically in computed results, conversions, prices, and measurements, not the leading digits.

Trailing digit chunks inside long multi-digit numbers. These are the later tokens after the first chunk, as in computed results, conversions, sequences and IDs. Activation is strongest deep in very long numbers.

43388.name: Nouns that name a quantity or numeric value, mostly monetary: amount, sum, cost, price, total, figure, value, number (also Italian/Portuguese equivalents like Subtotale and Valor). They fire most strongly on "sum"/"amount" in financial contexts such as "a sum of money" or "principal amount", and weakly on physical quantities like weight, distance and force.

Nouns that stand for a quantity or numeric value, especially monetary ones: "amount"/"amounts" (strongest, e.g. "amount due", "total amount"), plus "sum", "total", "number", "balance", "cost", "principal", "funds", "distance" and "how much". They usually appear in math word problems, financial text or code, and are often preceded by modifiers such as "total", "loan" or "maximum".

4340.name: The word "In" (sometimes with a following "the"/"a") at the start of a sentence or paragraph, opening an introductory prepositional or transitional phrase such as "In fact", "In this case", "In a paper". It activates most strongly right after a period or line break. Lowercase mid-sentence "in" and other sentence openers like "After" activate only weakly.

43423.name: Sports narrative about player and game performance, strongest in baseball and cricket recaps and stat descriptions (e.g., 'went 2-for-4', 'reaches base on a hit, walk', 'one batter after another'). It fires on the connective and function words, player names and verbs describing the action. Weak scattered activations appear on similar play-by-play text in other domains such as poker, casino games and card rules.

Sports play-by-play and game-recap narration, strongest in baseball. It fires on the function words and connective tokens that carry the action forward: prepositions, articles, commas, periods and phrases like "started with a", "after a single by", "hits a … to center field". It also lights up on numbers in stat lines such as "with 35 walks and 10 … in 61 games". Activation is highest in dense sequences of plays, and weak on isolated tokens in general sports text.

43444.name: Double newline that comes right after a blog or article header line, such as a date (strongest for full weekday-plus-date lines like "Monday, 21 November 2016"), an author name, or a read time, just before the post title or body begins.

The double newline right after a date line heading a blog post (e.g., "Monday, 29 June 2009"), marking where the post title or body begins. It fires most strongly on day-month-year (British-style) dates and dates at the very start of the text, and less on US-style dates following "Pages".

43683.name: Tokens spelling "it" in any form. Mostly the pronoun "it"/"It" (subject, object, expletive/dummy uses like "it is", "it turns out", "what it means"), but also case and orthographic variants such as "IT", ".it", "its", and "itch".

The word "it" (and variants such as "It", "its", and misused "it's"), most strongly when it opens a sentence or paragraph as a subject, often a dummy or expletive subject ("It's...", "It is said"). It also fires weakly on "IT" in the sense of Information Technology.

4394.name: Fires in news and article prose on markers of sourcing and discourse structure. The strongest hits are attribution phrases naming where information comes from: "Business Insider reports that", "Via BleepingComputer", "The Sun reported", "according to", "as per", "said", "news release", "NSA's guidance". It also fires on sentence-final punctuation followed by a paragraph break (".⏎⏎") at transitions between paragraphs or sections.

Discourse boundaries and source/attribution markers in news and blog text: paragraph breaks after headlines or sentence ends, closing punctuation of quotes, and phrases that cite or point to a source or the article itself (e.g. wire-service credits, 'reported', 'appeared at', 'Read more', 'Story continues below', 'read the rest of her post', publisher and edition info). Activations are generally weak and diffuse.

440.name: Separators within lists, enumerations and sequences of parallel items: commas, "and", periods, newlines, bullet dashes and pipes that sit between consecutive list elements, clauses or entries. Activation is strongest in long repetitive enumerations such as number lists, bulleted instructions and constructor initializer lists.

4402.name: Citation and reference markers: numeric tokens inside brackets/parentheses/superscripts referring to sources (e.g., [10], (29), [1]), plus final digits of years in author-year citations. Strongest on standalone bracketed reference numbers; weaker on other trailing numbers, IDs, and page markers.

44053.name: Connective tokens ("that" in "is that", colons, commas, periods, bullets, "because") right after a phrase introducing a drawback, limitation or problem ("the downside is", "disadvantages:", "unfortunately,", "however,"), at the point where the specific negative point is about to be stated. Weaker on similar slots before lists of features or other explanations.

Function words and punctuation (mostly "that", "is", "because", commas, colons, periods) at the point right after a statement introducing a problem, drawback, flaw, limitation or concern, just before the clause explaining what it is (e.g. "the problem is that…", "one drawback is that…", "has a fatal flaw:").

4406.name: Weak, diffuse activation on the start of a noun phrase serving as the object or complement of a preceding preposition or verb. Typical governing words are 'to', 'with', 'by', 'from', 'of', 'through', 'beyond', 'around' and 'meet'. Activation covers determiners and demonstratives ('the', 'this', 'that', 'its'), pronouns and the head noun or name, as in 'to the show', 'beyond this world', 'of the Danube River' and 'by Kathleen'. It is strongest right after the governing word and fades across the rest of the phrase.

4443.name: Names of news outlets and media sources, firing on the final or distinguishing token of the publication's name (Times, Post, Globe, Tribune, Weekly, Variety, Reuters, AP, AFP, Media, Eurogamer). It also responds to generic media words (newspapers, press, radio) and source attribution contexts such as photo credits and 'told X'. Weak activations occur on website domain pieces and dateline line breaks.

Names of news outlets and publications, especially the final word of a newspaper title (Post, Times, Herald, Independent, Advocate, Globe), plus words like "newspaper" and "press". Activation peaks when the token completes a paper's name and the outlet is cited as a source ("told the New York Times", "the Washington Post"). Other media brands such as radio stations, magazines, journals and websites fire weakly.

4453.name: Temporal prepositions and conjunctions that anchor a time relative to a reference event (since, after, following, once, upon, from, post-, when), strongest when marking time elapsed after an event (e.g. 'shortly after its arrival', 'years after his ouster').

Temporal prepositions and conjunctions that place something relative to a reference event, chiefly "after" and also "since", "upon", "following" and "within minutes of", together with the determiner, pronoun or auxiliary that follows them. Activation peaks on "after" when it comes right after a time expression such as "shortly", "long", "a week", "40 days", "months" or "immediately". Weaker activations land on other spatial or relational prepositions like "above", "of" and "from".

446.name: The last word of a clause or sentence, typically the head noun (or adverb/adjective/verb) that completes a phrase immediately before a period, comma, or conjunction. It fires most strongly on sentence-final nouns that close a prepositional or object phrase (e.g. "environment", "society", "horizon", "time").

Phrase-final words that complete a noun phrase, clause or idiomatic unit, typically the head noun or closing word right before punctuation, a preposition or a new clause (e.g. "memory usage.", "further assistance.", "after the fact.", "get there,"). The pattern holds across prose, code comments and several languages. Activations are weak on fragments in repetitive or garbled text.

4489.name: Comparison and relational operators, strongest for symbolic inequality operators (>, <, >=, <=) in code conditionals and math, weaker for LaTeX forms (\leq, \geq, >), word equivalents (above, below, exceeds, between, within, at least), and breadcrumb '>' separators.

4497.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly inside standardized publishing and legal boilerplate: copyright and permission notices ("strictly personal, individual use", "open content license", "reprint/republish… creating new collective works"), open-archive disclaimers ("deposit and dissemination"), citation and research-portal templates (closing quote before "Together they form a unique fingerprint"), and trademark or official-use disclaimers. It especially activates on words about using, reproducing, distributing or documenting works, and sometimes on year digits and punctuation in this kind of metadata. Elsewhere it fires sporadically on word fragments and stray tokens.

45113.name: Statements describing what will happen as a promise, reassurance or expected consequence (e.g. "then we will display it", "assured that improved wages would", "all would be well", "an attempt will be remade").
