62706.name: Words describing operations or changes applied to something (replace, add/remove, rearrange, transform, switch, double, modify, tilt, increase), plus the context of whether a result is invariant to or depends on such changes (e.g., "invariant with respect to the renormalization group", "depend on the choice of"). The feature is mostly in technical or mathematical writing and fires weakly on scattered tokens elsewhere.

Words about altering, transforming or freely choosing things: change, transform, deform, move, substitute, transpose, double, cut. It also covers arbitrariness or interchangeability ('any other', 'any two', 'either way', 'same thing on both sides', 'commutative', 'isomorphic'). The shared idea is applying an operation or variation and asking whether the result stays equivalent or invariant. It is strongest in mathematical contexts about equivalence under transformation.

62799.name: Subword fragments in the middle of rare, unfamiliar words, mostly foreign proper names (people, places, companies) and drug names, where a word is split into several uncommon pieces; the activation is on an internal fragment, before the word is finished.

Middle subword fragments inside rare, multi-token proper nouns (mostly unusual surnames, foreign given names, and place names), firing on the internal pieces after the first token and before the word ends.

6283.name: The final noun (or noun phrase) of a coordinated list or conjunction, mostly the item right after "and"/"or" or a list comma that closes the phrase, typically just before a period or comma.

The final noun or noun phrase in a coordinated list or pair, usually right after "and", "or", "but", a comma or "+". It marks the second or later item that completes a parallel series, such as "and Cowboys", "Diplo and Bieber", or "heart, lungs, and brain". Commas or periods that close the item are sometimes included.

62980.name: Words that follow a short imperative verb in website or interface boilerplate, such as "Cite this", "Cite this article as", "Export as", "Share as", "Run as", "Revision as of", "Posting as", "View As". The word "as" after such a command is by far the most frequent, and citation and reference prompts ("Cite this", "cite or link to") activate most strongly.

Function words, chiefly "as" plus "at", "using", "with", "by", that come right after a verb in website boilerplate and UI text, such as "Flag as inappropriate", "Revision as of", "referenced as", "Published at", "Log in using" and "Give as a gift". The words that complete a citation or attribution instruction ("cite the", "Preferred Citation") also activate. In each case the token links an action to the category, format or timestamp that follows it.

6314.name: Tokens inside proper names of places, mostly the later or completing subword piece of a geographic name (city, county, region, district, river, valley). Typical cases are Onondaga, Kitsap, Kingstown, Pradesh and Cape. Activation is weak and also spills onto a few other proper-name fragments, such as person or era names.

Geographic place names (cities, counties, states, regions, countries), with activation mostly on the final or later subword token of the name; strongest on regional/county-level names, especially those followed by words like "County".

63262.name: A weak, diffuse feature found in expository scientific and engineering prose about physical phenomena such as optics, fluids, materials, acoustics and circuits. It fires mostly on structural connectors where the explanation continues: sentence boundaries followed by a new sentence start ('. But', '. A', '. The'), clause commas, parentheses, and prepositions or articles like 'of', 'on the', 'that'. Occasionally it fires on technical nouns such as 'behaviour', 'distribution', 'design' and 'scenarios'.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across expository science and engineering text, such as research summaries, technology descriptions and environmental or physics explanations. It peaks on words that describe how something works, is designed or is studied: method and purpose phrases ("using", "so that", "to enhance", "included replacing", "aims at studying concepts to"), mechanism nouns ("noise reduction", "charge modulation") and fragments of technical names.

6402.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on function words, punctuation and delimiters at clause or list-item boundaries, such as semicolons, colons followed by line breaks, underscores in variable names, and newlines between dated entries. It is strongest in repetitive, templated text, like the repeated n_1, x_1, arr_1 assignments, cast lists, numbered sections and code. There it marks the point where the next parallel item or segment is about to begin.

64245.name: Words that express opposition or being against something, e.g. "oppose/opposed/opposing", "opposition (to)", "opponents of", "against", along with weaker antonymic or obstructive relations ("antithetical to", "obstructed", "in favor"). The strongest activations fall on forms of "oppose".

Words expressing opposition or a stance against something (oppose/opposed/opposing, against, opponents, opposition, at odds, object to), with the strongest activations on verbs like "opposed". Weaker activations appear on support or favor terms (support, favor, backs, all for) and on "opp" letter strings in unrelated words (Oppenheimer, Stoppard, oppression).

64251.name: Mostly numeric tokens in sequences or references: list/part numbers, citation superscripts, page numbers, years' final digits, dates and counts. These are often items in an ordered series (Part 8, 9, 10…; refs 16, 17). Weaker activation on sentence-ending periods/paragraph breaks and a few ordinal words ("second", "five").

Numbers (or the final digit/ordinal suffix of a number) that act as an identifier in a sequence or index: dates (day after a month, last digit of a year), citation/figure/item/issue numbers, "N of M" counters, list numbering and ordinals. Month names that precede a date also activate weakly.

64707.name: Words that introduce source attribution, citation or provenance information: e.g. "quoted in/by", "reprinted", "reproduced", "posted", "retrieved from", "via", "licensed under", "Wikimedia/Commons", "see", "author of". They usually follow a source name or comma in credits, bylines and references. Strongest on "quoted"; weak, scattered activation on other connective words.

Words in attribution, sourcing and provenance phrases, mostly passive verbs and prepositions saying where content was published, quoted, credited, found or distributed (e.g. via, quoted by, published, posted, seen, referred to, Associated Press, License Photo, Supported by). Strongest on 'via' and 'quoted by'.

64717.name: First names or initials of people, mostly in author/contributor lists (academic papers, bylines), with the strongest activation on given names that come after the first entry in a list of several people and sit just before the surname.

First names (or their first subword/initial token) of people, especially a second or later person in a list of authors, researchers or credited contributors (after commas, "and", "Dr.", or a line break), usually followed by a surname and affiliation.

64787.name: Tokens that open a variable placeholder or interpolation in code, shell commands, URLs, or templates, such as "(!" field references, "${", "={", "{{", "%" format specifiers, and "$". These are the positions where a variable name or value gets substituted into a string or expression. Much weaker activations occur on scattered ordinary tokens, notably "page" in the boilerplate "top of page".

Template placeholders and variable slots: the opening delimiters ({{, {, [[, [, <, $) and names of fill-in fields where text is meant to be substituted (e.g. {{amount}}, {table_name}, <name>, [post_name], [insert ...], $search). It fires most strongly on the opening bracket of these slots and also weakly on other code-like syntax and odd fill-in tokens.

64872.name: Diffuse, mostly weak activations in expository technical writing, mainly programming, math and software docs. They fire on words that define or describe an abstract entity and how it is referenced, passed or made available, e.g. "is an object", "available to your scripts as the context object", "a symbol (like x, y, or z)", variables, placeholders, arrays and values. The strongest hits fall on explanations of what an identifier or object represents.

Mostly technical/programming documentation describing what role an entity plays or where it goes, such as how a value is passed, represented, added or placed. It fires most on role nouns like 'argument', 'variables', 'parameter', 'Context', 'slots' and 'pronoun', and on role-assigning phrases like 'passed as the first argument', 'is represented by a' and 'added as a'. It also fires weakly on placeholder-like tokens such as 'None' and 'XXXX'.

649.name: Diffuse, low-level activation across tokens of generic, formulaic web prose, strongest and densest in SEO/marketing-style or boilerplate explanatory text (e.g., product pitches, business advice, health claims), with weaker spikes at sentence boundaries and transitional phrases (". This", "In fact", "Moreover"). Specific narrative or news content activates only sparsely.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires broadly on ordinary tokens (content nouns, verbs, connectives, punctuation) in generic expository or assistant-style text, such as tech and code explanations, tutorials, product descriptions, and essays, including garbled or non-English text. It has no specific lexical trigger. It peaks mildly on runs of descriptive or explanatory prose, for example marketing claims like 'boxes are both durable and safe'.

65114.name: Forms of the word "disclose" (disclose, disclosed, disclosure(s), undisclosed, and the "losure" piece of non-disclosure) in any sense: revealing information, legal or financial disclosure, and affiliate disclaimers. Weak activations appear on related revealing verbs such as "divulge" and "discussed".
Forms of the word "disclose" (disclose, disclosed, disclosure(s), undisclosed, Disclosure headers), i.e., revealing or making information known; weakly also fires on the similar-looking "discourse".

6521.name: Interrogative words (what, why, how, who) that open a question or a wh-clause, plus the words right after them (e.g., "What more could you", "What's wrong", "How to"). Activation is strongest on rhetorical or conversational questions and on free relative "what" clauses ("what really matters is"). It is weaker on headings such as "How to…" or "What is X?".

65400.name: The first symbol or token after an equals sign (or similar relation) in math, physics or code expressions, firing most strongly when the right-hand side repeats the variable or function name from the left side (e.g. u(0,x)=u(x), V=V_per+V_ω, ξ=ξ_S, f(x)=f(0)+…, y(0)=y(h), dp[i]=dp[…]).

The first token(s) on the right-hand side of a mathematical equation or definition (right after "=" or another relation), firing hardest when that symbol repeats the variable or function named on the left (e.g. "u = u(x,t)", "W = WΦ", "a = a'"). It fires weakly on similar relational slots in prose and code.

Math/code variables at the start of an expression's right-hand side (just after '=' or a relation), especially when they repeat a symbol from the left side, as in v = v_0 or f(a) = f(b). More weakly, any token that copies an earlier word or identifier (sacrificed the sacrifice, mute/unmute, repeated function names in code).

6564.name: Weak, diffuse feature on structural and technical text. It fires most strongly on generic placeholders or templates that describe a format rather than real content, such as "[Author names]. [Article title]", "name of author, name of recipient", "(ACCOUNT_LENGTH + 1)", "foo: f("foo")" and "/path/to". It also fires weakly on punctuation and delimiters in structured text: colons introducing a spec ("Received:", "rulestring: B"), braces, equals signs, tags, and code or math syntax.

6574.name: Words tied to schooling and education levels, such as school names, grade or year levels (high school, 10th grade, Class XII, elementary, varsity), degrees, majors and university names. Activation is strongest on terms for school stages like high school, grade and class, and weak on scattered unrelated word fragments.

6647.name: The conditional keyword "if"/"If" that begins a condition, strongest in code if-statements (e.g. "if (" / "if ($") and also common in sentence-initial prose "If" clauses. Weaker activation spreads onto the tokens of the condition expression, with faint scattered hits on other tokens.

Words opening a conditional clause, mainly sentence-initial "If"/"if" (also "Should", or a bare condition after "If"), especially when they lead into a branch or alternative outcome such as "If not…" or "if unsuccessful…". The pattern extends to comparison and condition operators in code ("!==", "<", "=").

6673.name: Words tied to the submission, filing, pending or publication status of documents. It is strongest on patent filings ("application", "Ser. No.", "divisional of", "filed") and also covers manuscripts or papers "submitted", "received", "preliminary", "ongoing", "pending" and "Manuscript". It also fires weakly on other metadata nouns such as paper, dissertation, publication, doi and arXiv.

670.name: A weak, diffuse feature firing on the opening words of a new sentence, title, or clause, often right after a heading or paragraph break. It covers the framing lead-in (subject, verb, and function words such as "I believe that if you want to", "Those who want to", "The funny thing is,", "Know Your Credit") up to, but usually not including, the main content noun.

A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires across stretches of ordinary running prose (function words, verbs, noun phrases mid-clause) rather than on specific tokens. It is strongest within explanatory or narrative clauses and is common in noisy, incoherent, or machine-generated-looking text, including prose fragments mixed into code or web boilerplate.

6702.name: A diffuse, weak feature with no clear semantic theme. It fires on ordinary mid-sentence tokens in running prose (and occasionally code), mostly function words and phrase-building words such as "the", "of", "to", "is", "with" and commas, plus verbs and nouns that open a continuing clause. Typical cases are "consider becoming a", "the options is to", "discover the most efficient one" and "impact of aquatic organism". Activation tends to rise slightly in multi-word stretches that lead into a complement or object, rather than on any particular topic or word.

6741.name: Fires most on the word "Sort", both as a capitalized command or label ("Sort by:", "Sort code") and in "a sort of". It fires more weakly on synonyms like "kind" and "type". It also responds weakly to related ideas of classifying, separating and working things out ("separation", "clustering", "discern", "figure out", "solved"). Scattered low activations elsewhere, often on verbs, appear to be noise.

6780.name: Clause or sentence boundaries, mostly the period (or period plus newline) ending a sentence and sometimes the first word of the next sentence, plus commas, semicolons and parentheses that close a clause. The strongest firing is on a sentence-final period after a completed statement, especially where the text continues with a new sentence.

Sentence and clause boundaries: mostly the period (or other end punctuation, often with following newlines) that closes a complete statement, plus clause-joining commas and conjunctions ("and", "while", "though", "But", "And") where one idea ends and the next begins. Activation is strongest at the end of short factual or listing statements.

6887.name: The second element of a hyphenated compound modifier (e.g., "-solving", "-energy", "-gas", "-quality"), i.e., the hyphen-prefixed token joining a word to the preceding word to form a compound adjective/noun modifier, usually before a head noun; weak scattered activations on other modifiers.

Tokens that join a word to the noun or word it modifies, mostly hyphenated compound pieces ("-meter", "-end", "-hour", "-abuse") forming compound modifiers. Possessive apostrophes ("trainers'", "day’s") also fire because they link a possessor to the following noun.

6889.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires most on words expressing equivalence, sameness or correspondence between things (equivalent, equal to, synonyms, identical, interchangeable, comparable, proportional, mappings, transformation, rename). It also gives faint activations on scattered word fragments and technical terms.

Words expressing sameness, equivalence or similarity between things (equivalent, same, isomorphism, synonyms, similarities, tantamount, twin, homogeneous, interchangeably, "amount to"), strongest on "isomorphism"; other activations are weak and scattered.

6912.name: Tokens deep inside long random-looking alphanumeric strings such as hex hashes, UUIDs, API keys, encoded URL parameters and long digit runs. Activation is strongest partway through the unpredictable character sequence, especially in hex and mixed letter-digit chunks. Weaker activation appears on IDs, DOIs, postal codes, numeric data and garbled-encoding text.

6981.name: References to the people or agents responsible for something: names of creators, founders, authors and speakers, along with the agentive phrases attached to them ("by the same authors", "co-founder", "producer of", "he established", "I"). Activation is strongest on personal names and creator or founder roles, especially after "by" or in appositives that introduce a person.

70.name: The very first token of a document, whatever it is (a title word, heading, byline, navigation text, newline or whitespace), marking the start of the text.

Fires on the very first token of a document or text sequence, whatever that token happens to be (a word, word fragment, symbol, code keyword, or whitespace/newline). Where the text opens with repeated filler like newlines or asterisks, the leading run is marked as well. The feature tracks sequence-start position, not content.

700.name: A broad, diffuse activation over ordinary running text: it covers long stretches of fluent prose, mostly in mid-sentence descriptive or explanatory clauses (marketing copy, narration, technical how-to). Activation tends to rise toward content words late in the clause. It is weaker or absent on code, boilerplate and identifiers, and is not tied to specific words.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature that spans runs of substantive content tokens in LLM/assistant-style technical text, such as code and markup, math formulas and worked calculations, problem statements, and clarification requests. It does not single out one specific word, and it is strongest on the core phrase of an explanation or definition.

7004.name: Words about updating or keeping current. The strongest are forms of "update" (updated, updates, Update), especially in "Last updated"/"Updated:" metadata, and "date" in "up to date". Weaker hits include related recency and newness terms such as latest, refresh, recent, upgrade, modern and advances.

7072.name: Weak activations on tokens inside predictable, boilerplate web and code text: navigation links and site chrome ("Skip to main content", "Login | Register", "Connect with us", "Leave a Reply"), metadata and licensing phrases ("Open Access", "Copyright", "Last Updated", "Issue"), and code file headers ("-*- coding", "Created on", package/import lines). The marked token is typically the word that completes the stock phrase.

7079.name: Marks where a conditional clause ends and its consequence begins: the comma, 'then', colon or brace and indentation after an if/once/given condition in prose or code (if…:, else, ') {'), plus the closing word of the condition itself (e.g. 'so', 'True', 'achieved'). Strongest on code colons and newlines following if statements.

7199.name: Section/chapter numbering and identifier tokens in structured references: digits and separators in chapter/section numbers, LaTeX \label{sec:intro}/{s1} keys, figure filenames, DOIs, URL path IDs, and index codes. Peaks on the number or key that names a section or item (e.g. the "1" in \label{s1}).

7216.name: Names of LaTeX text- and font-formatting commands written right after a backslash, such as \text, \mathrm, \operatorname, \mathbf, \textbf, \rm and \textit, usually in math mode just before a braced argument. Activation is strongest on \mathrm, the "name" part of \operatorname, and \text used in subscripts, units or labels. Other LaTeX command names (\url, \bibitem, \emph, \,) and HTML entities like ' activate only weakly.

7219.name: Past-participle attribution or permission words in legal and boilerplate notices (licensed, published, sponsored, certified, authorized, powered by, distributed). It is by far strongest on "Licensed" opening an Apache-style license comment at the top of a source-code file, and moderate on "licensed under" Creative Commons notices.

722.name: Boundaries between text segments, mostly newlines and sentence-ending punctuation followed by line breaks. It fires most strongly in structured metadata, such as citation and DOI blocks, key-value fields (Size:, Issue, Classification:) and section headers (Keywords, Index Terms). The first word of a new field or section often activates as well.

724.name: Fires on the tokens leading up to and starting a person's name (usually a surname): first names, initials, titles (Dr., Capt.), role nouns (historian), and introducers like "by", "said", "see", "and", commas and parentheses. It is strongest in academic citations and author lists, where it peaks on the opening parenthesis, list number, separator or "by" right before an author surname.

7271.name: Pieces of web and document metadata, especially URL parts ("://", "www", domains like ".com"/".org"/".edu", path segments), which activate most strongly. Weaker activations land on DOI numbers, file paths, citation fields (journal names, vol), site navigation, headers and names of sites or shows. Overall it tracks boilerplate reference and link text rather than ordinary prose.

7300.name: Boundary tokens (newlines, often fused with closing punctuation like '.', '?', '!', ')', '}', or stray spaces) that end one text segment, list item, or section right before an unrelated new segment, heading, or field begins. Strongest at abrupt topic/document shifts, e.g., before a new '###' heading or after a timestamp or "more" link.

7397.name: Weak, scattered activations on word pieces, often fragments, evoking hippie, new-age or wellness lifestyle culture: hippie, bohemian, Taoist, holistic, mindfulness, CBD, vegetarian/veggies, 'med' (as in meditate), harmonize, chill out, calm, trippin', workout/gyms and fasting. The strongest activations are on HIPPIE, med, mindfulness, CBD and Taoist.

7403.name: A weak, diffuse feature. It fires on words about whether something exists, is present, or can be found. Typical cases are finding, seeing, searching for or locating things, and existing or no longer existing. It also covers deleting, removing or destroying things, membership checks ('if … not in', 'exists', a count of 0), and memory or persistence ('memory', 'souvenir', 'toujours', '思念'). This holds in both prose and code.

7459.name: Operators and connective symbols that come right after a number (or variable) in math, LaTeX, or code. The strongest cases are multiplication signs (*, \cdot, ×) and the backslash starting a LaTeX command such as \pi or \times, especially in coefficient patterns like "2\pi" or "2 *". There is weaker activation on other separators that follow a numeric token.

7468.name: Tokens that close or end a structure, block, or segment, mainly closing markup: LaTeX \end{align*}/\end{eqnarray} (strongest), HTML closing tags (, , ), code fences, comment and region terminators, and closing brackets or quotes. It also fires weakly on the whitespace or newline at a boundary just before a new section or list item, such as the space before "1."

7482.name: Tokens that close a structured block: HTML/XML closing-tag openers ", , ), the brace after LaTeX \end, final closing braces of code classes/functions, and "End"/#endregion. Also weakly fires on boundary text after a section ends (e.g., "Leave a Reply", list labels).

7555.name: Weak, diffuse activations on tokens that cite or attribute information to media and publication sources: news articles, journals, press and source lines, URLs (https://www…), bylines, transcripts, interviews and 'according to'/'told'/'said' attributions.

Language about news media and the sourcing or attribution of reported information: news outlets and press items (news, media, press release/conference, story, edition, report, interview), attribution phrases ("according to", "reports say", "as the Guardian reports", "courtesy of", "via the", "photo credit"), and the punctuation or byline points where such a citation would begin or end.

7676.name: Places just before a name, label or identifier is given, mostly in code and technical text. It fires on words like "name", "title", "id", "class", "called", "Identifier:" and "username". It also fires on syntax that introduces a named value, such as function-call openings, string concatenations in paths, URL and DOI segments, and phone-number endings before an email address.

7700.name: The token "ion" as a standalone word or word piece in physics/chemistry terms (ion, ions, ionic, ionization, ionosphere, deionized), plus related charged-particle vocabulary (electrolyte, plasma, charged particle, proton, salt). Weaker matches come from unrelated words that merely contain "ion" or similar pieces, such as Deion, Hyperion and SERMION.

Mainly the token "ion"/"Ion" in any setting: chemistry and physics (ions, ionized, lithium ion, Ionosphere) as well as unrelated words containing it (Ionian Sea, Saturn Ion, Psion, Hyperion). Activation is weaker on related charged-particle or chemistry vocabulary (salts, electrolytes, particles, plasma, rays, radical, charged) and on look-alike fragments such as "lion", "aura" and "desal(ination)".

7785.name: Focusing, limiting and hedging adverbs and discourse modifiers (only, even, just, not, mainly, solely, often, almost, at least) that come right after a verb, noun or clause and come before the phrase they modify. The strongest cases are "only" and "not" restricting a following prepositional phrase or complement (e.g. "valid only if", "applied only to"). Parenthetical commas and hedge phrases ("kind of", "more or less", "I think") also activate weakly.

7858.name: A weak, diffuse feature that is strongest in source code, especially statements that load, read, parse or convert data: variable assignments like `data = np.genfromtxt(...)`, `Image.FromStream`, `FromStr`, Deserialize and loop bodies. In prose it fires faintly on words about handling data or structures (parsing dates, loaders reading XML, temperature data reconstructed). Elsewhere activations are scattered and low.

7898.name: Street address components, especially street-type suffixes (Road, Drive, Dr., Way, Street, Lane) and the house numbers or commas that follow the street name in postal addresses. Weaker activation appears on other structured metadata such as dates, phone numbers, emails, and separators in copyright or footer lines.

790.name: Phrases that introduce the contrasting or alternative counterpart in a comparison, e.g. after 'but', 'however', 'on the other hand', 'while', 'instead', 'in contrast to' or 'else'. The activation spans the second side of the opposition (symmetric vs asymmetric, junior vs senior, metal vs asphalt, responders vs non-responders, autoflowers vs photoperiods), including code branches like 'else' or 'rest'.

Weak, diffuse activation, mostly in technical, coding or explanatory text. It fires on phrases that set up a contrasting or alternative case against something stated just before. Typical triggers are words like "otherwise", "instead", "but here" and "usually". Examples include "with let, the value can be changed" after a const case, a modified condition after the original, "the second line has 4 spaces" after the first line, and "became strong" after "weak". Activation is strongest on the key contrasting content words (can, lighter, update, immutable, address).

7966.name: Section headings at the start of a document's body, mostly the first numbered heading ("1. Introduction", "I. INTRODUCTION", \section{Introduction}). The heading word and its numeral activate most strongly. Weaker activations fall on other numbered list or section starts and on page-header words such as "How", "Post" and "updated".

797.name: Words tied to programming, software code and computing. It fires most strongly on "code", "programming", "coding" and code-block markers or language tags (```golang, ```swift, "Code Implementation"). Weaker activation falls on source-code keywords and package names (package, namespace, System.Text, .github), on software/tech terms, and on generic technical or work-related nouns.

7988.name: Generic plural nouns (mostly groups of people like students, people, researchers, fans) used as the subject or agent of a clause, often right after a conjunction, comma, or sentence start, referring to a class of actors rather than specific individuals.

8123.name: Numbers inside in-text citations and cross-references, mostly the closing digit of a bracketed reference number ([1], [7]), the year in an author-year citation (Pavlov, 1927), or a figure/table number (Fig. 3). These usually come just before the closing bracket or parenthesis. Weaker activation falls on other trailing digits, such as phone numbers, zip codes and page numbers.

8140.name: Numbers or variables serving as the second operand right after an arithmetic or comparison operator (−, +, ×, ÷, /, ±, >, 'to'), mostly in math, code, or numeric comparisons. Activation is strongest after a minus sign in subtraction expressions.

8207.name: A weak, diffuse feature for chemistry and lab-science language. It fires most strongly in chemistry research abstracts: phrases like "is reported.", reagents, nucleophilic, carbocations, kJ mol units, chemical reactions, and chemistry laboratories. It also fires faintly on a scattering of other technical or scientific tokens, such as units, citations and terms from scientific prose.
The word "chemistry" (and, more weakly, nearby chemistry-related terms like chemical, elements, metal, spill). Other activations are faint and scattered.

8310.name: A weak, diffuse pattern centered on short symbolic tokens in structured or technical text. Most often these are single-letter variables, indices, subscripts, exponents or numbers inside LaTeX formulas, equations and code arguments (e.g. e^{-t}, n m, uf.join(5, 6)). It also fires on formatting fragments such as table tags and on highly predictable completions in boilerplate text (New Zealand, skip to navigation).

8313.name: Assignment/definition operators that follow a newly named identifier, mostly the " =" in code variable assignments (e.g. `x = ...`, `let y = ...`). Weaker activation falls on analogous separators that link a name to its value, type or definition: colons in type annotations or "key: value" fields, "->" return arrows, and "is"/"be a" in math definitions.

8342.name: Numeric tokens inside numbers (years, prices, measurements, codes, counts), especially multi-digit chunks containing or ending in the digit 3 (e.g. 33, 133, 933, 193, 203, or a final '3' in years like 2013). The strongest activations are on tokens with repeated 3s. A few non-numeric subword fragments, such as parts of Japanese names, also activate weakly.

8352.name: Weak and diffuse activations, peaking on the idea of conditionality: things that vary with or depend on circumstances. Typical triggers are “conditional logic” with :if, “depend on”, “condition-dependent”, “tailored to”, “different”/“various”/“split strategies”, and content that displays differently on desktop vs. mobile or at specific times. The many low-level activations on scattered function words, code and math tokens appear to be noise.

8365.name: A diffuse, weakly activating feature with no clear semantic focus. It fires sporadically on assorted tokens in ordinary prose (news, informational, and narrative text), mostly mid-sentence content words and function words, plus sentence- or paragraph-ending punctuation and line breaks. Activation is slightly stronger in short headline-like or descriptive passages, such as a snake breaking into a shop or a question about table manners.

8368.name: Tokens tied to sickness and medical symptoms, especially cold/flu-like illness: coughing (strongest), fever, high temperature, paracetamol, nasal drainage, infection, illness, vaccines and viral antigens, plus words like "cold" and "health". Weak activations on unrelated subword fragments look like noise.

839.name: Decimal points in numbers, firing most strongly on the period right after a leading zero ("0." before a fractional value such as 0.50, 0.375). Weaker activations appear on decimal points after other digits, the "0" itself, and assorted punctuation or separators (colons in times, stray commas or periods, sentence-ending breaks).

842.name: Tokens in the trailing elaboration at the end of a sentence, mostly infinitive purpose clauses ("to help you manage…"), relative clauses ("that could affect…") and prepositional phrases ("for the next generation of…") that extend a statement toward its final noun. Activation usually rises as the phrase approaches the closing period, and the very last word is often not marked.

A diffuse, weak feature on the trailing complement of a clause: the prepositional, infinitival or participial phrase that finishes a predicate (e.g. 'to improve the security', 'for subsequent steps', 'to successfully execute the code'). It fires on the function words and content words inside the phrase, and activation often rises toward the phrase's end, just before punctuation. This is common in technical and instructional text, which is often garbled or machine-generated.

8422.name: Capitalized word-start tokens within concatenated or CamelCase identifiers, chiefly code method and function names (Parse, Union, Find, Print, Message), plus Twitter handles, usernames, URLs and library names. Activation is strongest on the first capitalized piece of a code identifier. Weak, scattered activations also appear on title-cased words in ordinary prose.

8453.name: Language that reports study results and quantitative findings, especially sample counts and proportions (e.g., "Results:", "Out of 2757", "Of 2,460 … 38 patients", "25%", "Number of observations", "Fifty-two percent"). Activation peaks at the openings of results sections and on the numbers and phrases that set up counts and subsets.

85.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that activates across long runs of ordinary content tokens in factual prose rather than on any specific word. It is strongest in news-style reporting, such as statements of who announced, found or did something, attributions like 'a professor of… at… College', and statistics like '98 live births'. It fires weakly and sporadically on nouns and function words in general expository text, and barely at all in code or metadata.

A diffuse, weakly firing feature with no single clear trigger. It mostly lands on content words (usually nouns, sometimes verbs) that complete a phrase or clause, such as objects, complements and list items before a comma or period. The strongest activations come from descriptive or enumerative passages like item lists, quantities and title or summary headings.

8530.name: Tokens that open or mark a source attribution right after a claim: citation openers such as " (", " [", ".[", \cite and reference numbers, phrases like "according to", "discussed/consulted in" and "Figure", link syntax "](", and the closing punctuation of a quote before its speaker (",\"", ".\"", " –").

855.name: Sentence-ending boundaries: the period fused with following newline(s) (".⏎", ".⏎⏎") marking the end of a sentence/paragraph before a new section, list item, or paragraph; also other post-sentence break tokens like extra spaces, an opening parenthesis, or a dash after a sentence ends.

8607.name: Tokens (spaces, opening parentheses, punctuation, operators, newlines, short words) that immediately precede a number such as a year, measurement, count, price, or code. The feature seems to anticipate that a numeric token comes next.

8626.name: Words that mark intensity or how extreme or severe something is, mostly adjectives and adverbs such as severe, extreme, extremely, harsh, serious, intense, worse and worst, along with nouns like severity. It fires most strongly on "severe"/"severity" and "extreme", typically right before the noun or adjective they intensify.

8801.name: Completion tokens of proper nouns, mostly place names (cities, states, countries) as well as person, company and acronym names. Usually the final subword of a multi-token name (e.g. "ira" in Thyatira, "ell" in St Austell) or the second word of a multi-word name ("City", "York"). Activation is weak overall and strongest on locations.

8846.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on head nouns or word-piece continuations that complete multi-token technical terms, compound nouns and proper names, such as instrument and method names, institutions, software and surnames. It is strongest in scientific and technical text, e.g. the second or third part of terms like "Spin Rotation", "Box Score", "X-ray laser" and "Berkeley Mapper".

Weak, diffuse feature that fires on tokens completing a predictable word or fixed phrase: subword continuations of names and technical terms (S-ayers, Ros-etta, Borgh-ese, Bay-esian, Mucolipid-osis, Changes-et, Gnu-PG) and the second element of set compounds or named entities (pattern recognition, reverse engineered, patent prosecution, Press Standards, Proto Labs, AP poll).

8860.name: Separators and items inside enumerations and lists. The strongest activations are on the commas, semicolons and 'or'/'and' between items in a series (colors, elements, metals, keywords). It also fires on numbered list markers and bullets, and on sentence or paragraph breaks that lead into the next item.

8909.name: Items that sit inside an enumeration or sequence: the nouns, numbers, arguments or names that come after the first entry in a comma/slash/plus-separated list. Activation is highest on middle or later items such as "Weight", "Family", "stores", "readings" and "2MP", and on the separators or line breaks next to them. The same applies to repeated code arguments and number series.

8938.name: Mostly diffuse, low-level activations. The strongest and most consistent responses are to text layout and formatting terms, especially alignment and justification: align, justify/justified, aligned, alignment, orientation, left/center, and CSS flex/justify-content. Weaker hits fall on attribute or parameter names in code and markup, such as attachment, activation, orient, textStyle, Trim and sort.

8941.name: Phrases that define a target audience or the conditions under which a recommendation applies: who something is for or suits ("for those who…", "for someone who…", "freelancers looking to…", "families with…") and conditional clauses about a reader's preferences, needs or situation ("if you want to…", "if X isn't your thing", "your specific goals and needs"). Activation is generally weak and diffuse.

Conditional or target-audience qualifiers that state when, for whom, or under what circumstances something applies: phrases like "if you want/need…", "when you only have…", "for customers who need…", "in systems where…", and "for projects with…". These typically appear in recommendation or explanatory text, often in technical or assistant-style writing.

8986.name: Fires most strongly across spans of biblical or scriptural verse and archaic religious prose, such as quoted passages from Daniel, Luke, Psalms and Corinthians (e.g. 'thy', 'the flesh', 'Rahab and Babylon'), building up through the quoted phrase. There are weak, scattered activations on ordinary content words (verbs, nouns, adjectives) in other texts.

9012.name: Fires on the token right before a year number, most often the space, slash, dot, hyphen or opening parenthesis that separates the year from the month or day in dates (e.g. "May 2016", "9/23/2015", "08.03.2022", "(2015)"). It also fires on year-prefix tokens like "201", "202" and "200", including inside identifiers and URLs. The feature predicts that a four-digit year comes next.

9042.name: Tokens tied to Scandinavian/Nordic and broader Germanic (German, Dutch) origin, most strongly explicit Nordic references such as 'Scandinavian', the Norwegian domain '.no', Stockholm and Sweden. Weaker activations fall on pieces of surnames and words with that origin, e.g. Steensland, Anfinsen, Heisenberg, Vermeer, Arvid and Yuletide, plus German-language text.

9070.name: Enumeration labels in an ordered sequence: numbers, letters, roman numerals or superscripts marking a later item (typically the 3rd onward) in a numbered list, section/appendix/task/chapter heading, affiliation marker or parenthesized item, i.e. the continuation of a counting series.

9075.name: Marks the recipient or addressee of an action, request, or communication: the person or entity being asked, told, contacted, helped, or sent something (e.g. 'ask your husband', 'told his father', 'contact us', 'asked me', 'mentioned this to Owen', 'sent ... to him'). Strongest on nouns and pronouns that follow verbs like ask, tell, contact, or discuss with. Weaker activations fall on destination nouns that receive something (website, Tribunal, network) and on requested things (help, advice, attention).

9096.name: Fires weakly and diffusely on fragmented, disjointed or garbled web text: SEO keyword-stuffed spam, scraped boilerplate, metadata, URLs, product codes and incoherent run-on phrases. It is strongest on spammy strings of unrelated keywords (e.g. 'research posters phd researchers music recommender systems', 'essay on environmental awareness wikipedia pollution tuesday').

9104.name: Tokens that start a new structural unit in code or documents: keywords and annotations opening a definition (especially test markers like #[test], [Test], def test_, Scenario/Given/When, plus main, pub, fn, decorators), and section headings, step/item numbers, and bibliography entry fields. The strongest activations are on test attributes.

914.name: The indefinite article "an" (including capitalized "An" at sentence start) used before a vowel-initial noun phrase. Other determiners like "a" or "the" and stray fragments activate only weakly.

9206.name: Weak, diffuse activations on parts of technical names and terms, mostly in computing and software contexts: tool, OS and language names (Azure CLI/PowerShell, SSH, Solaris, R, edgeR), code identifiers and modules (csv.writer, /bin, ENV, .bat), and the second or later subword of multi-token proper nouns or brand names (Star Trek, Cartoon, Bashner). The strongest firing is on software tools and shell or CLI names.

9235.name: Words describing violent or physical events, motion, destruction and natural disasters: crashes, explosions, floods, plummeting, firing, attacks, collapse, ruins, projectiles. It is strongest on dramatic falling or impact sequences (e.g. a plane plummeting onto a house, crash landings). It also fires weakly on surrounding action verbs, connectives and some unrelated nouns.

924.name: Weak, diffuse activation on tokens inside repetitive, list-like or unstructured text that isn't ordinary prose: number and symbol sequences, code and URL fragments, keyword-stuffed tags, garbled spaced-out letters, line breaks in lists or verse, and math notation. It is strongest on repeated or sequential patterns such as "b b b 1 2 3", strings of underscores and dots, and runs of numbers.

Fires across garbled, nonsensical or highly repetitive token sequences: random symbol/number strings, repeated characters or words, mixed-language gibberish, malformed code and list-like fragments. Activation rises the longer and more patternless or repetitive the noise becomes, and stays low in coherent prose.

9246.name: Fires across news/wire-report style prose rather than on one specific word, peaking at structural and attribution points. These include dateline markers like "(AP) -", sentence and paragraph breaks between news paragraphs, and source-attribution phrases ("official said", "researchers found", "added in a written statement", "the report warns"). It also fires on temporal framing such as "hours after a", "yesterday", "Sept." and "Earlier", and on named entities or corporate suffixes (Obama, Erdogan, Inc, AG). Activation is weak on non-news text.

9358.name: A diffuse, mostly weak feature that fires on scattered structural tokens, mainly in code, markup and other formatted text (HTML/XML tags, code syntax, delimiters, whitespace and line breaks). It is strongest on the opening HTML list-item and anchor tag tokens (such as <li class=""><a) inside a navigation list. Activations on ordinary prose tokens are low and show no clear pattern.

9359.name: Items in the middle of an enumerated or sequential list, typically after the first one or two. These are often successive numbers, letters, ordinals, months or coordinate components (y, z). Activation is strongest deep in predictable progressions like 1, 2, 3, 4 or A B C D…, and weaker for loose comma lists of related nouns such as countries, games or chemical classes.

9383.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single topic. It fires most often on tokens inside repeated or parallel constructions, where the text mirrors an earlier pattern. Examples include the second element of a pair or list ("Sasha uses him", "the other finish of", "and Kurds", "breast cancer"), a repeated phrase ("Quote from an episode"), or code lines that echo a previous assignment or declaration ("second =", "string d", "else if"). It also fires lightly on word-piece completions and on punctuation or formatting tokens.

9416.name: Code tokens that emit a message: output, error and warning functions or operators (print, puts, printf, println, die, warn, fatalError, qDebug <<) that come right before a quoted string literal. Weaker activations land on miscellaneous tokens before quoted or explanatory text in prose.

Tokens immediately preceding a quoted string or message content, especially output/print calls and constructors in code (new Error(', cout <<, print, println, document.write) and keys/attributes before string values ("title":, title=). It also fires weakly on prose words that introduce communicated content (said X,; let us know; email us with; include your name).

9441.name: Verbs of speech, reporting, and attribution (said, says, described, claims, believes, reported) that follow a subject and introduce the content of a statement or opinion. Following words like "that" or ":" and attribution punctuation also activate. Activation is strongest for "said" and "says" attributing quotes to named people in news-style text.

9531.name: Words and phrases that introduce what something is made of or contains, such as "consist(s/ing) of", "composed of", "made (up) of", "comprise" and "combination of". The verbs "consist" and "compose" activate most strongly. Weaker activations come from looser relational links like "based on", "in the form of", "ranging" and "refers to".

9568.name: A weak, diffuse feature with no single clear trigger. It fires on content tokens that complete a phrase. These are mostly head nouns of noun or prepositional phrases ("roadway", "corner", "plasmid", "University of California, Berkeley"), plus the prepositions and articles leading into them. It also fires on named entities and on citation parentheticals such as "(Seamans 1929)" and "(Acharaya, 2004)".

9571.name: Tokens in technical or mathematical contexts that name or give the value of a scaling parameter, such as an exponent, power, slope, degree or dimension (e.g. "slope of 0.50", "the exponent is", "ε^{-η}"). The strongest activations fall on these scaling and exponent terms and their numeric values. Weak activations appear diffusely on other numbers, variables and technical nouns in scientific text and code.

9590.name: A diffuse, low-level feature that fires weakly on scattered mid-sentence tokens, mostly function words, nouns and verbs, in technical, instructional or explanatory prose. It is strongest inside code and formula syntax, such as function calls, parentheses, '#(' and 'sqrt(points', where the next tokens follow predictably from structure.

A diffuse, low-intensity pattern with no clear semantic theme. The strongest common thread is tokens that complete a predictable collocation or word given the preceding context: the noun after a modifier (plain flour, cell phone, set an alarm, Pillsbury biscuits), the second half of a set phrase (Terms and Concepts, Asia-Pacific), the verb after a modal (must place, have to win and), or a word-final subword (mathematic-ian, Gigg-les). Isolated stronger hits occur on regex bracket syntax.

9608.name: A diffuse, low-intensity feature that fires on text describing what a process, system or function outputs, produces or yields. The strongest activations are on input→output descriptions, such as 'inputs and predicts its continuation', 'will give off visible radiation', and C++ cout print statements. Weaker activations follow the same theme: 'output of two signals', 'maps to ℝ', 'should return', 'include the result', 'generating new ranges' and 'submit completed articles'.

9623.name: A diffuse feature that fires mostly in structured or technical text on short, slot-filling tokens. These include newly introduced single-letter variable names in code and math (g, h, z, q, x, D), page numbers after dotted leaders in tables of contents, and the '>' newline after '<thead' in HTML tables. It also fires weakly on scattered function words in prose (as, between, via, the).

9645.name: Concepts of supply and delivery of resources or utilities to something, especially electrical power (voltage figures, power sockets and supplies, charging, cutting off power), plus related inputs such as water, steam feeds, nutrients, internet access and network services. Strongest on "power" and voltage terms.

9693.name: Tokens in formal document metadata and front-matter boilerplate, such as author bylines and affiliations, addresses, submission and acceptance dates, "Key words" and "Corresponding author" labels, DOIs and ID numbers, and case or bill numbers. Often the token is the line break that separates a header field from the following text, or the punctuation within these reference strings. A weaker, similar response appears for news datelines and name and score formatting.

9699.name: Structural boundary tokens that end a block or begin a new one. In code these are mostly the indentation whitespace and closing braces/brackets (}, };, }), #endif) that close nested scopes, firing most strongly on deep stacks of closing braces. Weaker activations land on similar markers in other text: closing HTML tags, paragraph breaks after a sentence, list or step numbers, and transition words like 'Also' and 'On the other hand'.

9774.name: Narrative plot or premise descriptions (story synopses, blurbs, recaps, story openings) setting up characters, settings and conflicts. Activation spreads across function words, sentence boundaries and clauses that introduce a protagonist and situation, and is strongest at loglines and blurbs (e.g. 'a serial killer who wants to…', 'never wants to work as a lawman again. He's…').

9800.name: Tokens that repeat an identifier or word that appeared just before, most strongly a variable reused on the right side of its own reassignment (e.g. k = k^2, j = j + 1, line = line.strip(), m_hp = m_hpMax). Weaker activations fall on other near-copies of recent tokens, such as repeated names, terms, numbers or registers.

9807.name: Weak, diffuse feature that fires on words about physical parts, surfaces and contact or attachment between things. Typical hits are body or object parts and surfaces (bone, arms, fingernail, buckle, cursor, shoes, pockets, surface). It also catches attaching or contact verbs and the prepositions after them (attached to the, connected to, cling to, bite into, docked to, fit seamlessly with). A similar 'X linked to / value of Y' relation in code or API text (page_token must be the value of next_page_token) also activates it.

A weak, diffuse pattern centered on physical contact and spatial placement. It fires mostly on concrete nouns for body parts, object parts or surfaces (foot, elbow, shoulder, skin, side, back, chamber, banister, floor). It also fires on the prepositional phrases that locate or attach something to them ("on the top of the", "to the stone floor", "attached to the appropriate devices", "into the side of"). The strongest activations come in descriptions of something being placed on, pressed against or fastened to a surface.

982.name: Tokens that repeat or continue a pattern just established in the context: duplicated words or phrases ("cries and cries", "unite, unite", "many, many", "oh, oh", "end goal after the end goal"), runs of the same symbol or character ("- - - -", dot leaders, "9999", "WOOOOO"), and parallel list or sequence items (page numbers 1 2 3, "45µl, 55µl", "H + H", "\cdot"). Activation is strongest on clear repeats of a preceding token.

Tokens inside repetitive or predictable sequences: repeated symbols, numbers, words, or code fragments (e.g. "// // //", "1 1 1", "bodybody", "20-20-", backtick runs). Activation grows as the repetition continues, and there is weaker activation on simple continuations like counting lists.

983.name: Function words and connective glue, such as prepositions (of, to, in, for, between), articles (the, a), conjunctions (and, or, that) and commas. They fire most where a word is about to be followed by a noun phrase or complement, as in "using the", "use the" and "discussion of". This is a broad syntactic signal for introducing an upcoming object or argument rather than anything tied to meaning.

A diffuse feature with no single trigger word. It fires mostly on function words inside running prose that link one phrase to the next, especially "of", "the", "and", "to", "in", "with" and "by". Activation peaks on "of" in phrases like "effects of", "idea of" and "construction of a". Some content words also light up, mainly verbs and modifiers that set up a following phrase ("reducing", "activate", "implement"). It fires weakly on the analogous connecting symbols in code, lists and markup, such as "->", "=", bullets and list numbering.

9895.name: A weak, diffuse feature that fires on structural boundary tokens, where one unit ends and the next begins. These include sentence- and clause-ending punctuation (commas, periods followed by newlines) and line breaks. Its strongest activations are on code statement delimiters and connectors (braces, semicolons, 'or die', '&&', '->__', '())') and on transitions from prose into code. It also fires on short header or label words in web and page layouts.

Tokens at the boundary just before reported speech or program output, typically the punctuation, speaker name or pronoun that comes right before a speech verb or quotation (e.g. '...daughters, Obama said', 'He said, “...”', 'Mr. Trump tweeted:'). In code, the same thing happens around print and output statements and the closing of their strings (") ;", ")//").

991.name: Words naming a role, office, or job title, especially leadership, management, or authority positions (director, manager, president, chair, CEO, mayor), often with a following "of"/"in". Weaker hits on management/administration words and on organizational or academic units.

Job titles, offices and roles held by people (president, director, VP of, head of, mayor, editor, CEO, adviser to), usually in appositive or descriptive phrases identifying someone's position. The strongest activations come on senior or leadership titles, often including the trailing "of"/"to".

9920.name: Citation and reference markers, mostly the opening bracket or parenthesis and number of an inline citation (e.g. "[2]", "(1)", "(Hartman et al. 1999)", especially author-year digits) placed after a factual claim. It also fires weakly on other source and attribution cues such as "according to", figure numbers and URLs.

9958.name: Definitional or characterizing statements about a topic, especially in an expository or medical register. Activation falls on the copula and the words that open the description, e.g. "X is a common problem that…", "the disease is distinguished by…", or a parenthetical gloss like "(a rare cancer)". It is often triggered right after the subject noun (a disease, condition, process or concept) when a description or classification of it is about to follow.

996.name: A diffuse, low-intensity signal spread over long runs of ordinary prose in polished, expository or narrative writing (journalism, essays, marketing, fiction) and not tied to any specific word. It is strongest on wordy descriptive or rhetorical clauses, such as "would make history as the world's first," "a restful night's sleep is the foundation of," or "It is seamless, whole and complete." It is weak on isolated words and on proper names, numbers and list-like text.

A diffuse, weak feature that fires across spans of fluent, formulaic prose, strongest on mid-clause continuation words in generic, cliché, LLM-style phrasing such as stock narrative, marketing, advice or explanatory sentences (e.g. 'demand has been steadily rising', 'don't be afraid to think creatively', 'make every interaction effortless'). It fires only sporadically and weakly on isolated tokens in garbled or code-like text.

999.name: Tokens right before a capitalized word, usually a proper noun, personal name, brand or acronym (e.g. 'to' before Okta, 'from' before Mary Cassatt, 'Dr.' before Brei). Also name fragments mid-name ('Shish|u Qu', 'Rus|son Gilman'), and breaks, colons or bullets that start a new capitalized line or item.

A weak, diffuse feature that fires mostly on function words, punctuation and line breaks immediately before an upcoming proper noun or named entity, such as a brand, product, organization, team, person or place (e.g. 'in' before a place name, ', a spokeswoman for' before an airline, '.⏎⏎' before a product title). It also fires on early or partial tokens inside such names. In effect it anticipates that a capitalized name is coming next.
